title: ORDINARY OR WHITE CONSOMMÉ
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L)
ingredients: 3 lbs. (1360 g) of shin of beef
0.75 lb. (340 g) of leeks and 1 stick of celery
1 medium-sized onion with a clove stuck in it

instructions.title: Preparation
content: Put the meat into a stock-pot of suitable dimensions, after having previously strung it together; add the poultry carcase, five quarts (4.73 L) of water, and one-half oz. (14 g) of grey salt.
Place the stock-pot on a moderate fire in such a manner that it may not boil too quickly, and remember to stir the meat from time to time.

Under the influence of the heat, the water gradually reaches the interior of the meat, where, after having dissolved the liquid portions, it duly combines with them. These liquid portions contain a large proportion of albumen, and as the temperature of the water rises this substance has a tendency to coagulate. It also increases in volume, and, by virtue of its lightness, escapes from the water and accumulates on the surface in the form of scum.

Carefully remove this scum as it forms, and occasionally add a little cold water before the boil is reached in order that, the latter being retarded, a complete expulsion of the scum may be effected. The clearness of the consommé largely depends upon the manner in which this skimming has been carried out.

Then the vegetable garnishing is added. The scum from these is removed as in the previous case, and the edge of the stock-pot should be carefully wiped to the level of the fluid, so as to free it from the deposit which has been formed there.
The stock-pot is then moved to a corner of the fire where it may continue cooking slowly for four or five hours.

At the end of this time it should be taken right away from the fire, and, after half a pint (237 mL) of cold water has been added to its contents, it should be left to rest a few minutes with a view to allowing the grease to accumulate on the surface of the liquid, whence it must be carefully removed before the consommé is strained.
This last operation is effected by means of a very fine strainer, placed on the top of a white tureen (clean and wide), which should then be placed in a draught to hasten the cooling of the consommé.
The tureen should not on any account be covered, and this more particularly in summer, when rapid cooling is a precautionary measure against fermentation.

notes.title: Remarks upon the Different Causes which Combine to Influence the Quality of a Consommé
content: It will be seen that I have not made any mention in the above formula of the meat and the vegetables which have helped to make the consommé, my reason being that it is preferable to remove them from the stock-pot only after the broth has been strained, so as not to run the risk of disturbing the latter.

The quality of the meat goes a long way towards settling the quality of the consommé. In order that the latter be perfect, it is essential that the meat used should be that of comparatively old animals whose flesh is well set and rich in flavour. This is a sine quâ non, and the lack of meat coming from old animals in England accounts for the difficulty attaching to the making of a good consommé and savoury sauces in this country. Cattle in England are killed at an age varying from three to four years at the most; the meat thus obtained has no equal for the purpose of roasts and grills, and anything approaching it is rarely met with on the Continent. But when this same meat is used for boiling or braising, it does not contain enough juice or flavour to yield a satisfactory result.

This shortcoming is furthermore aggravated by a fault that many commit who are employed in the making of consommés and stock. The fault in question consists in cooking the bones simultaneously with the meat. Now to extract that gelatinous element from bone which produces the mellowness characteristic of all good consommés, it is necessary that the gelatigenous bodies should be cooked for twelve hours at least, and even after that time has elapsed they are still not entirely spent. On the Continent the quality of the meat easily compensates for this technical error, but such is certainly not the case in England, where five hours’ stewing only results in a flat and insipid consommé.

I therefore believe that, in the case of either consommé or stock, the formulæ of which I shall give later, it would be advisable for the bones to stew at least twelve hours, and this only after they have been well broken up, while the quantity of water used should be so calculated as to suffice exactly for the immersion of the meat that must follow. The contents of this first stock-pot should include half of the vegetables mentioned, and the consommé thus obtained, after having been strained and cooled, will take the place of the water in the recipe, in accordance with the directions I have given above.

notes.title: The Uses of White Consommé
content: White consommé is used in the preparation of clarified consommés, in which case it undergoes a process of clarifying, the directions for which will be given later. It also serves as the liquor for thick soups, poached fowls, &c. It must be limpid, as colourless as possible, and very slightly salted, for, whatever the use may be for which it is intended, it has to undergo a process of concentration.

section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: THE PREPARATION OF CLARIFIED CONSOMMÉ FOR CLEAR SOUPS
yield: Four quarts (3.79 L)
ingredients: 1.5 lbs. (680 g) of very lean beef
instructions: First, mince the beef and pound it in a mortar with the fowl’s carcase and the white of egg, adding a little cold white consommé.
Put the whole into a tall, narrow, and thick-bottomed stewpan; then gradually add the cold, white broth, from which all grease has been removed, that the whole may be well mixed. (Recipe 1)
Then the stewpan may be put on the fire, and its contents thoroughly stirred, for fear of their burning at the bottom.
When boiling-point is reached, move the stewpan to a corner of the fire, so that the soup may only simmer, for anything approaching the boil would disturb the contents.
A good hour should be enough to properly finish the consommé, and any longer time on the fire would be rather prejudicial than the reverse, as it would probably impair the flavour of the preparation.
Now carefully remove what little grease may have collected on the surface of the consommé, and strain the latter through muslin into another clean stewpan.
It is now ready for the addition of the garnishes that are to form part of it.

notes.title: Remarks upon Clarifications
content: For clarified consommés, even more than for the ordinary kind, it is eminently advisable that the meat should be that of old animals. Indeed, it is safe to say that one lb. of meat coming from an animal of eight years will yield much better consommé than two lbs. would, coming from a fattened animal of about three or four years. The consommé will be stronger, mellower, and certainly more tasty, as the flesh of young animals has absolutely no richness of flavour.

It will be seen that I do not refer to any vegetable for the clarification. If the white consommé has been well carried out, it should be able to dispense with all supplementary flavouring, and, the customary error of cooks being rather to overdo the quantity of vegetables—even to the extent of disguising the natural aroma of the consommé—I preferred to entirely abandon the idea of vegetable garnishes in clarifications, and thus avoid a common stumbling-block.

section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: CHICKEN CONSOMMÉ
introduction: White chicken consommé is prepared in exactly the same way as ordinary white consommé. The colour of chicken consommé should be lighter than that of the ordinary kind—namely, a light, amber yellow, limpid and warm.
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L)
ingredients: 1.5 lbs. (680 g) of shin of beef
1 old hen or a cock, slightly coloured on the spit or in the oven
0.75 lb. (340 g) of leeks and 1 stick of celery
1 medium-sized onion with a clove stuck in it

instructions.title: Preparation
content: Put the meat into a stock-pot of suitable dimensions, after having previously strung it together; add the hen/cock, poultry carcases, five quarts (4.73 L) of water, and one-half oz. (14 g) of grey salt.
Place the stock-pot on a moderate fire in such a manner that it may not boil too quickly, and remember to stir the meat from time to time.
Carefully remove scum as it forms, occasionally adding a little cold water to retard the boil and ensure complete expulsion of the scum.
Add the vegetable garnishing, remove any further scum, and wipe the edge of the stock-pot.
Move the stock-pot to a corner of the fire and let it cook slowly for four or five hours.
Remove from fire, add half a pint (237 mL) of cold water, and let it rest to allow grease to accumulate on the surface. Carefully remove the grease.
Strain the consommé through a very fine strainer into a tureen and place in a draught to cool rapidly. Do not cover the tureen.

instructions.title: Clarification
content: For clarification, increase the quantity of roast fowl-carcases used, provided they are not too fat. The process is the same as in the clarification of ordinary consommés. (Recipe 2)

section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: FISH CONSOMMÉ
introduction: These consommés are rarely used, for Lenten soups with a fish basis are generally thick soups, for the preparation of which the fish fumet should avail. (Recipe 11) Whenever there is no definite reason for the use of an absolutely Lenten consommé, it would be advisable to resort to one of the ordinary kind, and to finish off the same by means of a good fish essence extracted from the bones of a sole or whiting. An excellent consommé is thus obtained, more palatable and less flat than the plain fish consommé. If, however, one were obliged to make a plain fish consommé, the following procedure should be adopted.
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L)
ingredients: 4.5 quarts (4.26 L) of ordinary fish fumet having a decided taste
0.5 lb. (227 g) of good fresh caviare, or pressed caviare

instructions.title: Clarification of Fish Consommé
content: Pound the caviare and mix the resulting pulp with the cold fish fumet. (Recipe 11)
Put the whole into a saucepan, place it on the open fire, and stir with a spatula until the contents reach the boil.
Then move the saucepan to a corner of the fire, and let the consommé simmer gently for twenty minutes, after which strain it through muslin with great caution.
Keep it well covered and in the warmth, so as to prevent the formation of a gelatinous film on the surface.

notes: Fish consommés are greatly improved by the addition of such aromatics as saffron or curry, both of which considerably add to their quality.
section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: GAME CONSOMMÉ
introduction: The necks, breasts, and shoulders of venison and of hare, old wild rabbits, old pheasants, and old partridges may be used in the production of game consommés. An ordinary consommé may likewise be made, in which half the beef can be replaced by veal, and to which may be added, while clarifying, a succulent game essence. This last method is even preferable when dealing with feathered game, but in either case it is essential that the meat used should be half-roasted beforehand, in order to strengthen the fumet. The formula that I give below must therefore only be looked upon as a model, necessarily alterable according to the resources at one’s disposal, the circumstances, and the end in view.
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L) of Plain Game Consommé
ingredients: 3 lbs. (1360 g) of neck, shoulder, or breast of venison
4 oz. (113 g) of sliced carrots, browned in butter
0.5 lb. (227 g) of mushrooms, likewise browned in butter
1 medium-sized leek and 2 sticks of celery
1 bunch of herbs with extra thyme and bay leaves
1 onion, oven-browned, with 2 cloves stuck into it
instructions: Proceed in exactly the same way as for ordinary consommés (Recipe 1), taking care only to half-roast the meat, as I pointed out above, before putting it in the stewpan.
Add peppercorns ten minutes previous to straining the consommé.
Time allowed for cooking is three hours.

notes.title: The Clarification of Game Consommés
content: The constituents of the clarification of game consommés vary according to the kind of consommé desired. If it is to have a partridge flavour, one partridge should be allowed for each quart of the consommé, whereas if its flavour is to be that of the pheasant, half an old pheasant will be required per each quart of the liquid. Lastly, in the case of plain game consommés, one lb. (454 g) of lean venison, hare, or wild rabbit should be allowed for each quart of the required consommé.

Whatever be the kind of game used, the latter must be thoroughly boned and the meat well pounded, together with the white of an egg per four quarts (3.79 L) of consommé. About two oz. (57 g) per quart of dried mushrooms should now be added if they can be procured, while the bones and the remains or carcases of game should be browned in the oven and completely drained of all grease.

The whole can now be mixed with the cold game consommé. The clarification is then put over an open fire (stirring incessantly the while), and as soon as the boil is reached the saucepan must be moved to a corner of the fire, where its contents may gently boil for three-quarters of an hour.
The fat should then be removed, and the consommé strained through muslin, after which cover up until wanted.

section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: SPECIAL CONSOMMÉS FOR SUPPERS
introduction: The consommés whose formulæ I have just given are intended more particularly for dinners. They are always finished off by some kind of garnish, which, besides lending them an additional touch of flavour, gives them their special and definite character when they are served up in the diner’s plate. (Recipe 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

But the case is otherwise with the consommés served for suppers. These, being only served in cups, either hot or cold, do not allow of any garnishing, since they are to be drunk at table. They must therefore be perfect in themselves, delicate, and quite clear.

These special consommés are made in a similar manner to the others, though it is needful to slightly increase the quantity of meat used for the clarification, and to add to that clarification the particular flavour mentioned on the menu—to wit, a few stalks of celery, if the consommé is a celery one; a small quantity of curry, if the consommé is given as “à l’Indienne”; or a few old roast partridges if it is to be termed “Consommé au fumet de perdreau”; and so on.

The means by which one may vary the aroma of consommés are legion, but it is highly important, what aroma soever be used, that the latter be not too pronounced. It ought only to lend a distinctive and, at the same time, subtle finish to the consommé, which, besides sharpening the latter, should increase its succulence.

When the consommé is served cold it ought to have the qualities of an extremely light and easily-melting jelly, barely firm; but when it is too liquid, it rarely gives that sensation of perfection and succulence to the palate of the consumer which the latter expects. When too firm and too gelatinous it is positively disagreeable; therefore, if it is to be relished, it should be just right in respect of consistency.

title: BROWN STOCK OR “ESTOUFFADE”
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L)
ingredients: 4 lbs. (1814 g) of shin of beef (flesh and bone)
4 lbs. (1814 g) of shin of veal (flesh and bone)
0.5 lb. (227 g) of lean, raw ham
0.5 lb. (227 g) of fresh pork rind, rinsed in tepid water
0.75 lb. (340 g) of minced carrots, browned in butter
0.75 lb. (340 g) of minced onions, browned in butter
1 faggot, containing a little parsley, a stick of celery, a small sprig of thyme, and a bay leaf

instructions.title: Preparation
content: Bone and string the meat, and keep it in readiness for the morrow.
Break the bones as finely as possible, and, after having besprinkled them with a little stock-fat, brown them in an oven; also stir them repeatedly.

When they are slightly browned, put them in a conveniently large saucepan with the carrots, the onions, and the faggot. Add five quarts (4.73 L) of cold water, and put the saucepan on an open fire to boil.

As soon as the boil is reached skim carefully; wipe the edge of the saucepan; put the lid half on, and allow the stock to cook gently for twelve hours; then roughly remove the fat; pass the liquid through a sieve, and let it cool.
This being done, put the meat in a saucepan just large enough to hold it. Brown it a little in some stock-fat, and clear it entirely of the latter.

Add half a pint (237 mL) of the prepared stock, cover the saucepan, and let the meat simmer on the side of the fire until the stock is almost entirely reduced. Meanwhile the meat should have been repeatedly turned, that it may be equally affected throughout.

Now pour the remainder of the stock, prepared from bones, into the saucepan, bring the whole to the boil, and then move the saucepan to a corner of the fire for the boiling to continue very slowly and regularly with the lid off.
As soon as the meat is well cooked the fat should be removed from the stock, and the latter should be strained or rubbed through a sieve, after which it should be put aside to be used when required.

notes.title: Remarks Relative to the Making of Brown Stock
content: Instead of stringing the meat after having boned it, if time presses, it may be cut into large cubes before browning. In this case one hour and a half would suffice to cook it and to extract all its juice.

Whether brown or white, stock should never be salted, because it is never served in its original state. It is either reduced in order to make glazes or sauces—in which case the concentration answers the purpose of seasoning—or else it is used to cook meat which must be salted before being cooked, and which, therefore, imparts the necessary salt to its surrounding liquor.
Brown stock ought to be the colour of fine burnt amber, and it must be transparent. It is used in making meat-glazes after reduction, also to moisten meat for braising and to prepare brown sauces.

section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: BROWN GAME STOCK
introduction: Ordinary game consommé and brown game stock are one and the same thing. The distinction lies in the ultimate use of this preparation; it is clarified if it be intended for a clear soup, and it is used in its original state if it is to be used for a thick game soup, for a sauce, or for reducing. (Recipe 5)
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L) of Plain Game Consommé
ingredients: 3 lbs. (1360 g) of neck, shoulder, or breast of venison
4 oz. (113 g) of sliced carrots, browned in butter
0.5 lb. (227 g) of mushrooms, likewise browned in butter
1 medium-sized leek and 2 sticks of celery
1 bunch of herbs with extra thyme and bay leaves
1 onion, oven-browned, with 2 cloves stuck into it
instructions: Proceed in exactly the same way as for ordinary consommés (Recipe 1), taking care only to half-roast the meat before putting it in the stewpan.
Add peppercorns ten minutes previous to straining the consommé.
Time allowed for cooking is three hours.
section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: BROWN VEAL STOCK
introduction: This stock is mostly used as the liquor for poultry and poëled game, while it may also serve in the preparation of thickened veal stock. Being quite neutral in taste, it lends itself to all purposes, and readily takes up the aroma of the meat with which it may happen to be combined. It is admirably suited to the poaching of quails, and nothing can supplant it in this particular.
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L)
ingredients: 8 lbs. (3629 g) of shin of veal, or lean and fresh veal trimmings
1 or 2 fowls’ carcases, raw if they are handy
6 oz. (170 g) of onions stuck with a clove
4 oz. (113 g) of leeks strung with a stick of celery
1 faggot, including 1 oz. (28 g) of parsley, 1 bay leaf, and a small sprig of thyme
instructions: The time allowed for cooking is a little shorter, and this operation may be completed within eight hours.
section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: WHITE VEAL STOCK, AND POULTRY STOCK
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L)
ingredients: 8 lbs. (3629 g) of shin of veal, or lean and fresh veal trimmings
1 or 2 fowls’ carcases, raw if they are handy
6 oz. (170 g) of onions stuck with a clove
4 oz. (113 g) of leeks strung with a stick of celery
1 faggot, including 1 oz. (28 g) of parsley, 1 bay leaf, and a small sprig of thyme

instructions.title: Preparation
content: Bone the shins, string the meat, break up the bones as small as possible, and put them in a stewpan with the water.
Place on an open fire, allow to boil, skim carefully, and then move to a side of the fire to cook very gently for five hours.

At the end of this time put the stock into another stewpan, add the meat and the vegetables, add water, if necessary, to keep the quantity of liquid at five quarts (4.73 L), let it boil, and allow it to cook slowly for another three hours.
After which remove all grease from the stock, pass the latter through a fine strainer or a colander, and put it aside until wanted.

notes.title: Remarks upon White Stock
content: One should contrive to make this stock as gelatinous as possible. It is therefore an indispensable measure that the bones be well broken up and cooked for at least eight hours.
Veal never yields such clear stock as beef; nevertheless, the consommé obtained from veal should not be turbid. It must, on the contrary, be kept as clear and as white as possible.

notes.title: Poultry Stock
content: Poultry Stock is made by adding two old fowls to the above veal stock, and these should be put into the liquor with the meat.

section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: WHITE FISH STOCK
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L)
ingredients: 4 lbs. (1814 g) of trimmings and bones of sole or whiting
0.5 lb. (227 g) of sliced, blanched onions
2 oz. (57 g) of parsley, root or stalks

instructions.title: Preparation
content: Butter the bottom of a thick, tall stewpan, put in the blanched onions and the parsley-stalks, and upon these aromatics lay the fish remains.
Add the juice of a lemon, cover the stewpan, put it on the fire, and allow the fish to exude its essence, jerking the pan at intervals.
Moisten, in the first place, with the white wine; then, with the lid off, reduce the liquid to about half.
Now add four quarts (3.79 L) of cold water, bring to the boil, skim, and then leave to cook for twenty minutes, only, on a moderate fire.
The time allowed is ample for the purpose of extracting the aromatic and gelatinous properties contained in the bones, and a more protracted stewing would only impair the savour of the stock.

notes.title: Remarks upon White Fish Stock
content: The formula which I give above diverges considerably from that commonly used, for, as a rule, fish stock is diluted far too much, and is stewed for much too long a time. I have observed that fish stock may be greatly improved by rapid cooking, and it was this consideration that led me to dilute it scantily, so as to avoid prolonged reduction.

It is likewise necessary to remember that in order to make perfect fish stock, only the sole or whiting should be used. In a case of emergency, however, i.e., if the supply of the latter were to run short, a quarter of their weight of brill bones might be added to them. But all other kinds of fish should be avoided in the preparation.

section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: FISH STOCK WITH RED WINE
introduction: This stock is comparatively rarely used, because, in practice, it is naturally obtained in the cooking of the fish itself, as, for instance, in the case of the “Matelotes.” Be this as it may, with the recent incursion of a custom which seems to demand, ever more and more, the serving of fish without bones, the following formula will be worthy of interest, as it is likely that its need will henceforth be felt with increasing urgency. Fish fumet with red wine may be prepared from all fresh-water fish, as well as from the remains of sole, whiting, chicken-turbot, and brill. It is generally better, however, to have recourse to the bones and remains of that fish which happens to be constituting the dish—that is to say, the bones and trimmings of sole in a stock for fillet of sole, the bones and trimmings of a chicken-turbot in a fumet for a chicken-turbot, and so on. The preparatory formula remains the same, whatever the kind of fish used may be.
yield: Four Quarts (3.79 L) of Fumet with Red Wine
ingredients: 4 lbs. (1814 g) of bones, heads, and trimmings of the fish to be served
0.75 lb. (340 g) of minced white onions
instructions: Put all the above-mentioned ingredients in a thick and tall stewpan, boil, skim carefully, and allow to cook twenty to thirty minutes on a moderate fire.
Then strain the stock through a colander into a tureen, to be used when required.

notes.title: Remarks upon Fish Stock with Red Wine
content: This stock stands reduction far better than white fish stock. Nevertheless, I urge the advisability of trying to obtain the required quantity without reduction.
In its preparation, one may use some mushroom parings, as in the case of white stock, if these are handy, and they will be found to lend an agreeable flavour to the fish fumet.

section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: VARIOUS ESSENCES
introduction: As their name implies, essences are stock which hold a large proportion of a substance’s aroma in a concentrated form. They are, in fact, ordinary stock, only less diluted, with the idea of intensifying the flavour of the treated ingredients; hence their utility is nil if the stock which they are intended to finish has been reasonably and judiciously treated. It is infinitely simpler to make savoury and succulent stock in the first place than to produce a mediocre stock, and finally complete it by a specially prepared essence. The result in the first instance is better, and there is economy of time and material.

The most one can do is to recommend, in certain circumstances, the use of essences extracted from particularly well-flavoured products, as, for instance, mushrooms, truffles, morels, and celery. But it would be well to remember that, nine times out of ten, it is preferable to add the product itself to the stock during the preparation of the same than to prepare essences.
For this reason I do not think it necessary to dilate upon the subject of essences, the need of which should not be felt in good cooking.
section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: VARIOUS GLAZES
introduction: The various glazes of meat, fowl, game, and fish are merely stock reduced to the point of viscosity. Their uses are legion. Occasionally they serve in decking dishes with a brilliant and unctuous coating which makes them sightly; at other times they may help to strengthen the consistence of a sauce or other culinary preparation, while again they may be used as sauces proper after they have been correctly creamed or buttered.

Glazes are distinguished from essences by the fact that the latter are only prepared with the object of extracting all the flavour of the product under treatment, whereas the former are, on the contrary, constituted by the whole base of the substance itself. They therefore have not only its savour, but also its succulence and mellowness, whereby they are superior to the essences, and cooking can but be improved by substituting them for the latter. Nevertheless, many chefs of the old school do not permit the use of glazes in culinary preparations, or, rather, they are of opinion that each cooking operation should produce them on its own account, and thus be sufficient unto itself. Certainly, the theory is correct when neither time nor cost is limited. But nowadays the establishments are scarce where these theories may be applied, and, indeed, if one does not make an abuse of glazes, and if they be prepared with care, their use gives excellent results, while they lend themselves admirably to the very complex demands of modern customs.
section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: MEAT GLAZE
introduction: Meat glaze is made by reducing brown stock in a large stewpan upon an open fire. As often as the stock is appreciably reduced, during ebullition, it may be transferred to smaller stewpans, taking care to strain it through muslin at each change of stewpan. The glaze may be considered sufficiently reduced when it evenly veneers a withdrawn spoon. The fire used for reducing should gradually wane as the concentration progresses, and the last phase must be effected slowly and on a moderate fire. (Recipe 7)When it is necessary to obtain a lighter and clearer glaze, the brown veal stock should be reduced instead of the “Estouffade.” (Recipe 9)
section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: POULTRY GLAZE
introduction: Reduce the poultry base and proceed in exactly the same way as for meat glaze. (Recipe 10, 15)
section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: GAME GLAZE
introduction: Use the game base, and proceed as for meat glaze. (Recipe 8, 15)
section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: FISH GLAZE
introduction: This glaze is used less often than the preceding ones. As it is only used to intensify the savour of sauces, it is sufficient for this purpose to prepare a white fish stock, which may be diluted with the stock already prepared, and which may be reduced according to the requirements. The name of fish fumet or fish essence is given to this preparation; its flavour is more delicate than that of fish glaze, which it replaces with advantage. (Recipe 11)
section_path: The Principal Kinds of Fonds de Cuisine (Foundation Sauces and Stocks)

title: BROWN ROUX
yield: about 1 lb (454 g)

introduction.title: The Science of Roux
content: It is very important that brown roux should not be cooked too rapidly. As a matter of fact, among the various constituent elements of flour, the starch alone acts as the cohering principle. This starch is contained in little cells, which tightly constrain it, but which are sufficiently porous to permit the percolation of liquid and fatty substances. Under the influence of moderate heat and the infiltered butter, the cells burst through the swelling of the starch, and the latter thereupon completely combines with the butter to form a mass capable of absorbing six times its own weight of liquid when cooked.
When the cooking takes place with a very high initial heat the starch gets burned within its shrivelled cells, and swelling is then possible only in those parts which have been least burned.

The cohering principle is thus destroyed, and double or treble the quantity of roux becomes necessary in order to obtain the required consistency. But this excess of roux in the sauce chokes it up without binding it, and prevents it from despumating or becoming clear. At the same time, the cellulose and the burnt starch lend a bitterness to the sauce of which no subsequent treatment can rid it.

From the above it follows that, starch being the only one from among the different constituents of flour which really effects the coherence of sauces, there would be considerable advantage in preparing roux either from a pure form of it, or from substances with kindred properties, such as fecula, arrow-root, &c. It is only habit that causes flour to be still used as the cohering element of roux, and, indeed, the hour is not so far distant when the advantages of the changes I propose will be better understood—changes which have been already recommended by Favre in his dictionary.

With a roux well made from the purest starch—in which case the volume of starch and butter would equal about half that of the flour and butter of the old method—and with strong and succulent brown stock, a Spanish sauce or Espagnole may be made in one hour. And this sauce will be clearer, more brilliant, and better than that of the old processes, which needed three days at least to despumate.

instructions: Mix the flour and butter in a very thick stewpan, and put it on the side of the fire or in a moderate oven.

Stir the mixture repeatedly so that the heat may be evenly distributed throughout the whole of its volume. The time allowed for the cooking of brown roux cannot be precisely determined, as it depends upon the degree of heat employed. The more intense the latter, the speedier will be the cooking, while the stirring will of necessity be more rapid.
Brown roux is known to be cooked when it has acquired a fine, light brown colour, and when it exudes a scent resembling that of the hazel-nut, characteristic of baked flour.

title: PALE ROUX
yield: about 1 lb (454 g)
instructions: Mix the flour and butter in a very thick stewpan, and put it on the side of the fire or in a moderate oven.
Stir the mixture repeatedly so that the heat may be evenly distributed throughout the whole of its volume.
Cooking must cease as soon as the colour of the roux begins to change, and before the appearance of any colouring whatsoever.
notes: The observations made relative to brown roux, concerning the cohering element, apply also to pale roux. (Recipe 19)

title: WHITE ROUX
yield: about 1 lb (454 g)
introduction: White roux differs from pale roux in that the cooking is still more slighted, and that it is prepared in a different manner.
instructions: Mix the flour and butter in a very thick stewpan and cook over low heat.

Stir constantly for a few minutes. The time of cooking is limited, as it is only needful, in this case, to do away with the disagreeable taste of raw flour which is typical of those sauces whose roux has not been sufficiently cooked.
Do not allow the roux to take on any color.

title: BROWN SAUCE OR ESPAGNOLE
yield: 4 quarts (3.8 L)
ingredients: 6 quarts (5.7 L) of brown stock or estouffade
2 lbs (907 g) of fresh tomatoes, roughly cut up, or an equivalent quantity of tomato purée
1 quart (946 ml) of brown stock, for replacement
instructions: Dissolve the brown roux in a tall, thick saucepan with six quarts of brown stock.
Put the saucepan on an open fire, and stir the sauce with a spatula or a whisk, and do not leave it until it begins to boil.

Remove the spatula, and put the saucepan on a corner of the fire, letting it lean slightly to one side with the help of a wedge, so that boiling may only take place at one point, and the inert principles thrown out by the sauce during despumation may accumulate high up in the saucepan, whence they can be easily removed as they collect.
During despumation, change saucepans two or three times, straining every time, and adding a quart of brown stock to replace what has evaporated.
When the sauce begins to get lighter, and about two hours before finally straining it, add the fresh tomatoes and the Mirepoix.
Reduce the sauce so as to measure four quarts when strained.
After straining, pour it into a wide tureen, and stir until quite cool lest a skin should form on its surface.

notes.title: Despumation Time
content: The time required for the despumation of an Espagnole varies according to the quality of the stock and roux. With a concentrated stock and starch roux, one hour will suffice, in which case the Mirepoix and the tomato are inserted from the first. (Recipe 19) But much more time is required if one is dealing with a roux whose base is flour. In the latter case six hours should be allowed, provided one have excellent stock and well-made roux. More often than not this work is done in two stages, thus: after having despumated the Espagnole for six or eight hours the first day, it is put on the fire the next day with half its volume of stock, and it is left to despumate a few hours more before it is finally strained.

notes.title: Keys to Success
content: 1. Only use strong, clear stock with a decided taste.
2. Be scrupulously careful of the roux, however it may be made. By following these two rules, a clear, brilliant, and consistent Espagnole will always be obtained in a fairly short time.

title: HALF GLAZE
introduction: This is the Espagnole sauce, having reached the limit of perfection by final despumation.
yield: approx. 1 quart (946 ml)
ingredients: 1 quart (946 ml) of first-class brown stock
instructions: Combine one quart of Espagnole and one quart of first-class brown stock.
Reduce until its volume is reduced to nine-tenths of a quart (approx 900 ml).
Strain into a bain-marie of convenient dimensions.
Finish, away from the fire, with the excellent sherry.
Cover the bain-marie, or slightly butter the top to avoid the formation of a skin.
notes: This sauce is the base of all the smaller brown sauces.

title: LENTEN ESPAGNOLE
introduction: Practical men are not agreed as to the need of Lenten Espagnole. The ordinary Espagnole being really a neutral sauce in flavour, it is quite simple to give it the necessary flavour by the addition of the required quantity of fish fumet. It is only, therefore, when one wishes to conform with the demands of a genuine Lent sauce that a fish Espagnole is needed. And, certainly in this case, nothing can take its place.
ingredients: 6 quarts (5.7 L) of fish stock or fumet
2 lbs (907 g) of fresh tomatoes, roughly cut up
1 lb (454 g) of Mirepoix, prepared with mushroom parings instead of bacon
instructions: The preparation of this Espagnole does not differ from that of the ordinary kind, except that the bacon is replaced by mushroom parings in the Mirepoix, and that the sauce must be despumated for only one hour. (Recipe 22)
notes: This sauce takes the place of the ordinary Espagnole, for Lenten preparations, in every case where the latter is generally used, in Gratins, in the Genevoise sauce, &c. (Recipe 22)

title: ORDINARY VELOUTÉ SAUCE
yield: 4 quarts (3.8 L)
ingredients: 5 quarts (4.7 L) of white veal stock (Recipe 10)
0.25 lb (113 g) of nice white mushroom parings (optional)
instructions: Dissolve the roux in the cold white veal stock and put the saucepan containing this mixture on an open fire.
Stir the sauce with a spatula or whisk, so as to avoid its burning at the bottom.
Add salt, nutmeg, pepper, and mushroom parings, if handy.
Bring to a boil and move to a corner of the fire to despumate slowly for one and a half hours, at the same time observing the precautions advised for ordinary Espagnole. (Recipe 22)
Strain through muslin into a smaller saucepan, add one pint of white stock, and despumate for another half hour.
Strain it again through a tammy or a sieve into a wide tureen, and stir with a spatula until it is quite cold.
notes: I am not partial to garnishing Velouté Sauce with carrots, an onion with a clove stuck into it, and a faggot, as many do. The stock should be sufficiently fragrant of itself, without requiring the addition of anything beyond the usual condiments. The only exception I should make would be for mushroom parings, even though it is preferable, when possible, to replace these by mushroom liquor. But this is always scarce in kitchens where it is used for other purposes; wherefore it is often imperative to have recourse to parings in its stead. The latter may not, however, be added to the stock itself, as they would blacken it; hence I advise their addition to the Velouté during its preparation.

title: VELOUTÉ DE VOLAILLE
introduction: This is identical with ordinary Velouté, except that instead of having white veal stock for its liquor, it is diluted with white poultry stock. The mode of procedure and the time allowed for cooking are the same. (Recipe 25)
yield: 4 quarts (3.8 L)
ingredients: 5 quarts (4.7 L) of white poultry stock
0.25 lb (113 g) of nice white mushroom parings (optional)
instructions: Dissolve the roux in the cold white poultry stock and put the saucepan containing this mixture on an open fire.
Stir the sauce with a spatula or whisk, so as to avoid its burning at the bottom.
Add salt, nutmeg, pepper, and mushroom parings, if handy.
Bring to a boil and move to a corner of the fire to despumate slowly for one and a half hours, at the same time observing the precautions advised for ordinary Espagnole. (Recipe 22)
Strain through muslin into a smaller saucepan, add one pint of white stock, and despumate for another half hour.
Strain it again through a tammy or a sieve into a wide tureen, and stir with a spatula until it is quite cold.

title: FISH VELOUTÉ
introduction: This Velouté is the base of various fish sauces.
yield: 4 quarts (3.8 L)
ingredients: 5 quarts (4.7 L) of very clear fish fumet (Recipe 11)
0.25 lb (113 g) of nice white mushroom parings (optional)
instructions: Dissolve the roux in the cold fish fumet and put the saucepan containing this mixture on an open fire.
Stir the sauce with a spatula or whisk, so as to avoid its burning at the bottom.
Add salt, nutmeg, pepper, and mushroom parings, if handy.
Bring to a boil and move to a corner of the fire to despumate slowly for twenty minutes.
Strain through muslin into a smaller saucepan, add one pint of fish fumet, and despumate for another half hour.
Strain it again through a tammy or a sieve into a wide tureen, and stir with a spatula until it is quite cold.

title: ALLEMANDE SAUCE OR THICKENED VELOUTÉ
introduction: Allemande Sauce is not, strictly speaking, a basic sauce. However, it is so often resorted to in the preparation of other sauces that it is given here after the Veloutés, from which it is derived. (Recipe 25)
yield: 1 quart (946 ml)
ingredients: 1 pint (473 ml) of cold white stock
1 quart (946 ml) of Velouté, well despumated (Recipe 25)
instructions: Put the egg yolks, cold stock, Velouté, lemon juice, and mushroom liquor in a thick-bottomed sauté-pan and mix them carefully.
Put the pan on an open fire, and stir the sauce with a metal spatula, lest it burn at the bottom.
When the sauce has been reduced to about one quart, add the fresh cream to it, and reduce further for a few minutes.
Pass it through a fine strainer into a tureen and stir until quite cold.
notes: Prepared thus, the Allemande Sauce is ready for the preparation of the smaller sauces. Butter must only be added at the very last moment, for if it were buttered any earlier it would most surely turn. The same injunction holds good with this sauce when it is to be served in its original state; it should then receive a small addition of cream, and be buttered so that it may attain its required delicacy; but this addition of butter and cream ought only to be made at the last moment, and away from the fire. When a sauce thickened with egg yolks has any fat substance added to it, it cannot be exposed to a higher temperature than 140°F (60°C) without risking decomposition.

title: BÉCHAMEL SAUCE
yield: 4 quarts (3.8 L)
ingredients: 0.5 lb (227 g) of lean veal, cut into small cubes
instructions: Pour the boiling milk on the roux, which should be almost cold, and whisk it well so as to avoid lumps. Let it boil, then cook on the side of the fire.

Meanwhile, fry the lean veal with butter in a saucepan, together with the minced onion. When the veal has stiffened without becoming coloured, add it to the Béchamel, together with salt and the other aromatics.
Let the sauce boil slowly for about one hour in all.
Pass it through a tammy into a tureen; butter the top, lest a crust should form.

notes.title: Lenten Variation
content: When Béchamel is intended for Lenten preparations, the veal must be omitted.

notes.title: Alternate Method
content: There is another way of making the sauce. After having boiled the milk, the seasoning and aromatics should be added; the saucepan is then covered and placed on a corner of the stove, so as to ensure a thorough infusion. The boiling milk must now be poured on to the roux which has been separately prepared, and the sauce should then cook for one quarter of an hour only.

title: TOMATO SAUCE
yield: 4 quarts (3.8 L)
ingredients: 5 oz (142 g) of salted breast of pork, rather fat
6 oz (170 g) of carrots, cut into cubes
6 oz (170 g) of onions, cut into cubes
10 lbs (4.5 kg) of raw tomatoes or 4 quarts (3.8 L) of same, mashed
instructions: Fry the pork with the butter in a tall, thick-bottomed saucepan. When the pork is nearly melted, add the carrots, onions, bay leaf and thyme.
Cook and stir the vegetables, then add the flour, which should be allowed to cook until it begins to brown.
Add the tomatoes and white stock, mix the whole well, and set to boil on an open fire.
Add the salt, sugar, pepper, and crushed garlic.
Cover the saucepan, and place in a moderate oven, where it may cook for one and one-half hours.
At the end of this time, pass the sauce through a sieve or tammy, and bring to a boil while stirring.
Finally, pour it into a tureen, and butter its surface to avoid the formation of a skin.

notes.title: Tomato Purée
content: A purée of tomatoes is also used in cookery; it is prepared in precisely the same fashion, except that the flour is omitted and only one pint of white stock is added.

title: HOLLANDAISE SAUCE
yield: 1 quart (946 ml)
instructions: Put the salt, mignonette pepper, vinegar, and 3 tablespoons of water in a small saucepan, and reduce by three-quarters on the fire.
Move the saucepan to a corner of the fire or into a bain-marie, and add 1 spoonful of fresh water and the egg yolks.
Work the whole with a whisk until the yolks thicken and have the consistence of cream.
Remove the saucepan to a tepid place and gradually pour the melted butter on the yolks while briskly stirring the sauce.
When the butter is absorbed, the sauce ought to be thick and firm. It can be brought to the correct consistence with a little water, which also lightens it slightly, but this addition is optional.
Complete the sauce with a drop of lemon juice, and rub it through a tammy.
notes: The consistence of sauces whose processes are identical with those of the Hollandaise may be varied at will; for instance, the number of yolks may be increased if a very thick sauce is desired, and it may be lessened in the reverse case. Also similar results may be obtained by cooking the eggs either more or less. As a rule, if a thick sauce be required, the yolks ought to be well cooked and the sauce kept almost cold in the making. Experience alone—the fruit of long practice—can teach the various devices which enable the skilled worker to obtain different results from the same kind and quality of material.

title: SAUCE BIGARRADE
yield: This sauce is principally used to accompany braised and poëled ducklings.
notes: For braised ducklings: After having strained the braising sauce, completely remove its grease, and reduce it until it is very dense. Strain it once more through muslin, twisting the latter; then, in order to bring the sauce to its normal consistence, add the juice of six oranges and one lemon per quart (946 ml) of sauce. Finish with a small piece of lemon and orange rind cut regularly and finely, Julienne-fashion, and scalded for five minutes.

For poëled ducklings: Strain the poëling stock for ducklings or wild ducks through linen; entirely remove the grease, and add four pieces of caramel sugar dissolved in one tablespoonful (15 ml) of vinegar per one-half pint (237 ml) of stock, the juice of the oranges and the lemon and the Julienne of rinds, as for the braised-ducklings sauce indicated above.

title: SAUCE BORDELAISE
yield: It is especially suitable for grilled butcher’s meat.
ingredients: 2 oz (57 g) very finely minced shallots
4 oz (113 g) beef-marrow, cut into slices or cubes
3 oz (85 g) butter per pint of sauce (optional)
instructions: Put the minced shallots, red wine, mignonette pepper, and bits of thyme and bay into a vegetable-pan.
Reduce the wine by three-quarters, and add one-half pint (237 ml) of half-glaze.
Keep the sauce simmering for half an hour; despumate it from time to time, and strain it through linen or a sieve.
When dishing it up, finish it with the dissolved meat glaze, a few drops of lemon-juice, and the beef-marrow, cut into slices or cubes and poached in slightly salted boiling water.
notes: This sauce may be buttered to the extent of about three oz (85 g) per pint (473 ml), which makes it smoother, but less clear.

title: CHASSEUR SAUCE (Escoffier’s Method)
instructions: Peel and mince the mushrooms.
Heat the butter and olive oil in a vegetable-pan; put in the mushrooms, and fry them quickly until they are slightly browned.
Add the minced shallots, and immediately remove half the butter.
Pour the white wine and liqueur brandy into the stewpan; reduce this liquid to half.
Finish the sauce with the half-glaze, tomato sauce, and meat-glaze.
Set to boil for five minutes more, and complete with the chopped parsley.

title: BROWN CHAUD-FROID SAUCE
instructions: Put the half-glaze into a sauté-pan with the truffle essence.
Put the pan on an open fire, and reduce its contents; while reducing, add the jelly to the sauce in small quantities at a time.
The degree of reduction in this sauce is a good third. After the reduction, carefully taste, and rectify the seasoning if necessary.
Mix a little Madeira or Port with the sauce, away from the fire, and strain through muslin or, preferably, through a Venetian-hair sieve.
Stir the sauce now and then while it cools, until it is sufficiently liquid, and at the same time consistent enough, to coat immersed solids evenly with a film of sauce.
notes: To be certain of its consistence, a test may be made by allowing it to cool a little.

title: VARIETIES OF THE CHAUD-FROID SAUCE
introduction: The following are variations on the Brown Chaud-Froid Sauce. (Recipe 34)
notes: For Ducks: Prepare the sauce as above (Recipe 34), adding to it (for the prescribed quantity) one-half pint (237 ml) of duck fumet obtained from the carcases and remains of roast duckling, and finish it, away from the fire, with the juice of four oranges and a heaped tablespoonful (15 ml) of orange rind, cut finely, Julienne-fashion, and scalded for five minutes.

For Feathered Game: Treat the Chaud-Froid sauce as indicated in Recipe 34, adding one-half pint (237 ml) of the fumet of the game constituting the dish in order to lend it that game’s characteristic taste. Observe the same precaution for the cooling.

For Fish: Proceed as in Recipe 34, but (1) substitute the Espagnole of fish for the half glaze; (2) intensify the first Espagnole with one-half pint (237 ml) of very clear fish essence; (3) use Lenten jelly instead of meat jelly.

notes.title: Remarks upon the Use of Chaud-Froid Sauces
content: The chaud-froid sauce may be prepared beforehand, and when it is wanted it need only be gently melted without heating it too much. It ought simply to be made sufficiently liquid to give a good coating to substances immersed in it.

title: DEVILLED SAUCE
yield: This sauce may be served with grilled fowls or pigeons. It also forms an excellent accompaniment to re-dished meat which needs a spicy sauce.
instructions: Put the sliced shallots and white wine in a vegetable pan.
Reduce the wine to two-thirds, add the half-glaze, and reduce again to two-thirds.
Season strongly with cayenne pepper, and strain through muslin.

title: “ESCOFFIER” DEVILLED SAUCE
introduction: This sauce, which may be bought ready-made, is admirably fitted to accompany grilled fish and grills in general. In order to make it ready, all that is needed is to add its own volume of fresh butter to it, the latter being previously well softened so as to ensure its perfect mixture with the sauce.

title: GENEVOISE SAUCE
ingredients: 2 lbs (907 g) head of salmon and remains or bones of fish
A few drops of anchovy essence
4 oz (113 g) butter per quart of sauce
instructions: Heat the 2 oz (57 g) of butter in a stewpan; insert the Mirepoix. (Recipe 228)
Slightly brown, add the head of salmon and remains of fish, and stew with lid on for twenty minutes.
Let the stewpan lean slightly to one side, so that the butter may be drained; moisten with one bottle of red wine and reduce the wine by half.
Add one pint (473 ml) of Lenten Espagnole, and allow to cook gently for half an hour.
Rub the sauce through a sieve, pressing it so as to extract all the essence. Let it rest awhile; carefully remove the fat which has risen to the surface.
Add the burnt brandy, one-half pint (237 ml) of red wine, and as much fish fumet. Boil again, then move stewpan to the side of fire to despumate for one and one-half hours.
Frequently remove what the ebullition causes to rise to the surface. Strain it through muslin or tammy.
Finish at the last minute with a few drops of anchovy essence and four oz (113 g) of butter per quart (946 ml) of sauce.
notes: The Genevoise Sauce, like all red-wine sauces, may be served without being buttered. It is thus clearer and more sightly in colour, but the addition of butter in small quantities makes it mellower and more palatable.

title: REMARKS ON RED-WINE SAUCES
introduction: In the general repertory of cooking we also have, in the way of red-wine sauces, the “Bourguignonne,” “Matelote,” and “Red-Wine” sauces, which are closely allied to the “Genevoise,” and only differ from it in details of procedure.

The “Bourguignonne” Sauce is composed of red-wine accompanied by aromatics, and reduced by half. In accordance with ordinary principles, it is thickened by means of three oz (85 g) of manied butter per quart (946 ml) of reduced wine. This sauce is buttered with four oz (113 g) of butter per quart (946 ml), and is especially regarded as a domestic preparation for poached, moulded, and hard-boiled eggs.

“Matelote” Sauce is made from Court-bouillon, with red wine which has been used for cooking fish. This Court-bouillon, with the mushroom parings added, is reduced by two-thirds, and is thickened with one pint (473 ml) of Lenten Espagnole per pint (473 ml) of the reduced Court-bouillon. This sauce should be reduced by a third, strained through a tammy, and finished by means of two oz (57 g) of butter and a little cayenne per pint (473 ml) of sauce.

The Red-Wine Sauce resembles the two preceding ones in so far as it contains mirepoix browned in butter and diluted with red wine. The wine is reduced by half, thickened by a pint (473 ml) of Lenten Espagnole per pint (473 ml) of the reduction, and the sauce is despumated for about twenty minutes. It is strained through a tammy, and finished, when ready, by a few drops of anchovy essence, a little cayenne, and two oz (57 g) of butter per pint (473 ml) of sauce.

title: GRAND-VENEUR SAUCE
yield: This sauce is the proper accompaniment for joints of venison.
ingredients: 0.25 pint (118 ml) cream per pint of sauce
instructions: Take one pint (473 ml) of Poivrade Sauce and boil it, adding one pint (473 ml) of game stock to keep it light. (Recipe 49)
Reduce the sauce by a good third; remove it from the fire, and add the red-currant jelly.
When the jelly is well dissolved, complete the sauce by adding the cream.

title: ITALIAN SAUCE
notes: Ordinary Italian Sauce: Put into a stewpan six tablespoonfuls (90 ml) of Duxelles (Recipe 223), two oz (57 g) of very lean, cooked ham, cut very finely, brunoise-fashion, and one pint (473 ml) of half-glaze tomatée. Boil for ten minutes, and complete, at the moment of dishing up, with one teaspoonful (5 ml) of parsley, chervil, and tarragon, minced and mixed.

Lenten Italian Sauce: Same preparation, only (1) omit the Ham, and (2) substitute Lent Espagnole (combined with fish fumet made from the fish for which the sauce is intended) for half glaze with tomatoes.

title: THICKENED GRAVY
yield: The thickened gravy with the veal-stock base is used for choicest pieces of butcher’s meat; that with a poultry-stock base is for fillets of poultry.
ingredients: 1 pint (473 ml) poultry or veal stock
instructions: Boil one pint (473 ml) of poultry or veal stock (according to the nature of the dish the gravy is intended for).
Dilute the fecula cold with a little water or gravy.
Pour this liaison into the boiling gravy, being careful to stir briskly to thicken the sauce.

title: VEAL GRAVY TOMATÉ
yield: This gravy is for butcher’s meat.
instructions: Add the tomato purée and tomato juice to the veal stock.
Reduce by a fifth. Strain the gravy through linen.

title: LYONNAISE SAUCE
instructions: Finely mince the onions and brown them slightly in the butter.
Moisten with the white wine and vinegar; almost entirely reduce the liquid.
Add the clear half-glaze, and set to cook slowly for half an hour.
Rub the sauce through a tammy.
notes: The onion may be left in the sauce or not, according to the preparation for which it is intended and the taste of the consumer.

title: MADEIRA SAUCE
instructions: Put the half-glaze into a sauté-pan, and reduce it on a brisk fire to a stiff consistence.
When it reaches this point, take it off the fire and add the Madeira to it, which brings it back to its normal consistence.
Strain through a tammy, and keep it warm without allowing it to boil.

title: MARROW SAUCE
introduction: The Marrow Sauce is a variety of the Bordelaise. (Recipe 32)
ingredients: 1 quart (946 ml) Bordelaise Sauce base (minced shallots, red wine, pepper, thyme, bay, half-glaze)
6 oz (170 g) beef marrow, cut into cubes
instructions: Follow the proportions as indicated under “Sauce Bordelaise” for the necessary quantity of this sauce. (Recipe 32)
Finish it with the beef marrow, cut into cubes, poached and well drained, and the chopped, scalded parsley.
If the sauce is to accompany vegetables, finish it, away from the fire, with the butter, and then add the cubes of marrow and the parsley.

title: PIGNONS SAUCE
yield: This sauce is specially suited to joints of venison.
ingredients: 1 oz (28 g) raisins, stoned and washed
instructions: Take the necessary amount of Poivrade Sauce and let it boil. (Recipe 49)
Prepare an infusion of juniper berries, with the water and concassed berries.
Leave the stoned and washed raisins to soak in tepid water for about an hour.
Finish the sauce, when dishing up, by adding the infusion of juniper berries strained through linen, the grilled kernels, the soaked raisins, and the Madeira wine.

title: PÉRIGUEUX SAUCE
yield: It is used for numerous small entrées, timbales, hot pâtés, &c.
ingredients: 1 quart (946 ml) Madeira Sauce base (reduced half-glaze and veal stock)
instructions: Prepare a base similar to Madeira Sauce by reducing half-glaze with half its volume of very strong veal stock, keeping it a little denser than usual. (Recipe 44)
Finish this sauce by adding the truffle essence and chopped truffles per quart (946 ml) of sauce.

title: PIQUANTE SAUCE
yield: This sauce generally accompanies grilled or boiled pork, and cold meat re-dished and minced which needs spicy flavouring.
ingredients: 1 tsp (5 ml) mixed chervil, parsley, and tarragon, finely chopped
instructions: Put the minced shallots, vinegar, and white wine into a vegetable pan.
Reduce the liquid by a good half, and add the half-glaze.
Set the sauce to boil, and despumate it for half an hour.
At the last moment finish it, away from the fire, with the gherkins, capers, and mixed herbs.

title: ORDINARY POIVRADE SAUCE
yield: This sauce is suitable for joints marinaded or not.
instructions: Heat 2 oz (57 g) of butter in a stewpan, and insert the raw Mirepoix. Fry the vegetables until they are well browned. (Recipe 228)
Moisten with the vinegar and Marinade; reduce to two-thirds. (Recipe 169)
Add the Espagnole Sauce and cook for three-quarters of an hour.
Ten minutes before straining the sauce, put in the crushed peppercorns. If the pepper were put in the sauce earlier, it might make it bitter.
Pass the sauce through a strainer, pressing the aromatics; add a further one-half pint (237 ml) of Marinade, and despumate for one-quarter of an hour, keeping it simmering the while.
Strain again through tammy, and finish the sauce, when ready for dishing, with 2 oz (57 g) of butter.

title: POIVRADE SAUCE FOR VENISON
ingredients: 4 lbs (1.8 kg) well-broken bones and ground-game trimmings
4 oz (113 g) butter per quart of sauce (optional)
instructions: Fry, with the butter and oil, the raw Mirepoix to which are added the bones and game trimmings. (Recipe 228)
When the whole is well browned, drain the grease away, and dilute with the vinegar and white wine.
Reduce this liquid by three-quarters, then add the game stock and Espagnole Sauce. Boil, cover the saucepan, and put into a moderate oven for at least three hours.
Take out the saucepan and pour its contents into a fine sieve placed over a tureen; press the remains to expel all the sauce.
Pour the sauce into a tall, thick saucepan. Add enough game stock and Marinade, mixed in equal parts, to produce three quarts (2.8 L) in all of sauce.
Gently reduce the sauce while despumating it. As it diminishes in volume, pass it through muslin into smaller saucepans.
Stop the reduction when only a quart (946 ml) of sauce remains.
notes: This sauce, like red-wine sauces, may be served as it stands. It is brilliant, clear, and perhaps more sightly thus, but the addition of a certain quantity of butter (four oz (113 g) per quart (946 ml)) makes it perfectly mellow, and admirably completes its fragrance.

title: PROVENÇALE SAUCE
introduction: In reality, true Provençale is nothing but a fine fondue of tomatoes with garlic.
instructions: Peel, remove the seeds, press and concass the tomatoes.
Heat the oil in a sauté-pan until it begins to smoke a little.
Insert the tomatoes seasoned with pepper and salt; add the crushed garlic clove, a pinch of powdered sugar, and the chopped parsley.
Allow to melt gently for half an hour.

title: ROBERT SAUCE
yield: This sauce—of a spicy flavour—is best suited to grilled and boiled pork. It may also be used for a mince of the same meat.
instructions: Finely mince the onion and put it into a stewpan with butter.
Fry the onion gently without letting it acquire any colour.
Dilute with the white wine, reduce the wine by one-third, add the half-glaze, and leave to simmer for twenty minutes.
When dishing up, finish the sauce with the meat glaze, mustard, and powdered sugar.
notes: If, when finished, the sauce has to wait, it should be kept warm in a bain-marie, as it must not boil again.

title: ESCOFFIER ROBERTS SAUCE
introduction: This sauce may be bought ready-made. It is used either hot or cold. It is especially suitable for pork, veal, poultry, and even fish, and is generally used hot with grills after the equivalent of its volume of excellent brown stock has been added to it. It may also be served cold to accompany cold meat.

title: ROUENNAISE SAUCE
yield: Serve this sauce with duckling à la Rouennaise.
ingredients: 1 pint (473 ml) Bordelaise sauce base with excellent red wine
instructions: Prepare a “Bordelaise” sauce using an excellent red wine as the diluent. (Recipe 32)
For one pint (473 ml) of sauce, pass the raw ducks’ livers through a sieve.
Add the resulting purée to the Bordelaise, and heat the latter for a few minutes in order to poach the liver.
Be careful not to heat the sauce too much nor too long, lest the liver be overcooked.

title: SALMIS SAUCE
introduction: The base of this sauce, which rather resembles the cullis, is unchangeable. Its diluent only changes according to the kind of birds or game to be treated.
ingredients: Shin and chopped carcase of the bird under treatment
0.5 pint (237 ml) game stock or mushroom liquor
instructions: Cut and gently brown the Mirepoix in butter. (Recipe 228)
Add the shin detached from the limbs and the chopped carcase of the bird under treatment, and moisten with the white wine.
Reduce the wine to two-thirds, add the half glaze, and boil gently for three-quarters of an hour.
Pass through a strainer, while pressing upon the carcase and the aromatics, to extract their quintessence.
Thin the cullis thus obtained by means of the game stock or mushroom liquor (if the game be Lenten).

Now despumate for about one hour, finally reduce the sauce, bring it to its proper consistency with a little mushroom liquor and truffle essence, rub it through tammy, and butter it slightly at the last moment.

title: TORTUE SAUCE
instructions: Boil the veal stock, adding the sage, sweet marjoram, rosemary, basil, thyme, bay, mushroom parings, and parsley. Cover and allow to infuse for half an hour.
Two minutes before straining, add the concassed peppercorns.
After straining through fine linen, add the half-glaze and tomato sauce (away from the fire) with the sherry, truffle essence, and a good pinch of cayenne.
notes: As this sauce must be spicy, the use of cayenne suggests itself, but great caution should be observed, as there must be no excess of this condiment.

title: VENISON SAUCE
yield: Serve this sauce with big ground-game.
ingredients: 1 pint (473 ml) Poivrade sauce for game
instructions: Prepare a Poivrade sauce for game. (Recipe 50)
Finish this sauce with the red-currant jelly, previously dissolved, and mixed with the fresh cream per pint (473 ml) of sauce. This addition must be made away from the fire.

title: AMERICAN SAUCE
introduction: This sauce is that of lobster prepared “à l’Américaine”. (Recipe 939) As it generally accompanies a fish, the meat of the lobster or lobsters which have served in its preparation is sliced and used as the garnish of the fish.

title: ANCHOVY SAUCE
ingredients: 1 oz (28 g) anchovy fillets, washed, sponged, and cut into small pieces
instructions: Put the unbuttered Normande Sauce into a small stewpan. (Recipe 99)
Finish it, away from the fire, with the anchovy butter and anchovy fillets.

title: AURORE SAUCE
ingredients: 0.5 pint (237 ml) very red tomato purée (Recipe 29)
instructions: Into the boiling velouté, put the tomato purée and mix the two. (Recipe 29)
Let the sauce boil a little, pass it through a tammy, and finish, away from the fire, with the butter.

title: LENTEN AURORE SAUCE
ingredients: 0.5 pint (237 ml) very red tomato purée (Recipe 29)
instructions: This sauce is made like the preceding one (Recipe 60), with the same quantities of velouté and tomato purée, replacing ordinary velouté by fish velouté.

title: BÉARNAISE SAUCE
yield: Serve it with grilled, butcher’s meat and poultry.
instructions: Put the chopped shallots, tarragon stalks, chervil, mignonette pepper, salt, and vinegar into a small stewpan.
Reduce the vinegar by two-thirds, take off the fire, and let the stewpan cool a little.
Add the yolks of five eggs to this reduction.

Put the stewpan on a low fire and gradually combine the melted butter with the yolks. Whisk the sauce briskly to ensure the cooking of the yolks, which alone, by gradual cooking, effect the leason of the sauce.
When the butter is combined with the sauce, rub the latter through a tammy.
Finish it with the chervil parings and chopped tarragon leaves. Complete the seasoning with a suspicion of cayenne.
notes: This sauce should not be served very hot, as it is really a mayonnaise with butter. It need only be tepid, for it would probably turn if it were over-heated.

title: BÉARNAISE SAUCE WITH MEAT GLAZE, OTHERWISE VALOIS SAUCE OR FOYOT SAUCE
yield: Serve it with butcher’s meat.
ingredients: 3 tbsp (45 ml) dissolved pale meat glaze
instructions: Prepare a Béarnaise sauce as explained in Recipe 62.
Complete it with the dissolved pale meat glaze, which may be added in small quantities at a time.

title: BÉARNAISE TOMATÉE SAUCE OR CHORON SAUCE
yield: This is proper to “Tournedos Choron,” but it may accompany grilled poultry and white, butcher’s meat.
ingredients: 0.33 pint (156 ml) very red tomato purée
instructions: Proceed in exactly the same way as for Béarnaise Sauce. (Recipe 62)
When the sauce is made and rubbed through tammy, finish it with the very red tomato purée.
In this case the final addition of chervil and tarragon should not be made.

title: BERCY SAUCE
yield: Serve with medium-sized poached fish.
ingredients: 0.5 pint (237 ml) fish fumet or fish liquor
A few drops of fish glaze
instructions: Heat the chopped shallots.
Moisten with the white wine and fish fumet (or the liquor of a fish similar to the one the sauce is to accompany).
Reduce to a good third, add the velouté, let the sauce boil some time.
Finish it, away from the fire, with the butter (added by degrees), a few drops of fish glaze, the lemon juice, and the chopped parsley.

title: BUTTER SAUCE
instructions: Mix the sifted flour with the melted butter.
Dilute with the boiling, salted water. Stir briskly to ensure a perfect leason, and do not allow to boil.
Add immediately the egg yolks mixed with the cream and the lemon juice.
Rub through a tammy, and finish the sauce with the fresh butter.
notes: Be careful that the sauce does not boil after it has been thickened.

title: BONNEFOY SAUCE, OR WHITE BORDELAISE SAUCE
yield: Serve it with grilled fish and grilled white meat.
ingredients: 0.5 pint (237 ml) Graves, Sauterne, or any other excellent white Bordeaux
instructions: Put the minced shallots and white Bordeaux wine in a stewpan.
Reduce the wine almost entirely, add the velouté, let it simmer twenty minutes, and rub it through a tammy.
Finish it, away from the fire, with the butter and a little chopped tarragon.

title: CAPER SAUCE
yield: It frequently accompanies boiled fish of all kinds.
instructions: Prepare a Butter Sauce and add two tablespoonfuls (30 ml) of capers per pint (473 ml) of sauce. (Recipe 66)

title: CARDINAL SAUCE
yield: This sauce is poured over the fish.
ingredients: 3 oz (85 g) very red lobster butter (Recipe 149)
instructions: Boil the Béchamel, to which add the fish fumet and a little truffle essence, and reduce by a quarter.
Finish the sauce, when dishing up, with the cream and the very red lobster butter. (Recipe 149)

title: MUSHROOM SAUCE
notes: If this be intended for poultry, add one-fifth pint (95 ml) of mushroom liquor and eight oz (227 g) of button-mushroom heads turned or channelled and cooked, to one pint (473 ml) of very stiff Allemande Sauce.
If it be intended for fish, take one pint (473 ml) of fish velouté, thickened with the yolks of four eggs, and finish it with mushroom liquor, as above.
The sauce suggested for poultry may also be used for fish, after adding the necessary quantity of fish fumet.

title: CHÂTEAUBRIAND SAUCE
yield: Serve with grilled fillet of beef, otherwise “Châteaubriand.”
instructions: Put the chopped shallots, thyme, bay, mushroom parings, and white wine into a stewpan.
Reduce the wine almost entirely, add the veal gravy, and reduce again until the liquid only measures one-quarter pint (118 ml).
Strain through muslin, and finish the sauce away from the fire with the butter “Maître d’Hôtel” and a little chopped tarragon. (Recipe 150)

title: WHITE CHAUD-FROID SAUCE
ingredients: 0.75 pint (355 ml) melted white poultry jelly
instructions: Boil the velouté in a stewpan, and add the melted white poultry jelly.
Put the stewpan on an open fire, reduce the sauce by a third, stirring constantly the while.
Gradually add the cream. When the sauce has reached the desired degree of consistency, rub it through a tammy.
Stir it frequently while it cools, for fear of a skin forming on its surface.
When dishing up, this sauce should be cold, so that it may properly coat immersed solids and yet be liquid enough to admit of the latter being easily steeped into it.

title: ORDINARY CHAUD-FROID SAUCE
ingredients: 0.75 pint (355 ml) melted white poultry jelly
instructions: Proceed exactly as for White Chaud-Froid sauce (Recipe 72), substituting Allemande Sauce for the velouté, and reducing the quantity of cream to one-quarter pint.
Observe the same precautions while cooling.

title: CHAUD-FROID SAUCE, A L’AURORE
notes: Prepare a white Chaud-Froid. (Recipe 72)

The sauce may be coloured by the addition of fine red tomato purée—more or less to match the desired shade—or by an infusion of paprika, according to the use for which it is intended. Paprika is preferable when not too deep a shade is required.

title: CHAUD-FROID SAUCE, AU VERT-PRÉ
yield: Use this sauce for Chaud-froids of fowl, particularly that kind distinguished as “Printanier.”
ingredients: 0.75 pint (355 ml) melted white poultry jelly
instructions: Prepare an infusion: Boil the white wine, and add to it the chervil stalks, tarragon leaves, chives, and parsley leaves. Cover, allow infusion to proceed away from the fire for ten minutes, and strain through linen.
Add this infusion to the velouté of the white Chaud-Froid sauce at the same time as the jelly. (Recipe 72)
Treat the sauce as explained in Recipe 72, and finish with spinach-green. (Recipe 143)
The shade of the sauce must not be too pronounced, but must remain a pale green. The colouring principle must therefore be added with caution and in small quantities.

title: LENT CHAUD-FROID SAUCE
instructions: Proceed as for white Chaud-Froid (Recipe 72), using the same quantities, and substituting fish velouté for ordinary velouté, and white fish jelly for poultry jelly.
notes: I have adopted the use of this ordinary Chaud-Froid sauce for the glazing of fillets and escalopes of fish and Shell-fish, instead of cleared Mayonnaise, formerly used, which had certain inconveniences—not the least being the oozing away of the oil under the shrinkage of the gelatine. This difficulty does not obtain in the ordinary Chaud-Froid, the definite and pronounced flavour of which is better than that of the cleared Mayonnaise.

title: “ESCOFFIER” CHERRY SAUCE
introduction: This sauce may be bought ready-made. Like the Roberts Sauce, it can be served hot or cold. It is an excellent adjunct to venison, and even to small ground-game. Saddle of venison with this sauce constitutes one of the greatest dainties that an epicure could desire.

title: CHIVRY SAUCE
yield: Chivry Sauce is admirably suited to boiled or poached poultry.
ingredients: A large pinch of chervil pluches
A large pinch of tarragon leaves
A large pinch of parsley leaves
instructions: In the boiling poultry stock, put the chervil pluches, tarragon and parsley leaves, young pimpernel, and chives. Cover up, and let infusion proceed for ten to twelve minutes.
Add the liquid (strained through linen) to the velouté.
Boil, reduce by a quarter, and complete it with the Green Butter. (Recipe 143)

title: CREAM SAUCE
yield: Serve this sauce with boiled fish, poultry, eggs, and various vegetables.
ingredients: 0.25 pint (118 ml) very fresh cream for finishing
instructions: Boil the Béchamel Sauce, and add one-quarter pint (118 ml) of cream to it.
Reduce on an open fire until the sauce has become very thick; then pass through tammy.
Bring to its normal degree of consistency by gradually adding, away from the fire, another one-quarter pint (118 ml) of very fresh cream and a few drops of lemon-juice.

title: SHRIMP SAUCE
ingredients: 1 pint (473 ml) fish velouté or Béchamel sauce
0.25 pint (118 ml) very clear fish fumet
instructions: Boil the fish velouté or Béchamel sauce, and add to it the cream and very clear fish fumet.
Reduce to one pint, and finish the sauce, away from the fire, with the Shrimp Butter and shelled shrimps’ tails. (Recipe 145)

title: CURRY SAUCE
yield: Serve this sauce with fish, shell-fish, poultry, and various egg-preparations.
instructions: Slightly brown the onions, parsley roots, celery, thyme, bay, and mace in butter.
Sprinkle with the flour and curry pepper. Cook the flour for some minutes without letting it acquire any colour.
Dilute with the white stock. Boil, cook gently for three-quarters of an hour, and rub through a tammy.
Now heat the sauce, remove its grease, and keep it in the bain-marie.
notes: This sauce is sometimes flavoured with cocoa-nut milk in the proportion of one-quarter of the diluent.

title: DIPLOMATE SAUCE
ingredients: 3 tbsp (45 ml) lobster meat, cut into small tubes
3 tbsp (45 ml) truffles, cut into small tubes
instructions: Take one pint (473 ml) of Normande Sauce, prepared according to Recipe 99, and finish it with the lobster butter and the lobster meat and truffles cut into small, regular tubes.

title: HERB SAUCE
yield: Serve this sauce with boiled or poached fish.
ingredients: 1 tbsp (15 ml) parsley, chopped and mixed
1 tbsp (15 ml) chervil, chopped and mixed
1 tbsp (15 ml) tarragon, chopped and mixed
1 tbsp (15 ml) chives, chopped and mixed
instructions: Prepare one pint of white-wine sauce. (Recipe 111)
Finish it away from the fire with the shallot butter and the chopped and mixed parsley, chervil, tarragon, and chives.

title: GOOSEBERRY SAUCE
yield: This sauce is excellent with grilled mackerel and the poached fillets of that fish.
instructions: Prepare one pint of butter sauce. (Recipe 66)
Meanwhile put the green gooseberries into a small copper saucepan containing boiling water. Boil for five minutes, then drain.
Put the gooseberries in a little stewpan with the white wine and powdered sugar.
Gently cook the gooseberries, rub them through a tammy, and add the resulting pulp to the butter sauce.

title: HUNGARIAN SAUCE
yield: It forms an ideal accompaniment to choice morsels of lamb and veal, eggs, poultry, and fish.
ingredients: 1 pint (473 ml) ordinary or Lenten Velouté
instructions: Gently fry the chopped onions in butter, without colouring, seasoned with table-salt and paprika.
Moisten with the white wine, add the faggot, and reduce the wine by two-thirds. Remove the herbs.
Finish with the Velouté (ordinary or Lenten, according to use) and boil moderately for five minutes.
Rub the sauce through a tammy, and complete it with the 2 oz (57 g) of butter.
notes: Remember this sauce should be of a tender, pink shade, which it must owe to the paprika alone.

title: OYSTER SAUCE
ingredients: 0.25 pint (118 ml) reduced oyster liquor, strained
instructions: Take one pint of Normande Sauce, finish it as directed in that recipe (Recipe 99), and complete it with the reduced and strained oyster liquor and the poached and trimmed oysters.

title: IVORY SAUCE, OR ALBUFERA SAUCE
yield: Serve this sauce chiefly with poultry and poached sweet-bread.
ingredients: 4 tbsp (60 ml) dissolved, pale, meat glaze
instructions: Take the necessary quantity of Suprême Sauce, prepared as explained in Recipe 106a.
Add the dissolved, pale, meat glaze to lend the sauce that ivory-white tint which characterises it.

title: JOINVILLE SAUCE
introduction: As may be seen, Joinville Sauce differs from similar preparations in the final operation where crayfish and shrimp butter are combined.
ingredients: 1 oz (28 g) very black truffles cut Julienne-fashion (optional)
instructions: Prepare one pint of Normande Sauce as given in the first part of its formula. (Recipe 99)
Complete it with the shrimp butter and crayfish butter.

If this sauce is to accompany a fish à la Joinville, which includes a special garnish, it is served as it stands. If it is served with a large, boiled, ungarnished fish, the truffles cut Julienne-fashion should be added.

title: MALTESE SAUCE
yield: Maltese Sauce is the finest for asparagus.
instructions: To the Hollandaise Sauce, add, when dishing up, the juice of the blood oranges and the grated orange-rind. (Recipe 30)

title: MARINIÈRE SAUCE
