yield: Serve this with small poached fish and more particularly with mussels.
instructions: Take the necessary quantity of Bercy Sauce. (Recipe 65)
Add, per pint (473 ml) of sauce, the mussel liquor and a leason composed of the egg yolks.

title: MORNAY SAUCE
ingredients: 0.25 pint (118 ml) fumet of fish, poultry, or vegetable
instructions: Boil the Béchamel Sauce with the fumet of the fish, poultry, or vegetable which is to constitute the dish.
Reduce by a good quarter, and add the grated Gruyère and Parmesan cheese.
Put the sauce on the fire again for a few minutes, and ensure the melting of the cheese by stirring with a small whisk.
Finish the sauce away from the fire with the butter added by degrees.

title: MOUSSELINE SAUCE
instructions: To a Hollandaise Sauce, prepared as explained (Recipe 30), add, just before dishing up, the stiffly-whipped cream per pint of sauce.

title: MOUSSEUSE SAUCE
yield: This preparation, though classified as a sauce, is really a compound butter, which is served with boiled fish.
introduction: The heat of the fish alone suffices to melt it, and its appearance is infinitely more agreeable than that of plain, melted butter.
ingredients: 2 tbsp (30 ml) very firm, whipped cream
instructions: Scald and wipe a small vegetable-pan, and put into it the stiffly-manied butter, properly softened.
Season this butter with table-salt and a few drops of lemon-juice.
Whisk it while gradually adding the cold water.
Finish with the whipped cream.

title: MUSTARD SAUCE
yield: It is served with certain small grilled fish, especially fresh herrings.
instructions: Take the necessary quantity of butter sauce and complete it, away from the fire, with the mustard. (Recipe 66)
notes: If the sauce has to wait, it must be kept in a bain-marie, for it should not on any account boil.

title: NANTUA SAUCE
ingredients: 3 oz (85 g) very fine crayfish butter
1 tbsp (15 ml) small, shelled crayfishes’ tails
instructions: Boil the Béchamel Sauce, add one-half pint (237 ml) of cream, and reduce by a third.
Rub it through a tammy.
Finish it with a further addition of the 2 tbsp (30 ml) of cream, the crayfish butter, and the shelled crayfishes’ tails.

title: NEWBURG SAUCE - FIRST METHOD (WITH RAW LOBSTERS)
ingredients: 0.33 pint (156 ml) Marsala or old Sherry
instructions: Divide the lobster into four parts. Remove its creamy parts, pound them finely with 2 oz (57 g) of butter, and put them aside.
Heat the 1.5 oz (43 g) of butter and oil in a sautépan, and insert the pieces of lobster, well seasoned with salt and cayenne.
Fry until the pieces assume a fine, red colour; entirely drain away the butter.
Add the burnt brandy and Marsala or old Sherry.
Reduce the wine by two-thirds, and wet the lobster with the cream and fish fumet.
Now add a faggot, cover the sautépan, and gently cook for twenty-five minutes.
Drain the lobster on a sieve, remove the meat and cut it into cubes.
Finish the sauce by adding the creamy portions put aside from the first. Boil so as to ensure the cooking of these latter portions.
Add the meat, cut into cubes, and verify the seasoning.
notes: The addition of the meat to the sauce is optional; instead of cutting it into cubes it may be stewed and displayed on the fish constituting the dish.

title: NEWBURG SAUCE - SECOND METHOD (WITH COOKED LOBSTER)
introduction: Originally, these two sauces, like the American, were exclusively composed of, and served with, lobster. To obviate the difficulty of digesting lobster at night, I have made it a practice to serve lobster sauce with fillets or Mousselines of sole, adding the lobster as a garnish only.

By using such condiments as curry and paprika, excellent varieties of this sauce may be obtained, which are particularly suited to sole and other white Lenten fish. In either of these cases it is well to add a little rice “à l’Indienne” to the fish.
instructions: The lobster having been cooked in a Court-bouillon, shell the tail and slice it up.
Arrange these slices in a sautépan liberally buttered at the bottom; season them strongly with salt and cayenne, and heat them on both sides to effect the reddening of the skin.
Immerse, so as to cover, in a good Sherry, and almost entirely reduce same.
When dishing up, pour on to the slices a leason composed of the fresh cream and the egg yolks.
Gently stir, away from the fire, and roll the saucepan about until the leason is completed.

title: NOISETTE SAUCE
yield: Serve this with salmon, trout, and all boiled fish in general.
instructions: Prepare a Hollandaise Sauce according to the recipe under Recipe 30.
Add the hazel-nut butter at the last moment.

title: NORMANDE SAUCE
yield: This sauce is proper to fillet of sole “à la Normande,” but it is also frequently used as the base of other small sauces.
ingredients: 4 tbsp (60 ml) good cream for finishing
instructions: Put the fish velouté, mushroom liquor, oyster liquor, sole fumet, egg yolks, lemon-juice, and 0.25 pint (118 ml) of cream in a sautépan.
Reduce by a good third on an open fire.
Season with a little cayenne, rub through a tammy.
Finish with the butter and 4 tbsp (60 ml) of good cream.

title: ORIENTAL SAUCE
yield: Serve this sauce in the same way as American Sauce. (Recipe 58)
instructions: Take one pint of American sauce, season with curry, and reduce to a third. (Recipe 58)
Then add, away from the fire, the cream per pint of sauce.

title: POULETTE SAUCE
yield: Use this sauce with certain vegetables, but more generally with sheep’s trotters.
instructions: Boil the Sauce Allemande for a few minutes, and add the mushroom liquor.
Finish, away from the fire, with the butter, lemon-juice, and chopped parsley.

title: RAVIGOTE SAUCE
yield: This sauce accompanies boiled poultry and certain white “abats.”
instructions: Reduce the white wine with the vinegar by half.
Add the ordinary velouté, boil gently for a few minutes.
Finish with the shallot butter and the chopped chervil, tarragon, and chives.

title: REGENCY SAUCE
notes: If this sauce is to garnish poultry: boil one pint (473 ml) of Allemande Sauce with six tablespoonfuls (90 ml) of mushroom essence and two tablespoonfuls (30 ml) of truffle essence. Finish with four tablespoonfuls (60 ml) of poultry glaze.
If it is to garnish fish: substitute for the Allemande Sauce some fish velouté thickened with egg-yolks and the essences of mushroom and truffle as above. Complete with some fish essence.

title: SOUBISE SAUCE
ingredients: 2 lbs (907 g) finely-minced onions, scalded and dried
instructions: Stew the finely-minced, scalded, and well-dried onions in butter. This increases their flavour.
Add the thickened Béchamel; season with salt and powdered sugar.
Cook gently for half an hour, rub through a tammy.
Complete the sauce with some tablespoonfuls of cream and 2 oz (57 g) of butter.

title: SOUBISE SAUCE WITH RICE
yield: This sauce, being more consistent than the former, is used as a garnish just as often as a sauce.
ingredients: 2 lbs (907 g) minced onions, scalded and drained
instructions: Garnish the bottom and the sides of a tall, medium stewpan with the thin rashers of fat bacon.
Insert the onions, together with the Carolina rice, white consommé, powdered sugar, and necessary salt.
Cook gently in the front of the oven for three-quarters of an hour.
Then pound the onions and rice in a mortar, rub the resulting purée through a tammy.
Finish with cream and butter as in the preceding case. (Recipe 104)

title: SOUBISE SAUCE TOMATÉE
ingredients: Very red tomato purée (1/3 volume of Soubise)
instructions: Prepare a soubise in accordance with the first formula (Recipe 104), and add to it one-third of its volume of very red tomato purée.

notes.title: Remarks
content: 1. The Soubise is rather a cullis than a sauce; i.e., its consistence must be greater than that of a sauce.

2. The admixture of Béchamel in Soubise is preferable to that of rice, seeing that it makes it smoother. If, in certain cases, rice is used as a cohering element, in order to give the Soubise more stiffness.
3. In accordance with the uses to which it may be put, the Soubise Tomatée may be finally seasoned either with curry or paprika.

title: SUPRÊME SAUCE
introduction: The salient characteristics of Suprême Sauce are its perfect whiteness and consummate delicacy. It is generally prepared in small quantities only.
ingredients: 1.5 pints (710 ml) very clear poultry stock
instructions: Put the poultry stock and mushroom cooking liquor into a sautépan. Reduce to two-thirds.
Add the poultry velouté; reduce on an open fire, stirring with the spatula the while.
Combine one-half pint (237 ml) of cream with the sauce, adding it little by little.
When the sauce has reached the desired consistence, strain it through a sieve.
Add another one-quarter pint (118 ml) of cream and the best butter.
Stir with a spoon from time to time, or keep the pan well covered.

title: VENETIAN SAUCE
yield: This sauce accompanies various fish.
ingredients: 0.25 pint (118 ml) white wine and tarragon vinegar, mixed equally
instructions: Put the chopped shallots, chervil, and the white wine/tarragon vinegar mix into a stewpan.
Reduce the liquid by two-thirds; add the white wine sauce; boil for a few minutes. (Recipe 111)
Rub through a tammy, and finish the sauce with a sufficient quantity of Herb Juice and the chopped chervil and tarragon. (Recipe 183)

title: VILLEROY SAUCE
instructions: Put the Allemande Sauce, truffle essence, and ham essence into a sautépan.
Reduce on an open fire and constantly stir until the sauce is sufficiently stiff to coat immersed solids thickly.

title: VILLEROY SOUBISEE SAUCE
instructions: Put the Allemande Sauce and Soubise purée into a sautépan. (Recipe 105)
Reduce as in the preceding case (Recipe 108), as the uses are the same.
According to the circumstances, a few teaspoonfuls of very black, chopped truffles may be added.

title: VILLEROY TOMATÉE SAUCE
notes: Prepare the sauce as explained under Recipe 108, and add to it the third of its volume of very fine tomato purée. Reduce in the same way.

notes.title: Remarks
content: 1. Villeroy sauce, of whatsoever kind, is solely used for the coating of preparations said to be “à la Villeroy.”
2. The Villeroy Tomatée may be finally seasoned with curry or paprika, according to the preparation for which it is intended.

title: WHITE WINE SAUCE
notes: Method 1 (For glazed fish): Add one-quarter pint (118 ml) of fish fumet to one pint (473 ml) of thickened Velouté, and reduce by half. Finish the sauce, away from the fire, with four oz (113 g) of butter.

Method 2: Almost entirely reduce one-quarter pint (118 ml) of fish fumet. To this reduction add the yolks of four eggs, mixing them well in it, and follow with one lb (454 g) of butter, added by degrees, paying heed to the precautions indicated under sauce Hollandaise. (Recipe 30)

Method 3: Put the yolks of five eggs into a small stewpan and mix them with one tablespoonful (15 ml) of cold fish-stock. Put the stewpan in a bain-marie and finish the sauce with one lb (454 g) of butter, meanwhile adding from time to time, and in small quantities, six tablespoonfuls (90 ml) of excellent fish fumet. The procedure is exactly that of the Hollandaise, with fish fumet taking the place of water. (Recipe 30)

title: APPLE SAUCE
yield: Serve this sauce lukewarm with duck, goose, roast hare, &c.
instructions: Quarter, peel, core, and chop the apples.
Place them in a stewpan with the powdered sugar, cinnamon, and a few tablespoonfuls of water.
Cook the whole gently with lid on, and smooth the purée with a whisk when dishing up.

title: BREAD SAUCE
yield: This sauce is served with roast fowl and roast feathered game.
ingredients: 1 small onion with a clove stuck in it
instructions: Boil the milk, and add the bread-crumb, a little salt, the small onion with a clove, and the butter.
Cook gently for about a quarter of an hour.
Remove the onion, smooth the sauce with a whisk, and finish it with a few tablespoonfuls of cream.

title: CELERY SAUCE
yield: This sauce is suited to boiled or braised poultry. It is excellent, and has been adopted in French cookery.
ingredients: 1 onion with a clove stuck in it
instructions: Clean the celery stalks (only use the hearts), put them in a sautépan, wholly immerse in consommé, add the faggot and onion with a clove, and cook gently.
Drain the celery, pound it in a mortar, then rub it through a tammy and put the purée in a stewpan.
Thin the purée with an equal quantity of cream sauce and a little reduced celery liquor.
Heat it moderately, and, if it has to wait, put it in a bain-marie.

title: CRANBERRY SAUCE
yield: This sauce is mostly served with roast turkey.
instructions: Cook the cranberries with the water in a covered stewpan.
When the berries are cooked, drain them in a fine sieve through which they are strained.
To the purée thus obtained, add the necessary quantity of their cooking liquor to make a somewhat thick sauce.
Sugar should be added according to the taste of the consumer.
notes: This is to be bought ready-made, and, if this kind be used, it need only be heated with a little water.

title: FENNEL SAUCE
yield: This is principally used with mackerel.
instructions: Take one pint of butter sauce and finish it with the chopped fennel, scalded for a few seconds. (Recipe 66)

title: EGG SAUCE WITH MELTED BUTTER
ingredients: 3 hot hard-boiled eggs, cut into large cubes
1 tsp (5 ml) chopped and scalded parsley
instructions: Dissolve the butter, and add to it the necessary salt, a little pepper, the lemon juice, the hot hard-boiled eggs, and the chopped and scalded parsley.

title: SCOTCH EGG SAUCE
yield: This sauce usually accompanies boiled fish, especially fresh haddocks and fresh and salted cod.
ingredients: 3 hot hard-boiled eggs, cut into cubes
instructions: Make a white roux with the butter and flour.
Mix in the boiling milk, season with salt, white pepper, and nutmeg, and boil gently for ten minutes.
Then add the hot hard-boiled eggs, cut into cubes (the whites and the yolks).

title: HORSE-RADISH OR ALBERT SAUCE
yield: Serve this sauce with braised or roast beef—especially fillets.
ingredients: A good 0.5 pint (237 ml) of butter sauce
A good 0.5 pint (237 ml) of cream
A pinch of salt and pepper
instructions: Place the rasped horse-radish in a stewpan with the white consommé. Boil gently for twenty minutes.
Add the butter sauce, as much cream, and the bread-crumb; thicken by reducing on a brisk fire and rub through tammy. (Recipe 66)
Then thicken with the egg yolks.
Complete the seasoning with a pinch of salt and pepper, and the mustard dissolved in the vinegar.

title: PARSLEY SAUCE
instructions: This is the Butter Sauce, to which is added, per pint, a heaped tablespoonful of freshly-chopped parsley. (Recipe 66)

title: REFORM SAUCE
yield: This sauce is for mutton cutlets when these are “à la Reform.”
ingredients: 0.5 oz (14 g) hard-boiled egg white, Julienne-cut
instructions: Put the half-glaze sauce and ordinary Poivrade sauce into a small stewpan and boil.
Complete with a garnish composed of the gherkins, hard-boiled egg white, salted tongue, truffles, and mushrooms. All these to be cut Julienne-fashion and short.

title: AIOLI SAUCE, OR PROVENCE BUTTER
ingredients: A few drops of lemon juice
A few drops of cold water
instructions: Pound the garlic cloves as finely as possible in a mortar.
Add the raw egg yolk and a pinch of salt.
Gradually let the oil fall in a thread while wielding the pestle, so as to effect a complete amalgamation.
Add a few drops of lemon juice and cold water to the sauce as it thickens to avoid it turning.

notes.title: Note
content: Should it decompose while in the process of making or when made, the only thing to be done is to begin it again with the yolk of an egg.

title: ANDALOUSE SAUCE
ingredients: Very red and concentrated tomato purée (1/4 volume of Mayonnaise)
2 oz (57 g) capsicum, per pint of sauce
instructions: Take the required quantity of Mayonnaise sauce and add to it the quarter of its volume of very red and concentrated tomato purée. (Recipe 126)
Finally, add 2 oz (57 g) of capsicum cut finely, Julienne-fashion, per pint (473 ml) of sauce.

title: BOHEMIAN SAUCE
instructions: Put the cold Béchamel, egg yolks, a little table salt, and white pepper into a bowl.

While whisking briskly, gradually add the tarragon vinegar. When the vinegar is absorbed, slowly add the oil in a thin, continuous stream, whisking constantly until the sauce is fully emulsified and thickened.
Finish the sauce with the mustard.

title: GENOA SAUCE
yield: Serves with cold fish.
ingredients: 1 oz (28 g) fir-apple kernels (or sweet almonds)
3 tbsp (45 ml) purée of herbs (equal parts chervil, parsley, tarragon, fresh pimpernel)
instructions: Pound the pistachios and fir-apple kernels (or almonds) in a mortar to a smooth, fine paste.
Add the cold Béchamel and mix.
Put this paste into a bowl, add the egg yolks, a little salt and pepper.
While whisking briskly, gradually add the lemon juice. When the juice is absorbed, slowly add the oil in a thin, continuous stream, whisking constantly until the sauce is fully emulsified.
To prepare the purée of herbs, take equal quantities of chervil, parsley, tarragon, and fresh pimpernel. Scald for one minute, cool quickly, press to expel water, and pass through a fine sieve.
Complete the sauce with the prepared purée of herbs.

title: GRIBICHE SAUCE
yield: Chiefly used with cold fish.
instructions: In a basin, crush the yolks of the hard-boiled eggs and work them into a smooth paste with the French mustard, salt, and a little pepper.
Make up the sauce by gradually adding the oil as if making a mayonnaise.
Complete the sauce with the chopped parsley, chervil, tarragon, capers, and gherkins, all evenly mixed.
Add the hard-boiled whites of the eggs, cut into a short Julienne.

title: MAYONNAISE SAUCE
instructions: Put the yolks in a basin. Season them with table-salt and a little cayenne pepper.
Gradually pour the vinegar on the yolks while whisking them briskly.
When the vinegar is absorbed, add the oil, letting it trickle down in a thread, constantly stirring the sauce meanwhile.
Finish the sauce by adding the juice of a lemon and the boiling water. The water ensures the coherence of the sauce and prevents it from turning.
notes: Mayonnaise prepared in this way is rather liquid, but it need only be left to rest a few hours in order to thicken considerably. Unless it be exposed to too low a temperature, the Mayonnaise, prepared as above, never turns, and may be kept for several days. Merely cover it to keep the dust away.

notes.title: Prejudices Refuted
content: 1. If the sauce forms badly, or not at all, the reason is that the oil has been added too rapidly at first, before the addition of the vinegar, and that its assimilation by the yolks has not operated normally.

2. It is quite an error to suppose that it is necessary to work over ice or in a cold room. Cold is rather deleterious to the Mayonnaise, and is invariably the cause of this sauce turning in winter. In the cold season the oil should be slightly warmed, or, at least, kept at the temperature of the kitchen, though it is best to make it in a moderately warm place.
3. It is a further error to suppose that the seasoning interferes with the making of the sauce, for salt, in solution, rather provokes the cohering force of the yolks.

notes.title: Causes of the Disintegration of the Mayonnaise
content: 1. The too rapid addition of the oil at the start.
2. The use of congealed, or too cold, an oil.

3. Excess of oil in proportion to the number of yolks, the assimilating power of an egg being limited to 2.5 oz (71 g) of oil if the sauce be made some time in advance, and 3 oz (85 g) if it is to be used immediately.

notes.title: Means of Bringing Turned Mayonnaise Back to its Normal State
content: Put the yolk of an egg into a basin with a few drops of vinegar, and mix the turned Mayonnaise in it, little by little. If it be a matter of only a small quantity of Mayonnaise, 0.5 coffeespoonful (1.25 ml) of mustard can take the place of the egg-yolk.

notes.title: Acid Seasoning
content: A whiter sauce is obtained by the use of lemon juice instead of vinegar.

title: CLEARED MAYONNAISE SAUCE
ingredients: 0.5 pint (237 ml) cold, rather firm melting aspic jelly (Lenten or ordinary)
instructions: Take the necessary quantity of Mayonnaise and gradually add to it, per 1.5 pints (710 ml) of the sauce, 0.5 pint (237 ml) of cold and rather firm melting aspic jelly. (Recipe 126)
The type of aspic (Lenten or ordinary) should depend on the nature of the products for which the sauce is intended.
notes: It is this very Mayonnaise, formerly used almost exclusively for coating entrées and cold relevées of fish, filleted fish, escalopes of common and spiny-lobster, &c., which I have allowed the Lenten Chaud-froid to supersede. (Recipe 76)

title: WHISKED MAYONNAISE
yield: Used principally for vegetable salads.
ingredients: 1 tbsp (15 ml) rasped or finely-chopped horse-radish
instructions: Put the melted jelly, Mayonnaise, tarragon vinegar, and horse-radish into a copper basin or other bowl. (Recipe 126)
Mix the whole, place the utensil on ice, and whisk gently until the contents get very frothy.
Stop whisking as soon as the sauce begins to solidify, for it must remain almost fluid so as to enable it to mix with the products for which it is intended.

title: RAVIGOTE SAUCE, OR VINAIGRETTE
yield: Accompanies calf’s head or foot, sheep’s trotters, &c.
ingredients: 3 tbsp (45 ml) fine herbs (finely chopped onion, parsley, and half as much chervil, tarragon, and chives)
instructions: Put the oil, vinegar, a little salt, and pepper into a bowl.
Add the small capers and the fine herbs, comprising some very finely chopped onion, as much parsley, and half as much chervil, tarragon, and chives.
Mix thoroughly.
notes: Two or three tablespoonfuls of the liquor with which its accompanying solids have been cooked (e.g., calf’s head or sheep’s trotters liquor) are often added to this sauce when dishing up.

title: REMOULADE SAUCE
yield: Accompanies cold meat and poultry, and, more particularly, common and spiny lobster.
ingredients: 1 tbsp (15 ml) chopped and pressed capers
1 tbsp (15 ml) fine herbs (chopped parsley, chervil, and tarragon)
instructions: To one pint (473 ml) of Mayonnaise, add the mustard, gherkins, chopped and pressed capers, fine herbs, and anchovy essence. (Recipe 126)

title: GREEN SAUCE
yield: Suitable for cold fish and shell fish.
instructions: Take the necessary quantity of thick Mayonnaise with spicy seasoning, and add to it, per pint (473 ml) of sauce, one-third pint (156 ml) of herb juice. (Recipe 126, 132)

title: VINCENT SAUCE
instructions: Prepare and carefully wash all the herbs: parsley, chervil, tarragon, chives, sorrel-leaves, fresh pimpernel, water-cress, and spinach.
Put all these herbs into a copper bowl containing salted, boiling water. Boil for two minutes only.
Drain the herbs in a sieve and immerse them in a basin of fresh water.
When they are cold, drain them again until quite dry.
Finely pound the herbs with the yolks of the hard-boiled eggs.
Rub the purée thus obtained through a sieve first, then through a tammy.
Add one pint (473 ml) of very stiff Mayonnaise to it and finish the sauce with a dessertspoonful (10 ml) of Worcestershire sauce. (Recipe 126)

title: CAMBRIDGE SAUCE
yield: Suited to cold meats in general.
introduction: An Anglicised version of Vincent Sauce. (Recipe 132)
ingredients: 1 dessertspoonful (10 ml) mixed chervil, tarragon, and chives
instructions: Pound together the hard-boiled egg yolks, washed and dried anchovy fillets, capers, and the mix of chervil, tarragon, and chives.
When the whole forms a fine paste, add the mustard, oil, and vinegar, proceeding as for a Mayonnaise. (Recipe 126)
Season with a little cayenne.
Rub through a tammy, applying pressure with a spoon, and put the sauce in a bowl.
Stir it awhile with a whisk to smooth it, and finish with the chopped parsley.

title: CUMBERLAND SAUCE
yield: Serve with cold venison.
instructions: Scald the finely-chopped shallots for a few seconds and press them.
Cut the orange and lemon rind finely, Julienne-fashion, scald for two minutes, drain well, and cool.
Dissolve the red-currant jelly, to which are added the port wine, scalded shallots, prepared orange and lemon rinds, orange juice, and lemon juice.
Add the mustard, a little cayenne pepper, and as much powdered ginger.
Mix the whole well.

title: GLOUCESTER SAUCE
yield: Serve with all cold meats.
instructions: Take one pint (473 ml) of very thick Mayonnaise. (Recipe 126)
Add the juice of a lemon to the sour cream.
Combine the sour cream with the Mayonnaise by degrees.
Complete with the chopped fennel and Worcester sauce.

title: MINT SAUCE
yield: Special sauce for hot or cold lamb.
ingredients: Slightly less than 1 oz (28 g) white cassonade or castor sugar
instructions: Cut the mint leaves finely, Julienne-fashion, or chop them.
Put these in a bowl with the sugar, fresh vinegar, and water.

title: OXFORD SAUCE
notes: Make a Cumberland sauce, with the difference that the Julienne of orange and lemon rinds should be replaced by rasped or finely-chopped rinds, and that the quantities of same should be less, i.e., two-thirds of a teaspoonful (3.3 ml) of each. (Recipe 134)

title: HORSE-RADISH SAUCE
yield: Accompanies boiled and roast joints of beef.
ingredients: 1 lb (454 g) bread-crumb, steeped in milk and pressed
instructions: Dilute the mustard with the vinegar in a basin.
Add the finely-rasped horse-radish, powdered sugar, a little salt, cream, and the pressed bread-crumb.
Serve this sauce very cold.

title: BERCY BUTTER
yield: Principally served with grilled beef.
ingredients: 2 oz (57 g) beef marrow, cubed and poached
instructions: Put the white wine and finely-chopped, scalded shallots into a small stewpan.
Reduce the wine by one-half.
Add the butter softened into a cream, the chopped parsley, and the beef marrow (cut into cubes, poached in slightly salted water, and well drained).
Add the necessary table-salt, and, when dishing up, a little ground pepper and a few drops of lemon-juice.
This butter must not be completely melted.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: CHIVRY OR RAVIGOTE BUTTER
yield: Used to complete Chivry sauce and others containing herb juices, like Venetian.
ingredients: 6 oz (170 g) mixed herbs (equal parts chervil, parsley, tarragon, fresh pimpernel, chives)
instructions: Put the mixed herbs and chopped shallots into a small saucepan of salted, boiling water.
Boil quickly for two minutes, then drain and cool in cold water.
Press in a towel to completely remove the water, and pound in a mortar.
Add the half-melted butter, mix well with the purée of herbs, and pass through a tammy.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: CHÂTEAUBRIAND BUTTER
instructions: Reduce by two-thirds the white wine containing the chopped shallots, fragments of thyme and bay, and mushroom parings.
Add the veal gravy and reduce the whole to half.
Rub it through a tammy.
Finish it away from the fire with Maître d’Hôtel butter and the chopped tarragon. (Recipe 150)
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: COLBERT BUTTER
yield: Serve with fish prepared à la Colbert.
ingredients: 6 tbsp (90 ml) dissolved, pale meat glaze
instructions: Take 1 lb (454 g) of Maître d’Hôtel butter and add the dissolved meat glaze and chopped tarragon. (Recipe 150)
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: RED COLOURING BUTTER
introduction: This butter is made from shell-fish remains to create a colored and flavored butter.
ingredients: Available remains of shell-fish (e.g., lobster, crayfish shells)
notes: Put any available remains of shell-fish onto a dish after having thoroughly emptied and well dried them in the oven.
Pound them until they form a fine powder.
Add their weight of butter.
Put the whole into a saucepan and melt in a bain-marie, stirring frequently.
When the butter is quite clarified, strain it through muslin, twisting the muslin over a tureen of iced-water in which the strained butter solidifies.
Put the congealed butter in a towel, press it heavily to expel the water, and keep cool in a small bowl.

A very fine and decided red colour is obtained by using paprika as a condiment for sauces intended for poultry and certain butcher’s meats, in accordance with the procedure I recommend for the Hongroise. But only the very best quality should be used—that which is mild and at the same time produces a nice pink colour without entailing any excess of the condiment. Among the various kinds of paprika on the market I can highly recommend that of Messrs. Kotangi, which I have invariably found satisfactory.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: GREEN COLOURING BUTTER
introduction: This green butter should in all cases take the place of the liquid green found on the market.
ingredients: Butter (half the weight of the resulting spinach solids)
notes: Peel, wash, and thoroughly shake 2 lbs (907 g) of spinach to get rid of every drop of water.
Pound it raw and then press it in a strong towel, twisting it to extract all the vegetable juice.
Pour this juice into a sautépan, let it coagulate in a bain-marie.
Pour the coagulated juice onto a serviette stretched over a bowl in order to drain away the water.
Collect the remains of the colouring substance on the serviette using a palette-knife and put these into a mortar.
Mix with half their weight of butter, strain through a sieve or tammy, and put aside to cool.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: VARIOUS CULLISES
yield: Serves as a refining principle in certain fish sauces.
introduction: This cullis is prepared just in time for dishing up.
ingredients: Creamy parts and spawn of common and spiny lobsters
0.25 pint (118 ml) rich cream per 1 lb (454 g) of remains
notes: Finely pound shrimp and crayfish shells.
Combine with these the available creamy parts and spawn of the common and spiny lobsters.
Add 0.25 pint (118 ml) of rich cream per 1 lb (454 g) of the above remains.
Strain, first through a fine sieve and then through a tammy.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: SHRIMP BUTTER
instructions: Finely pound any available shrimp remains.
Add to these their weight of butter.
Strain through a tammy, place in a bowl, and put aside in the cool.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: SHALLOT BUTTER
yield: Accentuates the savour of certain sauces, such as Bercy, Ravigote, &c. (Recipe 139, 129)
instructions: Put the roughly minced shallots in the corner of a clean towel and wash them quickly in boiling water.
Cool, and press them heavily.
Then pound them finely with their own weight of fresh butter and strain through a tammy.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: CRAYFISH BUTTER
ingredients: Remains and shells of crayfish cooked in Mirepoix
instructions: Pound, very finely, the remains and shells of crayfish cooked in Mirepoix.
Add their weight of butter.
Strain through a fine sieve, and again through a tammy, to avoid the presence of any shell particles. This latter precaution applies to all shell-fish butters.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: TARRAGON BUTTER
instructions: Quickly scald and cool the fresh tarragon.
Drain, press in a towel, and pound in a mortar.
Add the butter, strain through a tammy, and put aside in the cool if it is not to be used immediately.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: LOBSTER BUTTER
ingredients: Spawn, shell, and creamy parts of lobster
instructions: Reduce to a paste in the mortar the spawn, shell, and creamy parts of lobster.
Add their equal in weight of butter and strain through a tammy.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: BUTTER A LA MAÎTRE D’HÔTEL
yield: Serve with grills in general.
instructions: First manie and then soften the butter into a cream.
Add the chopped parsley, a little salt and pepper, and a few drops of lemon-juice.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: MANIED BUTTER
introduction: This butter is made immediately before the time of dishing up and is used for quick liaisons like Matelotes, &c.
notes: Mix the butter and sifted flour until perfectly combined.
The sauce to which manied butter has been added should not boil if this can possibly be avoided, as it would thereby acquire a very disagreeable taste of raw flour.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: MELTED BUTTER
introduction: This preparation, which is used principally as a fish sauce, should consist of butter, only just melted, and combined with a little table-salt and a few drops of lemon-juice. It should therefore be prepared only at the last minute; for, should it wait and be allowed to clarify, besides losing its flavour it will be found to disagree with certain people.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: BUTTER A LA MEUNIÈRE
introduction: This butter is proper to fish “à la Meunière” and is always served on the fish.
notes: Put the necessary quantity of butter into a frying-pan and cook it gently until it has acquired a golden tint and exudes a slight smell of nut.
Add a few drops of lemon-juice.
Pour on the fish under treatment, which should have been previously sprinkled with concassed parsley.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: MONTPELLIER BUTTER
yield: Used to deck large fish, such as salmon and trout, but also for smaller pieces and slices.
ingredients: 6 oz (170 g) total mixed herbs (equal parts watercress leaves, parsley, chervil, chives, tarragon)
instructions: Put the mixed herbs, chopped shallots, and spinach leaves into a saucepan containing boiling water. Boil for two minutes.
Drain, cool, and press in a towel to expel water.
Pound in a mortar with the pressed capers, gherkins, garlic clove, and washed anchovy fillets.
Mix this paste with the butter.
Then add the yolks of three boiled eggs and two raw eggs.
Finally pour in the oil by degrees.
Strain through a fine sieve or through a tammy.
Put the butter into a basin and stir it well with a wooden spoon so as to make it smooth.
Season with table-salt and a little cayenne.
notes: When this butter is specially prepared to form a coat on fish, the oil and the egg yolks are omitted and only butter is used.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: BLACK BUTTER
notes: Put the necessary amount of butter into a frying-pan and cook it until it has assumed a brown colour and begins to smoke.
At this moment, add a large pinch of concassed parsley leaves and spread it immediately over the object to be treated.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: HAZEL-NUT BUTTER
ingredients: A few drops of cold water
instructions: Put the shelled hazel-nuts in the front of the oven for a moment to slightly grill their skins and make them easily removable.
Crush the nuts in a mortar until they form a paste, adding a few drops of cold water to prevent their producing any oil.
Add their equivalent in weight of butter and rub through a tammy.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: PISTACHIO BUTTER
instructions: Put the pistachios into boiling water and keep them on the side of the fire until the peel may be easily removed.
Drain, cool in cold water, and clean the pistachios.
Finely pound them while moistening with a few drops of water.
Add the butter and pass through a tammy.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: PRINTANIER BUTTER
introduction: These butters are made from all early-season vegetables, such as carrots, French beans, peas, and asparagus heads.
notes: For green vegetables: Cook quickly in boiling, salted water, drain, dry, pound with their weight of butter, and rub through a tammy.
For carrots: Mince and cook with consommé, sugar, and butter until the diluent is quite reduced. After cooling, they are pounded with their own weight of butter and rubbed through a tammy.
section_path: Compound Butters for Grills and for the Completion of Sauces

title: ORDINARY ASPICS
yield: Four Quarts (3.8 L)

ingredients.title: Stock
content: 4 lbs (1.8 kg) of strung knuckle of veal
3 lbs (1.4 kg) of strung knuckle of beef
3 lbs (1.4 kg) of veal bones, well broken up
3 calf’s feet, boned and blanched
0.5 lb (227 g) of fresh pork rind, well blanched and with fat removed
8 quarts (7.6 L) of cold water
1 oz (28 g) of salt
0.5 lb (227 g) of carrots
6 oz (170 g) of onions
2 oz (57 g) of leeks
1 stick of celery
1 large faggot

ingredients.title: Clarification
content: A few leaves of gelatine (optional, if needed for firmness)
2 lbs (907 g) of lean beef, minced then pounded
1 egg white
A little chervil and tarragon
A few drops of lemon-juice

ingredients.title: Flavouring (per quart of aspic)
content: 0.2 pint (95 ml) of liqueur wine (Sherry, Marsala, Madeira, etc.)
OR 0.25 pint (118 ml) of other wine (champagne, hock, etc.)

instructions.title: Stock Preparation
content: Put the meats in a very clean and well-tinned stockpot or stewpan. Add the cold water, boil, and skim. (Recipe 1)
Having well skimmed the stock, add the salt, put it on the side of the fire, and let it boil gently for four hours.
Remove the meat, taking care not to disturb the stock.
Carefully remove the fat, and garnish with the carrots, onions, leeks, celery, and a large faggot.
Put the whole back on to the fire and cook gently for a further two hours.
Strain through a sieve into a very clean basin and leave to cool.

instructions.title: Clarification of Aspic
content: When the stock has cooled, remove the grease that has formed on its surface.
Pour the stock off gently into a stewpan of convenient size, preventing the deposit at the bottom of the basin from mixing with the clear liquor.
Test the consistence of the aspic. If it is not firm enough, add a few leaves of gelatine steeped in cold water, being careful not to overdo the quantity.
Add to the stock the lean beef (pounded with the egg white), a little chervil and tarragon, and a few drops of lemon-juice.
Place the saucepan on an open fire, stir its contents with a spatula until the liquid begins to boil.
Remove it from the fire, and place it on the side of the stove, where it may boil gently for half an hour.
Take the saucepan off the fire and remove what little grease has formed on the aspic while cooking.
Strain through a serviette stretched and fastened across the legs of an overturned stool. Repeat the straining process until the aspic becomes quite transparent.

instructions.title: Flavouring the Aspic
content: Allow the aspic to become quite tepid.
Add the choice wine according to the quantities specified. The wine used should be very clear, free from any deposit, and as perfect as possible in taste.

title: CHICKEN ASPIC
ingredients: 4 lbs (1.8 kg) of strung knuckle of veal
3 lbs (1.4 kg) of strung knuckle of beef
3 lbs (1.4 kg) of veal bones, well broken up
0.5 lb (227 g) of fresh pork rind, well blanched and with fat removed
2 oven-browned hens, or their equivalent in weight of roasted fowl carcases
For clarification: Roasted-fowl carcases, well freed from fat
instructions: Prepare the stock with the hens and giblets in the same manner as for ordinary aspic. (Recipe 158)

The clarification follows the same rules as that of the ordinary aspic, except that a few roasted-fowl carcases, previously well freed from fat, are added to the clarification ingredients. (Recipe 158)
notes: In the case of this particularly delicate aspic, it is more than ever necessary not to overdo the amount of gelatine. It should be easily soluble to the palate in order to be perfect.

title: GAME ASPIC
ingredients: Game meats (deer, roebuck, doe, hare, or wild rabbit, previously browned in the oven) to substitute for beef
A few old specimens of feathered game (partridges or pheasants)
For clarification: Meat of the specific game for a defined flavor (e.g., partridge, pheasant, hazel-hen), or available ground game and roast carcases of feathered game for a general flavor
A small quantity of old brandy (optional)
instructions: Prepare this aspic stock in exactly the same way as that of ordinary aspic, substituting the browned game for the beef. (Recipe 158)

The clarification changes according to the different flavours to be given to the aspic. If it is not necessary to give it a special characteristic, prepare it with the meat of that ground game which happens to be most available, adding roast carcases of feathered game.
If the aspic is to have a well-defined flavour, the meat used for the clarification should be that producing the flavour in question (i.e., partridge, pheasant, etc.).
If desired, flavor the aspic with a small quantity of old brandy.
notes: Rather than use an inferior kind of brandy, it is advised to omit it entirely. Without aromatisation the aspic, though imperfect, is passable; but aromatised with bad brandy it is invariably spoilt.

title: FISH ASPIC WITH WHITE WINE
ingredients: Stock ingredients as per fish stock (Recipe 1)
Up to 8 leaves of gelatine per quart (946 ml) of aspic (if necessary)
Fresh or pressed caviare for clarification
Dry champagne, or a good Bordeaux or Burgundy
4 little crayfish à bisque per quart (946 ml) of aspic (optional, for flavor)
instructions: Prepare the stock in precisely the same manner as fish stock, but the stewpan need not be buttered. (Recipe 1)
If the aspic is not required to be quite white, a little saffron may be added.
When the stock is prepared, test its consistence and rectify, if necessary, with gelatine.
Clarify the stock with fresh or pressed caviare, following the same quantities and procedure as for the clarification of fish consommé. (Recipe 4)
For a special flavor, cook crayfish as for bisque, then pound them, and add them to the fish stock ten minutes before straining. (Recipe 11)
Flavor the aspic by adding the chosen wine only when the aspic is already cold and on the point of coagulating.
notes: The less gelatine is used, the better the aspic will be.
The wine used must be of unquestionably good quality.
Adding the wine when the aspic is cold is the only means of preserving all the aroma of the wine.

title: FISH ASPIC WITH RED WINE
yield: Intended for fish such as trout, salmon, carp, or pike.
ingredients: Court-bouillon with red wine, used for cooking fish (Recipe 165)
1 egg white, half-whisked, per quart (946 ml) of stock
A few drops of liquid carmine or vegetable red (optional)
instructions: Take the Court-bouillon with red wine that has been used for cooking the fish. (Recipe 165)
Thoroughly remove all grease from the stock. Pour it off carefully, reduce if necessary, and add the required quantity of gelatine. Test for firmness by cooling small quantities in ice.
For clarification, add the half-whisked egg white to the cold stock.
Put the stock over an open fire and stir with a spatula. As soon as it boils, pour the aspic through a serviette fixed on to the legs of an overturned stool.
Repeat the straining process until the required clearness is obtained.
If the wine has lost its color, add a few drops of liquid carmine or vegetable red to achieve a sombre pink color.
notes: The aspic should not be too firm.
The color of red-wine aspic must never be deeper than a sombre pink.

title: COURT-BOUILLON WITH VINEGAR
yield: Five Quarts (4.7 L). This court-bouillon is principally used for cooking trout and salmon, as well as for various shell-fish.
instructions: Put into a saucepan the water, salt, vinegar, minced carrots and onions, and the parsley, thyme, and bay, gathered into a bunch.
Boil, then allow to simmer for one hour.
Add the peppercorns twelve minutes before the end of the simmering time.
Rub through a tammy, and put aside until wanted.
notes: If the pepper were in for too long a time it would give a bitterness to the preparation. This rule also applies to the formulæ that follow, in which the use of peppercorns is also required.

title: COURT-BOUILLON WITH WHITE WINE
yield: Two Quarts (1.9 L). This preparation is principally used for poaching fresh-water fish.
instructions: Put into a saucepan the white wine, water, salt, minced onions, and the faggot.
Boil, then allow to simmer for thirty minutes.
Add the peppercorns twelve minutes before the end of the simmering time.
Strain through a tammy.
notes: If the court-bouillon has to be reduced the quantity of salt should be proportionately less.

title: COURT-BOUILLON WITH RED WINE
yield: The uses of court-bouillon with red wine are similar to those of the white-wine kind.
ingredients: 1.33 quarts (1.26 L) of excellent red wine
instructions: Put into a saucepan the red wine, water, salt, minced carrots and onions, and the faggot.
Boil, then allow to simmer for thirty minutes.
Add the peppercorns twelve minutes before the end of the simmering time.
Strain through a tammy.
notes: If the court-bouillon is to be reduced, the salt should be less accordingly.
When the court-bouillon with red wine is to constitute an aspic stock, fish fumet with enough gelatine takes the place of the water.

title: PLAIN COURT-BOUILLON
yield: Used with large pieces of turbot and brill.
introduction: The quantity of court-bouillon is determined by the size of the piece which it is to cover.
ingredients: Salt (a little less than 0.5 oz per quart of water)
Milk (0.25 pint per quart of water)
1 thin slice of peeled lemon (per quart of water)
instructions: Immerse the fish in the cold liquor, composed of the water, salt, milk, and lemon.
Very slowly bring the liquor to a boil.
As soon as boiling is reached, move the receptacle to the side of the fire, where the cooking of the fish is completed.
notes: This court-bouillon is never prepared beforehand.

title: SPECIAL COURT-BOUILLON, OR BLANC
yield: Five Quarts (4.7 L). Used for calf’s head or foot, sheep’s trotters, cocks’ kidneys or combs, or vegetables like salsify, cardoon, &c.
introduction: This preparation is a genuine court-bouillon, though it is not used in cooking fish.
ingredients: A little less than 2 oz (57 g) of flour
The juice of 3 lemons or 0.125 pint (59 ml) of good vinegar
instructions: Gradually mix the flour and the water.
Add the salt and the lemon juice, and pass through a strainer.
Set to boil, and stir the mixture the while, in order to prevent the flour from precipitating.
As soon as the boil is reached, immerse the objects to be treated.

title: COOKED MARINADE FOR VENISON
yield: Five Quarts (4.7 L)
ingredients: 1 faggot (including 1 oz parsley stalks, 2 sprigs of rosemary, 2 sprigs of thyme, and 2 bay leaves)
instructions: Heat the oil in a stewpan, add the carrots and onions, and fry them while stirring frequently.
When they begin to brown, add the shallots, the garlic, and the faggot.
Add the vinegar, white wine, and water. Cook this marinade for twenty minutes.
Add the salt, peppercorns, and brown sugar.
Ten minutes afterwards, pass it through a strainer and let it cool before inserting the meats.
notes: In summer the marinade very often decomposes, because of the blood contained by the meat under treatment in it. The only means of averting this is to boil the marinade every two or three days at least.

title: RAW MARINADE FOR BUTCHER’S MEAT OR VENISON
introduction: This marinade is prepared immediately before using and is very active.
notes: Salt and pepper the meat on all sides.
Put the meat in a receptacle just large enough to hold it, and lay it on a litter of aromatics (carrots, onions, shallots, parsley, thyme, and bay).
Sprinkle the meat copiously with oil and half as much vinegar.
Cover the dish with oil-paper, and put it somewhere in the cool.
Turn the meat over three or four times a day, covering it each time with a layer of vegetables.

This marinade is admirably suited to all butcher’s meat and venison, provided these be not allowed to remain in it for too long a time. The time varies according to the size and quality of the joints, and the taste of the consumer. All that can be said is that three hours should be sufficient to marinade a cutlet or escalope of roebuck, and that for big joints such as saddle or leg the time should not exceed four days.

title: MARINADE FOR MUTTON, ROEBUCK-STYLE
ingredients: 1 faggot (including 1 oz parsley stalks, rosemary, wild thyme, basil, and bay leaves)
instructions: Heat the oil in a stewpan, add the carrots and onions, and fry them while stirring frequently.
When they begin to brown, add the shallots, garlic, juniper berries, and faggot.
Add the vinegar, white wine, and water. Cook this marinade for twenty minutes.
Add the salt, peppercorns, and brown sugar.
Ten minutes afterwards, pass it through a strainer and let it cool before inserting the meats.

title: MARINADE WITH RED WINE FOR MUTTON
introduction: An excellent marinade for mutton which in summer enables one to preserve meat, otherwise perishable, for some days.
ingredients: Slightly increased quantity of minced carrots
Slightly increased quantity of minced onions
1 faggot (including 1 oz parsley stalks, rosemary, wild thyme, basil, and bay leaves)
instructions: Heat the oil in a stewpan, add the carrots and onions, and fry them while stirring frequently.
When they begin to brown, add the shallots, garlic, juniper berries, and faggot.
Add the vinegar and red wine. Cook this marinade for twenty minutes.
Add the salt, peppercorns, and brown sugar.
Ten minutes afterwards, pass it through a strainer and let it cool before inserting the meats.

title: BRINE
yield: Fifty Quarts (47.3 L)
instructions: Put the salt and the water in a tinned copper pan, and put it on an open fire.
When the water boils, throw in a peeled potato. If the potato floats, add water until it begins to sink. If the potato sinks immediately, reduce the liquid until it is able to buoy the tuber up.
At this stage, add the sugar and saltpetre; let them dissolve.
Remove the brine from the fire and allow it to cool.
Pour it into a receptacle of slate, stone, cement, or well-jointed tiles. Place a wooden lattice at the bottom for the meats to rest on.
For large pieces of meat, inoculate them with brine using a special syringe to ensure even salting. Allow eight days for salting a piece of beef over 8-10 lbs (3.6-4.5 kg).
For ox-tongue, trim the cartilage, beat it, and prick it on all sides with a string-needle before immersing. A medium-sized tongue needs about seven days.
notes: Though brine does not turn as easily as the cooked marinades, it would be well, especially in stormy weather, to watch it and occasionally to boil it. As boiling concentrates the brine, a little water should be added each time, and the test of the potato should always be resorted to.

title: ANCHOVIES (FILLETS OF)
introduction: Whether they be for hors d’œuvres or for culinary use, it is always best to have these handy.
notes: Wash and well wipe the anchovies to remove the white powder from their scales.
Neatly trim them to the shape of extended oblongs.
Detach the fillets from the bones by gentle pulling.
Divide each fillet lengthwise into three or four smaller fillets.
Put the smaller fillets into a small narrow dish or a little bowl, and cover them with oil.
The fillets may also be kept whole with a view to rolling them into rings.

title: ANGLAISE (FOR EGG-AND-BREAD-CRUMBING)
introduction: It is well to have this always ready for those dishes which are to be panés à l’anglaise, or as many of the recipes direct: treated à l’anglaise.
ingredients: 1 dessertspoonful (10 ml) of oil per couple of eggs
instructions: Whisk the eggs well with salt, pepper, and oil.

notes.title: Its Uses
content: The solids to be panés à l’anglaise are dipped into the Anglaise preparation, taking care that the latter coats them thoroughly. Whereupon, according to the requirements, they are rolled either in bread-crumbs or in fine raspings.

This combination of egg with bread-crumbs or raspings results in a kind of coat which, at the moment of contact with the hot fat, is immediately converted into a resisting crust. In croquettes this crust checks the escape, into the fat, of the substances it encloses.
A solid prepared à l’anglaise and cooked in fat should always be put into the latter when this is very hot, so as to ensure the instantaneous solidification of the egg and bread-crumbs.

notes.title: N.B.
content: Objects to be treated à l’anglaise are generally rolled in flour before being immersed in the anglaise, for the flour helps the foregoing to adhere to the object. The crust formed over the solid thus acquires a density which is indispensable.

title: AROMATICS
introduction: Aromatics play a very prominent part in cookery, and their combination with the condiments constitutes, as Grimod de la Reynière said, “the hidden soul of cooking.” Their real object, in fact, is to throw the savour of dishes into relief, to intensify that savour, and to give each culinary preparation its particular stamp.
They are all derived from the vegetable kingdom; but, while some are used dry, others are used fresh.

notes.title: Dry Aromatics (Permanent Kitchen Stock)
content: sage, basil, rosemary, sweet marjoram, thyme, and bay
Also: cinnamon, ginger, juniper-berries, nutmeg, cloves, mace, and vanilla

notes.title: Fresh Aromatics
content: parsley, chervil, tarragon, pimpernel, and common savory
Also: bits of common- and Seville-orange rind and zests of lemon rind

title: SEASONING AND CONDIMENTS
introduction: Seasonings are divided into several classes, which comprise:

notes.title: Saline seasonings
content: Salt, spiced salt, saltpetre.

notes.title: Acid seasonings
content: Plain vinegar, or the same aromatised with tarragon; verjuice, lemon juice, and common- or Seville-orange juices.

notes.title: Hot seasonings
content: Peppercorns, ground or concassed pepper, or mignonette; paprika, curry, cayenne, and compound spices.

notes.title: Saccharine seasonings
content: Sugar and honey.

notes.title: The pungents
content: Onions, shallots, garlic, chives, and horseradish.

notes.title: Hot condiments
content: Mustard, gherkins, capers, English sauces, such as Worcester, Harvey, Ketchup, Escoffier’s sauces, &c.; the wines used in reductions and braisings; the finishing elements of sauces and soups.

notes.title: Fatty substances
content: Most animal fats, butter, vegetable greases (edible oils and cocoanut butter).

notes.title: Remarks
content: In cookery it should be borne in mind that both excellence and eatableness depend entirely upon a judicious use and a rational blending of the aromatics, seasonings, and condiments. And, according as the latter have been used and apportioned, their action will be either beneficial or injurious to the health of the consumer. In the matter of seasoning there can be no question of approximation or half measures; the quantities must be exact, allowing only of slight elasticity in respect of the various tastes to be satisfied.

title: CLARIFIED BUTTER
introduction: A certain quantity of clarified butter should always be kept ready and handy.
notes: Put 1 lb (454 g) of butter to melt in a saucepan large enough to hold twice that amount.
Place the saucepan on the side of the fire, over moderate heat.
Remove all the scum which rises to the surface.
When the butter looks quite clear and all foreign substances have dropped to the bottom, put the liquid carefully away and strain it through muslin.

title: FAGGOTS (BOUQUETS GARNIS)
yield: 1 ounce (28 g) faggot
introduction: The name “faggot” is given to those little bunches of aromatics.
ingredients: 0.8 oz (22.7 g) of parsley stalks and roots
instructions: Put the various aromatics neatly together so that no sprig of the one sticks out beyond the others, and string them together properly.

title: CHERVIL
notes: Chopped Chervil: Clean the chervil and remove the stalks; wash, dry it well while tossing it, then chop it finely and put it aside on a plate in the cool, if it is not for immediate use.

Concassed Chervil: Proceed as above, except that, instead of chopping it, compress it between the fingers and slice it after the manner of a chaff-cutter. Concassed and chopped chervil are, if possible, only prepared at the last moment.

Chervil Pluches: The pluches are the serrated portions only of the leaves, which are torn away to show no trace of the veinings. They are immersed in water, and at the last moment withdrawn, so as to be added, raw, to either soups or boiling consommés.

title: RASPINGS
notes: Golden raspings are obtained by pounding and passing through a fine sieve bread-crusts which have been previously well dried in the oven.
White raspings are similarly prepared, except that very dry, white crumb is used.

title: PEELED, CHANNELLED, AND ZESTED LEMONS
introduction: Lemons are greatly used in cookery, as dish and comestible garnish.
notes: Peeled: When a whole lemon is used for marinades or 'blancs', peel it to the pulp, removing the peel and all of the underlying white. The lemon is then cut into slices.

Zested: Flatten the removed rind, inside uppermost, and with a very sharp and flexible knife, remove all the white. Slice the remaining peel (zest) into strips about one inch (2.5 cm) wide, and cut these laterally in fine julienne-fashion. Scald the resulting bits for five minutes, cool, and drain them. Zest may also be finely chopped.

Channelled: Using a channel knife, excise parallel ribbons from the surface of the rind. A lemon channelled in this way is cut in two, lengthwise, its ends removed, and the two halves are cut laterally into thin, regular slices to look like serrated half-discs.
For Garnish: The simplest way is to cut the lemon through the centre, after having trimmed the two ends quite straight, and then to remove the rind roughly from the edge.

For whatever purpose the lemon be intended, it should be, as far as possible, only prepared at the last moment. If it must be prepared beforehand, it would be well to keep it in a bowl of fresh water.

title: SHALLOTS
notes: Chopped Shallots: Clean the shallots and, with a very sharp knife, cut them lengthwise into thin slices, letting them cling together at the root. Turn them half round and proceed in the same way at right angles. Finally, cut them laterally to produce very fine and regular, small cubes.
Ciseled Shallots: These are merely laterally sliced shallots, resulting in a series of thin, regular discs.
Ciseled or chopped shallots should, when possible, only be prepared when required; if, however, they must be treated in advance, they should be kept somewhere in the cool until wanted.

title: SPICES
introduction: Strictly speaking, spices include cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, mace; and the many varieties of peppers and pimenta, cayenne, paprika, &c. These various condiments need only be kept dry in air-tight boxes.

But there is another kind of preparation, in cookery, to which the name of spice or all-spice is more especially given. The following is a recipe for the spice in question, which would be found useful if it had to be prepared at a moment’s notice:
ingredients: 5 oz (142 g) of bay leaves, very dry
3 oz (85 g) of thyme (half wild, if possible), very dry
3 oz (85 g) of coriander, very dry
4 oz (113 g) of cinnamon, very dry
6 oz (170 g) of nutmeg, very dry
4 oz (113 g) of cloves, very dry
3 oz (85 g) of ginger-root, very dry
3 oz (85 g) of mace, very dry
10 oz (283 g) of mixed pepper (half black and half white), very dry
1 oz (28 g) of cayenne, very dry
instructions: Put all these ingredients into a mortar and pound them until they are all able to pass through a very fine sieve.
Put the resulting powder into an air-tight box, which must be kept dry.
notes: Before being used, this spice is generally mixed with salt. (Recipe 188)

title: FLOUR
introduction: For whatever use the flour is intended, it is always best to sift it. This is more particularly necessary in the case of flour used for coating objects to be fried; for the latter, being first dipped into milk, must of necessity let a few drops of that liquid fall into the flour they are rolled in. Lumps would therefore form, which might adhere to the objects to be fried if the flour were not sifted.

title: HERB JUICE
introduction: This is to finish or intensify certain preparations.
instructions: Throw equal quantities of parsley, chervil, tarragon and chive leaves into a small saucepan of boiling water.
Set to boil for two minutes, drain, and cool.
Press the herbs in a towel, twisting the latter.
Pound very finely, and extract the juice from the resulting paste by twisting a strong towel round it.
Keep this juice in the cool.

title: BREAD-CRUMBS
notes: Thoroughly rub some stale, well-broken-up bread-crumb in a closed towel.
Pass it through a fine sieve or colander, according as to whether it is required very fine or not.
Put it aside in a convenient receptacle.

title: CHOPPED ONION
notes: Cut the onion finely, like the shallots.
If it is to be minced even finer, it should be freed of its pungent juice to prevent blackening.
To do this, put the chopped onion in the corner of a towel, pour plenty of cold water over it, and twist the towel to express the water. By this means the onion remains quite white.

title: TURNED OR STONED OLIVES
notes: Using a special stoning instrument or the point of a small knife, cut the fruit spirally from the stone.
Keep the olives in slightly salted water.

title: PARSLEY
notes: Chopped Parsley: If parsley is properly chopped, no juice should be produced. If the operation is performed badly, expressing juice, wash the choppings in fresh water and press in a towel to expel the water.
Concassed Parsley: This is roughly chopped parsley. When used, it should be added a few moments before serving to undergo a slight cooking process.
Parsley Sprays: Used for garnishing. Use the curled-leaf kind, after removing the long stalks. Keep the sprays in fresh water until required.

Fried Parsley: Consists of sprays, well drained of water, immersed for an instant in very hot fat. The moment it is fried, carefully drain it, salt it, and place it in a clean towel to remove superfluous grease. It is used to dress fried viands.

Parsley, when quite fresh and used in moderation, is an excellent thing; but, should it have remained too long in the heat, it becomes quite insufferable. It is wiser to discard it entirely than to use it when not fresh.

title: SALT
introduction: Two kinds of salt are used in cooking, viz., grey, or sea-salt, and rock-salt.
notes: Grey-salt: Used more especially for Brines and in the preparation of ices. For roasts and grills, it is crushed with a roller, without being pounded, so every grain is perceptible. This salt, in melting, imparts a supplementary flavour.

Rock-salt: Found as cooking and table-salt. If using cooking salt, the required quantity should be dried, pounded in the mortar, passed through a fine sieve, and then put aside in a dry place. Even table-salt sometimes needs drying and sifting.
Spiced Salt: This is obtained from a mixture of 1 lb (454 g) of table salt with 3.5 oz (99 g) of spices. (Recipe 181). This salt should be kept in a very dry place.

title: VARIOUS PANADAS FOR STUFFINGS
introduction: Panadas are those preparations which go to make the leason of forcemeats and which ensure their proper consistence when they are cooked. They are not necessary to every forcemeat; for the mousseline kind, which are the finest and lightest, do not require them.

Nevertheless, they are useful for varying the taste and the uses of forcemeats, and I thought it advisable to introduce them here. The reader will thus be able to use either forcemeats with a panada base or mousseline forcemeats; in accordance with the requirements and his resources.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: A. BREAD PANADA
ingredients: 0.5 lb (227 g) of the crumb of bread
instructions: Put the bread crumb and salt into the boiling milk.
When the crumb has absorbed all the milk, place the saucepan over a brisk fire and stir with a spatula until the paste has become so thick as not to cling any longer to the end of the spatula.
Turn the contents of the saucepan into a buttered platter, and lightly butter the surface of the panada to avoid its drying while it cools.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: B. FLOUR PANADA
instructions: Put the water, a little salt, and the butter into a small saucepan.
When the liquid boils, add the sifted flour, stirring the while over a brisk fire until it reaches the consistence where it no longer clings to the spatula.
Cool as in the preceding case. (Recipe 190)
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: C. FRANGIPAN PANADA
ingredients: A little salt, pepper, and nutmeg
instructions: Put the sifted flour, egg yolks, salt, pepper, and nutmeg into a stewpan.
Add the melted butter by degrees and dilute with the boiled milk.
Pass through a strainer, stir over the fire until the boil is reached.
Set to cook for five minutes while gently wielding the whisk, and cool as in the preceding cases. (Recipe 190, 191)
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: CHICKEN FORCEMEAT WITH PANADA AND BUTTER
ingredients: 1 lb (454 g) of chicken-meat, tendons removed
0.5 lb (227 g) of very cold Bread Panada (Recipe 190)
instructions: Cut the chicken-meat into cubes, pound it, and add the salt, pepper, and nutmeg.
When the meat is well pounded, remove it from the mortar.
Place the cold panada in the mortar and pound it finely. (Recipe 190)
Add the butter, taking care that the two ingredients mix thoroughly.
Put in the chicken-meat, and wield the pestle vigorously until the whole mass is completely mixed.
Finally, add consecutively the whole eggs and the egg yolks, stirring incessantly and ensuring each egg is fully incorporated before adding the next.
Rub through a sieve, put the forcemeat into a basin, and smooth it with a wooden spoon.
Test the forcemeat by poaching a small portion in salted, boiling water to rectify seasoning and consistence. If too light, add a little white of egg; if too stiff, add a little softened butter.
notes: By substituting for chicken veal, game, or fish, &c., any kind of forcemeat may be made; for the quantities of the other ingredients remain the same whatever the basic meat may be.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: CHICKEN FORCEMEAT WITH PANADA AND CREAM (FOR FINE QUENELLES)
ingredients: 1 lb (454 g) of chicken-meat, tendons removed
2 oz (57 g) of white of egg
instructions: Finely pound the chicken-meat with the salt, pepper and nutmeg.
When the meat has been reduced to a fine paste, add, very gradually, the white of egg.
Finish with the Frangipan panada, and work vigorously with the pestle until amalgamated. (Recipe 192)
Strain through a fine sieve, put the forcemeat into a vegetable-pan, and place it on ice for a good hour.
Stir the forcemeat on the ice for a few seconds with a wooden spoon, then add, in small quantities, the raw cream.
Complete the preparation by adding the whipped cream.
Test as directed in the preceding recipe (Recipe 193), and add a little white of egg if it be too light, and a little cream if it be too stiff.
notes: This forcemeat may be prepared from all butcher’s meats, game, or fish.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: FINE CHICKEN FORCEMEAT OR “MOUSSELINE”
ingredients: 1 lb (454 g) of chicken-meat, tendons removed
1 pint (473 ml) of thick, fresh cream
instructions: Trim and cut the chicken-meat into cubes. Season with salt, pepper, and nutmeg.
Finely pound, and, when it is reduced to a paste, gradually add the whites of two eggs, vigorously working with the pestle.
Strain through a fine sieve, put the forcemeat into a vegetable-pan, and stir it for a moment with a wooden spoon.
Combine with it, gradually, the thick, fresh cream, working with great caution and keeping the receptacle on ice.

notes.title: Remarks Relative to Mousseline Forcemeat
content: This, like the preceding forcemeats, may be prepared from any kind of meat. The addition of the white of egg is not essential if the meats used already possess a certain quantity of albumen; but without the white of egg the forcemeat absorbs much less cream.

This forcemeat is particularly suited to preparations with a shell-fish base. Incomparably delicate results are obtained by the process, while it also furnishes ideal quenelles for the purpose of garnishing soup. In a word, it may be said of mousseline forcemeat that, whereas it can replace all other kinds, none of these can replace it.

notes.title: N.B.
content: Mousseline forcemeats of all kinds, with meat, poultry, game, fish, or shell-fish, may be made according to the principles and quantities given above.

section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: PORK FORCEMEAT FOR DIVERS USES
yield: Used for ordinary pies and terrines. Strictly speaking, it is “sausage-meat.”
ingredients: 2 lbs (907 g) of fillet of pork, tendons removed
2 lbs (907 g) of fresh, fat bacon
instructions: Cut the fillet of pork and fresh, fat bacon into large cubes.
Season with spiced salt. (Recipe 188)
Chop the fillet and bacon up, together or separately, then pound them finely in the mortar.
Finish with the eggs and brandy.
notes: The inclusion of eggs in this forcemeat really only obtains when it is used to stuff joints that are to be braised, such as stuffed breast of veal; or in the case of pies and terrines. The addition of the egg in these cases prevents the grease from melting too quickly, and thus averts the drying of the forcemeat.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: FORCEMEAT FOR GALANTINES, PIES AND TERRINES
ingredients: 1 lb (454 g) of fillet of veal, tendons removed
1 lb (454 g) of fillet of pork, tendons removed
2 lbs (907 g) of fresh, fat bacon
instructions: Cut the veal, pork, and bacon into cubes.
Season with spiced salt, chop the three ingredients together or apart, and then finely pound them.
Finish with the eggs and burnt brandy.
Strain through a sieve, and place in a basin.

When about to serve, add to it a little fumet corresponding with the meat that is to constitute the dish. For terrines, pies, and galantines of game, one-quarter or one-fifth of the forcemeat’s weight of gratin stuffing is added.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: VEAL FORCEMEAT WITH FAT OR GODIVEAU
ingredients: 1 lb (454 g) of fillet of veal, tendons removed
2 lbs (907 g) of very dry fat of kidneys of beef
14 oz (397 g) of very clean ice (in small pieces) or iced water
instructions: Cut the veal into cubes. Pare the beef fat by detaching skin and filaments.
Chop them separately, then combine and pound them in the mortar.
Season with salt, pepper, and nutmeg, and pound until the veal and fat become a homogeneous mass.
Add the eggs consecutively, at intervals of a few minutes, without ceasing to pound, ensuring each egg is mixed in before adding the next.
Spread the forcemeat on a dish, and put it on ice until the next day.
The next day, pound once more, and add the ice or iced water little by little.
Poach a small portion in boiling water to test its consistence. If too firm, add more ice; if too flimsy, add a little white of an egg.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: VEAL FORCEMEAT WITH FAT AND CREAM
ingredients: 1 lb (454 g) of very white fillet of veal, tendons removed
1 lb (454 g) of the fat of pared kidney of beef
instructions: Chop the veal and the beef fat finely and separately.
Combine them in the mortar, and pound until they form a fine and even paste.
Season with salt, pepper, and nutmeg.
Add consecutively the whole eggs and egg yolks, as in the preceding recipe. (Recipe 198)
Strain through a sieve, spread the forcemeat on a dish, and keep it on ice until the next day.
The next day, pound the forcemeat again for a few minutes, and add to it, little by little, the cream.
Test as before, and rectify if necessary by adding cream or thickening with the white of an egg.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: CHICKEN FORCEMEAT FOR GALANTINES, PIES AND TERRINES
introduction: The exact weight of chicken-meat used as the base of this forcemeat determines the quantities of its other ingredients. Thus the weight of meat afforded by a fowl weighing four lbs is estimated at twenty oz after deducting the fillets which are always reserved.
instructions: Chop up, either together or apart, the chicken-meat, the veal, the pork, and the bacon.
Put all these into the mortar, pound them very finely with the seasoning.
Add the eggs consecutively, and, last of all, pour in the brandy.
notes: 1. The quantity of spiced salt varies according as to whether the atmosphere be dry or damp.
2. According to the purpose of the forcemeat, one may add a little raw trimmings of foie gras, not exceeding one-fifth of the forcemeat in weight.
3. As a rule, forcemeat should always be rubbed through a sieve so as to ensure its being fine and even.
4. Chicken forcemeat may always be completed with 2 or 3 oz (57-85 g) of chopped truffles per lb (454 g) of its volume.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: GAME FORCEMEAT FOR PIES AND TERRINES
introduction: This follows the same principles as the chicken forcemeat, i.e., the weight of the game-meat determines the quantities of the other ingredients. The proportions, procedure, and appended remarks are the same as for chicken forcemeat. (Recipe 200)
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: GRATIN FORCEMEAT FOR ORDINARY HOT, RAISED PIES
ingredients: 0.5 lb (227 g) of fresh, fat bacon
0.5 lb (227 g) of fillet of veal
0.5 lb (227 g) of pale, calf’s liver
1 oz (28 g) of truffle parings (raw if possible)
0.33 pint (156 ml) of cold, reduced Espagnole
instructions: In a sautépan with very hot butter, quickly brown the bacon cut into large cubes, then drain on a dish.
In the same butter, quickly brown the veal cut like the bacon, and drain.
Rapidly brown the calf’s liver, also cut into large cubes.
Return the veal and bacon to the sautépan with the liver. Add salt, pepper, mushroom parings, truffle parings, shallots, thyme, and bay. Put on the fire for two minutes.
Drain the bacon, veal, and liver, and put the gravy aside.
Swill the sautépan with the Madeira.
Pound the bacon, veal, and liver quickly and finely, while adding consecutively 6 oz (170 g) of butter, the egg yolks, the reserved gravy, the cold Espagnole, and the Madeira.
Strain through a sieve, place in a tureen, and smooth with a wooden spoon.
notes: To make a gratin forcemeat with game, substitute for the veal that game-meat which may happen to be required.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: PIKE FORCEMEAT FOR QUENELLES A LA LYONNAISE
introduction: Forcemeats prepared with the flesh of the pike are extremely delicate. Subject to circumstances, they may be prepared according to any one of the three formulæ (Recipe 193, 194, 195). There is another excellent method specially used for the preparation of pike forcemeat à la Lyonnaise.
ingredients: 1 lb (454 g) of the meat of a pike, without skin or bones
0.5 lb (227 g) of melted beef-fat (or half beef-fat and half beef-marrow/butter)
instructions: Pound the pike meat in a mortar.
Combine with the stiff frangipan, season with salt and nutmeg, pass through a sieve, and return to the mortar.
Vigorously work the forcemeat to make it cohere.
Gradually add the melted beef-fat (or fat/marrow/butter mixture).
When the forcemeat is very fine and smooth, withdraw it from the mortar and place it in a bowl surrounded with ice until wanted.
section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: SPECIAL STUFFINGS FOR FISH
introduction: These preparations are used to stuff fish such as mackerel, herring, shad, &c., lending a condimentary touch that makes them more agreeable and digestible.

notes.title: First Method
content: ingredients: 4 oz (113 g) of raw, chopped milt 2 oz (57 g) of bread-crumb, steeped in milk and pressed 1.5 oz (43 g) of mixed fine herbs (chives, parsley, chervil, shallots, sweet basil), finely chopped 0.5 garlic clove, crushed 2 whole eggs Salt, pepper, and nutmeg
instructions: Put all ingredients into a bowl and chop them together to mix thoroughly.

notes.title: Second Method
content: ingredients: 4 oz (113 g) of bread-crumb steeped in milk and pressed 0.5 oz (14 g) of onion, slightly cooked in butter, and cold 0.5 oz (14 g) of chopped shallots, slightly cooked in butter, and cold 1 oz (28 g) of raw mushrooms, chopped and pressed 1 tbsp (15 ml) of chopped parsley A piece of garlic the size of a pea, crushed Salt, pepper, and nutmeg 2 eggs
instructions: Mix all ingredients in a bowl as above.

section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: FORCEMEAT BALLS OR QUENELLES
introduction: Whatever be the required size or shape of quenelles there are four ways of making them: (1) By rolling them; (2) by moulding them with a spoon; (3) by forming them with a piping-bag; (4) by moulding them by hand into the shape of a kidney.

notes.title: 1. To roll quenelles
content: This requires a stiff forcemeat. Place one-quarter lb (113 g) of forcemeat on a floured board.
With floured hands, roll the forcemeat into a sausage shape.
Cut the sausage laterally with a floured knife into sections.
Roll each section until its length is thrice its diameter.
Place on a floured tray.

To poach: Gently tilt the balls into a saucepan of boiling, salted water. Cover and keep on the side of the fire until the balls rise to the surface. Remove with a skimmer and place in cold water to cool. Drain on a cloth.

notes.title: 2. To Mould Quenelles with a Spoon
content: Butter a sautépan or tray and let the butter cool.
Use two coffee-spoons. Keep one in hot water.
With the other spoon, take up enough forcemeat to fill it.
Use the hot, wet spoon to smooth the top surface and then scoop the quenelle out, placing it on the buttered tray. The quenelle will be shaped like a large olive.

To poach: Pour enough boiling, salted water over the quenelles to cover them. Leave them to poach until they have swollen and seem soft and firm. Drain and use immediately or cool as previously described.

notes.title: 3. To Form Quenelles with a Piping-bag
content: This is recommended for small, fine soup garnishes. Butter a tray or sautépan.
Put the forcemeat into a piping bag fitted with a grooved or smooth pipe of the desired size.
Squeeze out the quenelles onto the tray, laying them very closely.
To poach: Poach in the same way as spoon-moulded ones.
