To poach Godiveau quenelles: Pipe onto fine, buttered paper on a buttered tray. Push into a very moderate oven for a few minutes until a thin dew of grease glistens on their surfaces. Remove from oven, overturn the tray onto a marble slab, and when nearly cold, carefully remove the paper.

notes.title: 4. To Mould Forcemeat with the Fingers
content: Place a saucepan three-quarters full of boiling, salted water on the edge of a table.

Tie a 2 lb (907 g) weight to a one-yard doubled string, creating a loop. Place the loop around the saucepan handle and draw the string diametrically across the opening, letting the weight pull it taut.
With the left hand, take some forcemeat. With the right index finger, remove a portion from the spoon.
Scrape the finger across the taut string, letting the ball of forcemeat fall into the boiling water.
When all stuffing is moulded, place the saucepan on the fire to complete poaching as in the preceding methods.

section_path: 2. The Various Kinds of Garnishes for Soups, Relevés, and Entrées, Hot or Cold

title: ORDINARY ROYALE
instructions: Put the chervil into the boiling consommé, cover the saucepan, and let infuse away from the fire for twenty minutes.
Pour this infusion over the eggs and yolks, beaten briskly in a basin, and mix with the whisk.
Strain through muslin, and carefully remove the froth that has formed.
Pour into buttered 'Charlotte' moulds (large or small).
Poach in a bain-marie, ensuring the water does not boil.
Allow 35-40 minutes for large moulds, and about 15 minutes for small moulds.
Always let the royale cool in the moulds before turning out.

title: DESLIGNAC OR CREAM ROYALE
instructions: Boil the thin cream and pour it, little by little, over the egg and yolks, well whisked in a basin.
Season with a little salt and nutmeg.
Strain through muslin.
For the poaching, follow the directions given above. (Recipe 206)

title: CHICKEN ROYALE
ingredients: 3 oz (85 g) of cooked white chicken-meat
instructions: Finely pound the cooked white chicken-meat and add the cold Béchamel.
Put this paste in a bowl, season with a little salt and a dash of nutmeg.
Dilute with the cream, and strain through a tammy.
Thicken this preparation with the egg and yolks.
Poach in small or large moulds, in accordance with the procedure already described. (Recipe 206)

title: GAME ROYALE
ingredients: 3 oz (85 g) of cooked meat of the chosen game
3 tbsp (45 ml) of cold Espagnole Sauce
instructions: Finely pound the cooked game meat and add the cold Espagnole Sauce and rich cream in small quantities at a time.
Warm the seasoning with a very little cayenne.
Strain through a tammy, thicken with the egg and yolks, and poach as before. (Recipe 206)

title: FISH ROYALE
ingredients: 4 oz (113 g) of fillet of sole (or other suitable fish)
instructions: Stew the fish, cut into cubes, in butter. Cool.
Pound finely, and add, little by little, the cold Béchamel and cream.
Season with salt and a pinch of nutmeg, and strain through a tammy.
Thicken by means of the egg yolks, and poach in large or small moulds. (Recipe 206)

title: CARROT OR CRÉCY ROYALE
ingredients: 5 oz (142 g) of the red part only of carrots
A few drops of vegetable red
instructions: Stew the carrots gently in butter. Cool.
Crush in a mortar, and gradually add the Béchamel and rich cream.
Season with table-salt and a pinch of castor sugar, and deepen the tint with a few drops of vegetable red.
Strain through a tammy, thicken with the egg and yolks, put into moulds, and poach. (Recipe 206)

title: FRESH PEAS OR ST. GERMAIN ROYALE
ingredients: 0.5 lb (227 g) of fresh, small peas
A few leaves of fresh mint
The liquor the peas were cooked in
instructions: Cook the peas in boiling water with the chervil and mint.
Pass through a sieve.
Dilute the resulting purée with two-fifths of its volume of the cooking liquor and one-fifth of cream.
Add a little sugar and the necessary salt.
Add the egg and yolks, pass through a fine strainer, and poach in well-buttered moulds. (Recipe 206)

title: VARIOUS ROYALES
introduction: Royales may also be made with leeks, celery, &c.
ingredients: 6 or 7 oz (170-198 g) of the chosen vegetable
notes: Finely mince the chosen vegetable.
Stew the same gently and thoroughly in butter, and strain through a tammy.
Add to the resulting purée the Béchamel, cream, eggs, and yolks.
Put into large or small moulds, and poach. (Recipe 206)

In order that these royales may have the required delicacy, I should urge the reader not to exceed the prescribed quantities of eggs and yolks, these being so calculated as to exactly produce the density required.

title: THE DIVIDING-UP OF ROYALES
introduction: When the poaching is done, take the mould or moulds out of water, and leave the royale to cool in them. Do not turn out the moulds whilst the preparation is hot, as it would surely scatter. It only assumes the necessary solidity for being divided up by means of the aggregation and contraction of its various constituents during the cooling process.
notes: If the royale has been poached in small moulds, slightly trim the cylinders of royale, divide them up laterally into discs, and stamp them uniformly with a plain or indented fancy cutter.

If the royale has been poached in large moulds, withdraw it from these, and place it on a serviette; trim the tops, cut into half-inch (1.27 cm) slices, and stamp with small, fancy cutters of different shapes. These little divisions of royale must always be stamped very neatly and quite regularly.

title: CHIFFONADE
introduction: The name “Chiffonade” is given to a mince of sorrel or lettuce, intended as a complement for such soups as “Potage de santé,” “le Germiny,” &c., or various clear consommés like “Julienne.”
notes: First carefully shred the sorrel or lettuce, and remove therefrom all the leaf-ribs.
Carefully wash the leaves, and squeeze the latter tightly between the fingers of the left hand and the table.
Now cut them into fine strips with a sharp knife.
If the chiffonade be intended for a consommé, add it to the latter half an hour before dishing up; it is thus actually cooked in the soup itself.

If, as is most often the case, it be intended for a thick soup, it is better to let it melt well in butter, to moisten it with a little consommé, and to let it boil for ten minutes before adding it to the soup.
Whatever the purpose be for which it is made, chiffonade should always be prepared with very tender sorrel or lettuce.

title: DIRECTIONS FOR SOUP WITH PASTES
notes: Vermicelli and the various Italian pastes should measure about 3 oz (85 g) per quart (946 ml) of consommé. They should first be thrown into boiling, salted water, where they are left to poach for three minutes, whereupon they are drained, cooled, and their cooking is completed in the consommé. The parboiling is necessary to get rid of flour which would otherwise make the consommé cloudy.

Tapioca, sago, salep, &c., should also be apportioned at about 3 oz (85 g) per quart (946 ml). These products need no parboiling; they are merely sprinkled into the boiling consommé while stirring, and are left to cook until the soup is quite clear. The boiling should be gentle, and the scum should be removed as often as it forms. The absolute transparency of the consommé is an infallible sign of its having been completed.
Brazilian, Japanese, and other pearls are used in the same quantities, but they should poach for thirty minutes if required to be very transparent.

title: THREADED EGGS
instructions: Beat up the eggs in a bowl, season with salt and pepper, and strain through a sieve.
Pour the eggs into a fine strainer, hold same over a sautépan containing some boiling consommé.
Shift it about in such wise as to let the egg fall in threads into the boiling liquid beneath, where it will immediately coagulate.
Drain the egg-threads very carefully lest they break.

title: PROFITEROLLES FOR SOUPS
introduction: These consist of little choux about the size of a large hazel-nut, stuffed with some kinds of purée, such as that of foie gras with cream, or of chicken, or of vegetables, &c. Four profiterolles should be allowed for each person.
instructions: Put a few tablespoonfuls of “pâte à choux” without sugar into a piping-bag fitted with a smooth pipe, whose orifice should be about one-quarter inch (0.64 cm) in diameter. (Recipe 2374)
Squeeze out portions of the preparation on to a tray, so as to form balls about the size of a small hazel-nut.
Gild by means of beaten egg applied with a fine brush, and cook in a moderate oven.
Do not take the profiterolles from the oven until they are quite dry.

title: POTATO CROQUETTES
ingredients: 2 lb (907 g) of potatoes, peeled and quartered
instructions: Cook the potatoes quickly in salted water. As soon as they are soft, drain them, and dry them in the front of the oven for a few minutes.
Press the potatoes through a sieve onto a cloth.
Place the purée in a sautépan; season with salt, pepper, and nutmeg; add the butter, and stir over a brisk fire until the purée becomes a consistent paste.
Take off the fire, complete with the egg yolks, mixing well.
Turn the paste out onto a buttered dish in a rather thin layer to cool quickly. Butter the surface to prevent drying.
Take equal portions of this paste (about 1.5 oz or 43 g each) and roll them on a flour-dusted board into the shape of a cork, a ball, or a quoit.
Dip these into an Anglaise and roll in bread-crumbs or raspings, patting the coating on well. (Recipe 174)
Plunge into hot fat and fry until they have acquired a fine, golden colour.

title: DAUPHINE POTATOES
ingredients: 1 lb (454 g) of potato croquette paste (Recipe 219)
6 oz (170 g) of pâte à choux without sugar (Recipe 2374)
instructions: Prepare the potato paste as for croquettes. (Recipe 219)
Add the pâte à choux without sugar and mix the two constituents thoroughly. (Recipe 2374)
Mould in the shape of small cylinders, and treat them à l’Anglaise, like the croquettes. (Recipe 219)

title: DUCHESSE POTATOES
introduction: These are the same as the croquettes, though they are differently treated. (Recipe 219)
notes: Prepare the potato paste as for croquettes. (Recipe 219)
Shape the paste on a floured board into diminutive cottage-loaves, little shuttle-shaped loaves, small quoits, lozenges, or rectangles.
Gild with beaten egg.
If shaped as quoits, rectangles, or lozenges, streak them with a small knife to prevent the gilding from blistering.
Bake in the oven for a few minutes before using them to dress the dishes they accompany.

title: MARQUISE POTATOES
ingredients: 6 oz (170 g) of very red, reduced tomato-purée
instructions: Take 1 lb (454 g) of croquette paste and add the tomato purée. (Recipe 219)
Pour this mixture into a bag fitted with a large, grooved pipe.
Squeeze it out upon a baking-tray in shapes resembling large meringues.
Slightly gild their surfaces with beaten egg, and put them into the oven for a few minutes before using them to dress the dish.

title: ORDINARY OR DRY DUXELLE
introduction: The uses of Duxelle are legion.
ingredients: 1 tbsp (15 ml) of butter and oil mixed
4 tbsp (60 ml) of mushroom stalks and parings, chopped and pressed
instructions: Slightly fry the onions in the butter and oil mixture.
Add the chopped and pressed mushroom stalks and parings.
Stir over a brisk fire until the moisture has completely evaporated.
Season with salt, pepper, and nutmeg, and add the chopped parsley, mixing thoroughly.
Transfer to a bowl, cover with a piece of white, buttered paper, and put aside until wanted.

title: DUXELLE FOR STUFFED VEGETABLES (Tomatoes, Mushrooms, &c.)
ingredients: 3 tbsp (45 ml) of half-glaze sauce with tomato
Crushed garlic the size of a pea
1 tbsp (15 ml) of fine, fresh bread-crumbs (optional)
instructions: Put the dry duxelle into a small stewpan. (Recipe 223)
Add the half-glaze sauce with tomato, crushed garlic, and white wine.
Set to simmer until the required degree of consistence is reached.
A tablespoonful of fine, fresh bread-crumbs may be added to thicken it.

title: DUXELLE FOR GARNISHING SMALL PIES, ONIONS, CUCUMBERS, ETC.
ingredients: 4 tbsp (60 ml) of ordinary pork forcemeat (Recipe 196)
instructions: Combine the dry duxelle with the ordinary pork forcemeat. (Recipe 223, 196)

title: MAINTENON (preparation used in stuffing preparations à la Maintenon)
ingredients: 4 tbsp (60 ml) of minced mushrooms, cooked
instructions: Put the Béchamel and Soubise into a vegetable-pan and reduce to half while stirring over a brisk fire. (Recipe 104)
Thicken, away from the fire, by means of the egg yolks.
Add the minced mushrooms, either cooked in the ordinary way or stewed in butter.

title: MATIGNON
introduction: This preparation serves chiefly for covering certain large joints of butcher’s meat, or fowl, to which it imparts an appropriate flavour.
ingredients: 2 medium carrots (red part only), finely minced
2 sticks of celery (from the heart), finely minced
1 tbsp (15 ml) of raw lean ham, cut paysanne-fashion
instructions: Combine the minced carrots, onions, celery, ham, thyme, and bay leaf.
Stew in butter.
Finally, swill the saucepan with the Madeira.

title: MIREPOIX
introduction: The purpose of Mirepoix in culinary preparations is the same as that of Matignon, but its mode of use is different. (Recipe 227)
Its constituents are the same as those of the Matignon, but instead of being minced they are cut up into more or less fine dice, in accordance with the use for which the preparation is intended.
Instead of the ham, fresh and slightly-salted breast of pork may be used, while both the ham and the bacon may be excluded under certain circumstances.

title: FINE OR BORDELAISE MIREPOIX
introduction: This chiefly serves as an adjunct to crayfish and lobsters and is made in advance.
ingredients: 4 oz (113 g) of the red part only of carrots, diced or chopped
4 oz (113 g) of onion, diced or chopped
1 oz (28 g) of parsley stalks, diced or chopped
instructions: Cut the carrots, onion, and parsley stalks into dice. For a finer Mirepoix, they may be chopped and then thoroughly pressed in a towel to squeeze out their moisture.
Put the ingredients into a small stewpan with the butter and a little powdered thyme and bay.
Stew until all are well cooked.
Turn the preparation out into a small bowl, heap it together, cover it with a piece of white, buttered paper, and put aside until wanted.

title: VARIOUS SALPICONS
introduction: This term stands for a certain preparatory method applied to a series of preparations.

Salpicons are simple or compound. Simple if they only contain one product, such as the meat of a fowl, game, butcher’s meat, foie gras, fish, ham, tongue, mushrooms, truffles, &c. Compound if they consist of two or more suitable ingredients.
The preparatory method consists in cutting the various ingredients into dice.
The series of preparations arises from the many possible combinations of the products, each bearing its own name (e.g., Royal, Financier, Chasseur, Parisien, Montglas, &c.).
Salpicons are always incorporated with a vehicular sauce which is in accordance with their constituents.

title: BATTER FOR VARIOUS FRITTERS
ingredients: 1 tbsp (15 ml) of oil or melted butter
2 egg whites, whisked to a froth
instructions: Put the flour, salt, and oil/butter into a bowl. Add the necessary quantity of lukewarm water.
If the batter is to be used at once, mix the ingredients by turning them over and over without stirring with a spoon to avoid elasticity.
If the batter is prepared beforehand, it may be stirred, as it loses its elasticity when left to stand.
Before using, add the whisked egg whites.

title: BATTER FOR VEGETABLES (Salsify, Celery, &c.)
ingredients: 2 tbsp (30 ml) of oil or melted butter
instructions: Put the flour, salt, and oil/butter into a bowl.
Dilute with the egg and the necessary quantity of cold water.
Keep this batter somewhat thin, do not stir it, and let it rest for a few hours before using.

title: BATTER FOR FRUIT AND FLOWER FRITTERS
ingredients: 2 tbsp (30 ml) of oil or melted butter
2 egg whites, whisked to a froth
instructions: Put the flour, salt, and oil/butter into a bowl.
Dilute gradually with the beer and a little tepid water.
When about to use the batter, mix therewith the whisked egg whites.
notes: Keep this batter thin, if anything, and above all do not stir overmuch.

title: BATTER FOR OVEN-GLAZED FRUIT FRITTERS
instructions: Mix the flour with the oil, salt, eggs (added one after the other), the necessary quantity of water, and the sugar.
Keep this preparation in a lukewarm place to let it ferment.
Stir it with a wooden spoon before using it to immerse the solids.
notes: Batter for fruit fritters may contain a few tablespoonfuls of brandy, in which case an equal quantity of the water must be suppressed.

title: PROVENÇALE (preparation for stuffing cutlets à la Provençale)
ingredients: A crushed piece of garlic as large as a pea
instructions: Put the Béchamel into a vegetable-pan and reduce it until it has become quite dense.
Thicken it with the egg yolks.
Finish it away from the fire with the crushed garlic and grated cheese.

title: CLEAR SOUPS
introduction: Clear soups, of whatever nature the base thereof may be, whether butcher’s meat, poultry, game, fish, shell-fish, or turtle, &c., are made according to one method only. They are always clear consommés to which has been added a slight garnish in keeping with the nature of the consommé.

title: THICK SOUPS
introduction: These are divided into three leading classes as follows:—(1) The Purées, Cullises, or Bisques. (2) Various Veloutés. (3) Various Creams.
notes: Though the three preparations of the first class are practically the same, and, generally speaking, the Cullises and the Bisques may be considered as purées of fowl, game, or shell-fish, it is advisable to distinguish one from another by giving each a special name of its own.

Thus the word Purée is most suitably applied to any preparation with a vegetable base. The term Cullis is best fitted to preparations having either poultry, game, or fish for base, while bisque, in spite of the fact that in former days it was applied indiscriminately to purées of shell-fish, poultry, pigeons, &c., distinctly denotes a purée of shell-fish (either lobster, crayfish, or shrimp, &c.).
In short, it is imperative to avoid all ambiguities and to give everything its proper name, or, at least, that name which identifies it most correctly.

title: PURÉES
introduction: Farinaceous vegetables, such as haricot-beans and lentils, and the floury ones, such as the potato, need no additional thickening ingredient, since the flour or fecula which they contain amply suffices for the leason of their purées.
On the other hand, aqueous vegetables like carrots, pumpkins, turnips, celery, and herbs cannot dispense with a thickening ingredient, as their purées of themselves do not cohere in the least.

notes.title: Cohering or Thickening Elements; their Quantities
content: In order to effect the coherence of vegetable purées, either rice, potato, or bread-crumb cut into dice and fried in butter may be used. The proportion of these per pound (454 g) of vegetables should be respectively 3 oz (85 g), 10 oz (283 g), and 10 oz (283 g).

notes.title: The Dilution of Purées
content: Generally this is done by means of ordinary white consommé, though in certain cases, as, for instance, if the soup is a Lenten one, milk is used.

notes.title: The Finishing
content: When the purées have been strained and brought to the required consistence they should be boiled and stirred. Then they are placed on the side of the fire to simmer for twenty-five or thirty minutes. It is at this stage that they are purified by means of the careful removal of all the scum that forms on their surface. When dishing up complete them, away from the fire, with 3 oz (85 g) of butter per quart (946 ml) of soup, and pass them once more through a strainer.

notes.title: Purée Garnishes
content: These are usually either small fried crusts, small dice of potato fried in butter, a chiffonade, some kind of little brunoise, or, more generally, chervil pluches.

title: CULLISES
introduction: Cullises have for their base either poultry, game, or fish.

notes.title: Thickening Ingredients
content: For fowl, 2 or 3 oz (57-85 g) of rice, or 0.75 pint (355 ml) of poultry velouté per lb (454 g) of fowl.
For game, 3 or 4 oz (85-113 g) of lentils, or 0.75 pint (355 ml) of game Espagnole per lb (454 g) of game.
For fish, a clear panada made up of French bread soaked in boiling salted milk. Use 5 oz (142 g) of bread and 1 good pint (473 ml) of milk per lb (454 g) of fish.

notes.title: Finishing
content: Having strained and made up the Cullises, boil them while stirring (except in the case of fish cullises, which must not boil, and must be served as soon as they are made), then place them in a bain-marie and butter their surfaces lest a skin should form. At the last moment complete them with 2 or 3 oz (57-85 g) of butter per quart (946 ml).

notes.title: Garnish
content: The garnish of poultry or game cullises consists of either small dice of game or fowl-fillets, which should be kept aside for the purpose; a fine julienne of these fillets, or small quenelles made from the latter, raw.
The garnish of fish cullis is generally fish-fillets poached in butter and cut up into small dice or in julienne-fashion.

title: BISQUES
notes: The invariable base of Bisques is shell-fish cooked in mirepoix. (Recipe 228)

Their thickening ingredients are rice, fish velouté, or crusts of bread fried in butter, the proportion being 3 oz (85 g) of rice, 10 oz (283 g) of bread-crusts, or 0.75 pint (355 ml) of fish velouté per lb (454 g) of shell-fish cooked in mirepoix. (Recipe 228)
When the soup is strained, treat it in precisely the same way as the cullises. (Recipe 240)
The garnish consists of small dice of the meat from the shell-fish used. These pieces should have been put aside from the first.

title: THE VELOUTÉS
introduction: These differ from the purées, cullises, and bisques in that their invariable thickening element is a velouté whose preparation is in harmony with the nature of the ingredients of the soup, these being either vegetables, poultry, game, fish, or shell-fish.

notes.title: The Preparation of the Velouté
content: Allow 3.5 oz (99 g) of white roux per quart (946 ml) of the diluent. This diluent should be ordinary consommé for a velouté of vegetables or herbs, chicken consommé for a poultry velouté, or very clear fish fumet for a fish or shell-fish velouté. The procedure is exactly the same as that described under Recipe 25 of the leading sauces.

notes.title: The Apportionment of the Ingredients
content: In general, the quantities of each constituent are in the following proportion:—Velouté, one-half; the purée of the substance which characterises the soup, one-quarter; the consommé used to bring the soup to its proper consistence, one-quarter. In respect of finishing ingredients, use, for thickening, the yolks of 3 eggs and 0.2 pint (95 ml) of cream per quart (946 ml) of soup.

notes.title: Rules Relative to the Preparation
content: If the velouté is to be of lettuce, chicory, celery, or mixed herbs, these ingredients are scalded for five minutes, drained, gently stewed in butter, and added to the prepared velouté in which their cooking is completed.
If carrots, turnips, onions, &c., are to be treated, finely mince them, stew them in butter without allowing them to acquire any colour, and add them to the velouté.
If fowl be the base, cook it in the velouté. This done, withdraw it, remove the meat, finely pound same, and add it to the velouté, which is then rubbed through tammy.
In the case of fish the procedure is the same as for fowl.
For game, roast or sauté the selected piece, bone it, finely pound the meat, and combine the latter with the velouté, which should then be rubbed through tammy.
For shell-fish, cook these in a mirepoix, finely pound them together with the latter, add to the velouté, and pass the whole through tammy.

notes.title: The Completing of Velouté
content: Having passed the soup through tammy, bring it to its proper degree of consistence with the necessary quantity of consommé, boil while stirring, and place in a bain-marie. At the last moment finish the soup with the leason and 2 oz (57 g) of butter per quart (946 ml) of liquid.

notes.title: Garnish for Velouté
content: For vegetables: Chiffonade, fine printaniers, or brunoise.
For fowl and game: The fillets of one or the other, poached and cut into small dice or in julienne-fashion; little quenelles made with the raw fillets, or either fowl or game royales.
For fish: Small dice or fine julienne of fish fillets poached in butter.
For shell-fish: Small dice of cooked shell-fish meat put aside for the purpose.

notes: In certain circumstances these garnishes are increased by means of 3 tbsp (45 ml) of poached rice per quart (946 ml) of the soup.

title: THE CREAMS
introduction: Practically speaking, the preparation of the creams is the same as that of the veloutés, but for the following exceptions:
notes: 1. In all circumstances, clear Béchamel is substituted for velouté.
2. The correct consistence of the soup is got by means of milk instead of consommé.
3. Creams do not require egg-yolk leasons.
4. They are not buttered, but they are finished with 0.2 or 0.4 pint (95 or 189 ml) of fresh cream per quart (946 ml).
Creams allow of the same garnishes as the veloutés. (Recipe 242)

title: SPECIAL SOUPS AND THICKENED CONSOMMÉS
introduction: These are of different kinds, though their preparation remains the same, and they do not lend themselves to the requirements of veloutés or creams. I should quote as types of this class the Ambassador, à l’Américaine, Darblay, Faubonne, &c. The same holds good with thickened consommés, such as “Germiny,” “Coquelin,” &c.

title: VEGETABLE SOUPS
introduction: These soups, of which the “Paysanne” is the radical type, do not demand very great precision in the apportionment of the vegetables of which they are composed; but they need great care and attention, notwithstanding.
The vegetables, in the majority of cases, must undergo a long stewing in butter, an operation the object of which is to expel their vegetable moisture and to saturate them with butter.
In respect of others which have a local character, the vegetables should be cooked with the diluent, without a preparatory stewing.

title: FOREIGN SOUPS
introduction: In the course of Part II. of this work I shall allude to certain soups which have a foreign origin, and whose use, although it may not be general, is yet sufficiently common. If only for the sake of novelty or variety, it is occasionally permissible to poach upon the preserves of foreign nations; but apart from this there exist among the recipes of foreigners many which can but enrich their adopter, besides being generally appreciated.

title: ORDINARY BRAISINGS
introduction: Of all the various culinary operations, braisings are the most expensive and the most difficult. Long and assiduous practice alone can teach the many difficulties that this mode of procedure entails, for it is one which demands extraordinary care and the most constant attention. Over and above the question of care and that of the quality of meat used, there are also these conditions to be fulfilled in order that a good braising may be obtained, namely, that excellent stock should be used in moistening, and that the braising base be well prepared.

notes.title: Meats that are Braised
content: Mutton and beef are braised in the ordinary way. The best for the purpose is that derived from an animal of 3 to 6 years of age in the case of beef, and 1 to 2 years in the case of mutton.

notes.title: The Larding of Meats for Braising
content: Meats like rumps or leg of mutton that are not sufficiently fat are larded with square strips of bacon fat (about 0.5 inch or 1.27 cm thick). These strips are seasoned with pepper, nutmeg, spices, parsley, and marinaded for two hours in brandy. Insert them into the meat equidistantly using larding needles. The proportion of fat to meat should be about 3 oz (85 g) per lb (454 g).

notes.title: To Marinade Braisings
content: Season meats with salt, pepper, and spices. Place them in a receptacle between two litters of aromatics, cover them with white or red 'vin ordinaire' in the proportion of 0.25 pint (118 ml) per lb (454 g) of meat, and leave them to marinade for about six hours, turning them three or four times.

notes.title: The Aromatics or Base of the Braising
content: These are thickly sliced and fried carrots and onions, in the proportion of 1 oz (28 g) per lb (454 g) of meat, one faggot, including one garlic clove and 1.5 oz (43 g) of fresh, blanched bacon-rind.

notes.title: To Fry, Prepare, and Cook Braised Meat
content: Drain the marinaded meat and wipe it dry. Heat clarified fat in a thick saucepan and, when hot, put the meat in to acquire colour on all sides.
Withdraw the meat, cover it with slices of larding-bacon if it is lean, and string it.
Pour the marinade into the braising-pan, and place the meat on a litter of the vegetables the marinade contained. Cover the pan and rapidly reduce the wine to a syrup.
Add sufficient brown stock to cover the meat, set to boil, and then put it in a moderate oven. Cook until a braiding needle may be deeply pricked without any blood being drawn. (First Phase)
Transfer the meat to another clean utensil. Then choose one of the following:

1. For a clear liquor: Strain the liquor over the meat through muslin. Place the pan in the oven to complete cooking, basting from time to time. Thicken the liquor with arrow-root as for an ordinary thickened gravy. (Recipe 41)

2. For a sauce: Reduce the liquor to half before returning to the meat. Restore its volume by means of two-thirds of its quantity of Espagnole sauce and one-third of tomato purée. Complete the cooking in this sauce, basting as before. When cooked, withdraw the meat, strain the sauce, let the grease settle, and carefully remove it. Rectify the sauce's consistency if necessary.

notes.title: The Glazing of Braised Meat
content: Place the cooked meat in the front of the oven, sprinkle it slightly with its cooking liquor, and push it into the oven so this liquor may dry and form a glaze. Repeat this operation eight or ten times.

notes: The explanations on the theory of braising, including the two phases of cooking and the critique of the 'pinçage' method, are lengthy but crucial for understanding the process. The first phase concentrates juices in the center of the meat, while the second phase involves the disaggregation of tissues and the exchange of juices between the meat and the sauce.

title: BRAISING OF WHITE MEATS
introduction: White braisings are made with the neck, the saddle, the loin, the fillets, the fricandeaus, and the sweet-bread of veal, young turkeys and fat pullets, and sometimes, relevés of lamb. The procedure is the same for all these meats; the time of cooking alone varies. The aromatics are the same as those of the brown braisings, but the frying of them is optional. The moistening liquor is brown veal stock. (Recipe 9)
notes: Except for veal sweet-bread, which is always blanched, the meats may be slightly stiffened and browned in butter. This is not essential.
Place them in a utensil just large enough to hold them, with aromatics underneath.
Moisten with a little veal stock, set to boil on a moderate fire, and reduce the stock with the lid on.
When this stock has assumed the consistency of a glaze, add a further similar quantity of fresh stock, and reduce as before.
The third time, moisten the veal until it is half covered, and push the pan into a moderate oven.
Baste constantly while it cooks.
Braised white meat is known to be cooked when, after being deeply pricked, it exudes an absolutely colourless liquid.
White braised meats are generally glazed.

title: POACHINGS
introduction: The best possible definition of a poaching is a boiling that does not boil. The term extends to all slow processes of cooking which involve the use of a liquor, however small.

The unalterable principle is that the poaching liquor must not boil, though it should reach a degree of heat as approximate as possible to boiling-point. Another principle is that large pieces of fish or poultry be set to boil in cold liquor. All other preparations whose mode of cooking is poaching gain by being immersed in liquor which has reached the required temperature beforehand.

notes.title: Poaching Poultry
content: Properly prepare the piece of poultry and truss it. If stuffing, do so before trussing. If larding, rub with lemon and dip the relevant portions in boiling white stock to stiffen the skin.
Place the poultry in a receptacle just large enough to hold it, and moisten with excellent white stock.
Set to boil, skim, put the lid on, and continue the cooking at a low simmer.
The fowl is known to be cooked when, after pricking the thick of the leg close to the 'drumstick', the issuing liquid is white.

notes: The need for a properly sized receptacle is to ensure the piece is wholly immersed and that the resulting sauce is concentrated and flavourful.
The white stock used should be prepared beforehand and be very clear. Cooking the poultry with the raw stock ingredients would result in a savourless sauce as the cooking times do not align.

title: POËLINGS
introduction: Poëlings are, practically speaking, roasts, for the cooking periods of each are the same, except that the former are cooked entirely or almost entirely with butter.

notes.title: Preparation of Poëled Meats
content: Place a layer of raw matignon in the bottom of a deep and thick receptacle. (Recipe 227)
Place the seasoned meat or poultry on the vegetables and sprinkle copiously with melted butter.
Cover the utensil, and push it into a moderately hot oven. Cook gently, like a stew, and frequently sprinkle with melted butter.
When cooked, uncover the utensil so the meat may acquire a fine colour. Then transfer to a dish and keep covered.
Add a sufficient quantity of brown veal stock to the vegetables in the pan. (Recipe 9) Set to boil gently for ten minutes.
Strain through a serviette, carefully remove all grease, and serve the stock in a sauceboat with the meat.

notes.title: Special Poëlings known as 'En Casserole' or 'En Cocotte'
content: These are actual poëlings cooked and served in special earthenware utensils.

'En casserole' preparations are simply cooked in butter, without vegetables. When cooked, the piece is withdrawn, excellent brown veal stock is poured into the utensil, simmered, and skimmed of butter before the piece is returned. (Recipe 9)

'En cocotte' preparations are the same, but the piece is garnished with vegetables (mushrooms, artichoke bottoms, small onions, etc.) which are half-cooked in butter before being added to complete their cooking with the meat.

notes: It is of paramount importance that poëlings not be moistened during cooking, except for feathered game like pheasants, which may have a small quantity of burnt brandy added when nearly cooked.
Do not remove the grease from the vegetables before the moistening stock is added, as the butter contains much of the flavour.

title: THE SAUTÉS
introduction: What characterises the process we call “sauté” is that the object treated is cooked dry—that is to say, solely by means of a fatty substance such as butter, oil, or grease. All products treated in this way must be frizzled—that is to say, they must be put into the fat when it is very hot in order that a hardened coating may form around them which will keep their juices within.

notes.title: Fowl and Game Sautés
content: After frizzling, complete cooking on the stove or in the oven with the lid off, basting with butter like a roast. Withdraw the pieces to swill the utensil, then return them to the sauce or garnish just to warm through.

notes.title: Red Meat Sautés (tournedos, cutlets, etc.)
content: Always effected on the stove in a small quantity of clarified butter. The thinner the piece, the more rapid the frizzling. When blood appears on the raw side, turn it over. When drops of blood appear on the second side, it is cooked.

notes.title: White Meat Sautés (veal, lamb)
content: Must also be frizzled in hot fat, but their cooking must be completed gently on the side of the fire, often with the lid on.

notes.title: Swilling the Utensil
content: After removing the product, remove the grease and pour a condimentary liquid (like wine) into the saucepan. Set to boil to dissolve the solidified gravy, and add this liquid to the prepared sauce or garnish.

title: LARDING BACON FOR ROASTS
introduction: Poultry and game to be roasted ought generally to be partly covered with a large thin slice of larding bacon, except those pieces of game which in special cases are larded.

The object and use of these slices are not only to shield the fillets of fowl and game from the severe heat of the fires but also to prevent these from drying while the legs, which the heat takes much longer to penetrate than the other parts, are cooking. The slices of bacon should therefore completely cover the breasts of fowl and game, and they should be tied on to the latter by means of string.
In some cases roasts of butcher’s meat are covered with layers of veal- or beef-fat, the object of which is similar to that of the bacon prescribed above.

title: SPITTED ROASTS
introduction: The whole theory of roasts on the spit might be condensed as follows:—

In the case of butcher’s meat, calculate the intensity of the heat used according to the piece to be roasted, the latter’s size and quality, and the time it has hung. Experience, however, is the best guide...
The three following rules will be found to cover all the necessary directions for spitted roasts:

1. All red meats containing a large quantity of juice should be properly set, and then, according to their size, made to undergo the action of a fire capable of radiating a very penetrating heat with little or no flame.
2. In the case of white meats, whose cooking should be thorough, the fire ought to be so regulated as to allow the roast to cook and colour simultaneously.
3. With small game the fuel should be wood, but whatever fuel be used the fire ought to be made up in suchwise as to produce more flame than glowing embers.

title: OVEN ROASTS
introduction: The degree of heat used for each roast must be regulated according to the nature and size of the latter after the manner of spitted roasts.

An oven roast, in the first place, should always be placed on a meatstand, and this should be of such a height that at no given moment during the cooking process the meat may come in contact with the juices and fat which have drained from it into the utensil beneath. Failing a proper stand, a spit resting upon the edges of the utensil may be used.

No liquid of any kind, gravy or water, need be put in the baking-pan. The addition of any liquid is rather prejudicial than otherwise, since by producing vapour which hangs over the roast it transforms the latter into a stew.
notes: Whether spitted or in the oven, a roast must always be frequently basted with a fatty substance, but never with any other liquid.

title: THE GRAVY OF ROASTS
notes: The real and most natural gravy for roasts is made from the swilling of the baking- or dripping-pan. To obtain this, neither the utensils nor the gravy ought to have burned.

When a greater quantity is required, prepare a stock beforehand from bones and trimmings of a similar nature to the roast. Place these in a pan with fat and roast them. Transfer to a saucepan, moisten to cover with tepid, salted water, add the swillings of the roasting pan, boil, skim, and cook gently for 3-4 hours. Strain and put aside for swilling.

notes.title: Swilling
content: Having removed the roast, take off a portion of the grease from the pan, and pour into it the required quantity of prepared gravy. Reduce by half, strain, and almost entirely remove grease.

notes: It is a mistake to remove all the grease from, and to clarify, the gravy of roasts. Treated thus they are certainly clearer and more sightly, but a large proportion of their savour is lost, and it should be borne in mind that the gravy of a roast is not a consommé.

title: THE DRESSING AND ACCOMPANIMENTS OF ROASTS
introduction: As a rule, a roast ought not to wait. It ought only to leave the spit or oven in order to be served. All roasts should be placed on very hot dishes, slightly besprinkled with fresh butter, and surrounded by bunches of watercress (this is optional). The gravy is invariably served separately.
Roasts of butcher’s meat and poultry are dished up as simply as possible.
Small roasted game may be dished up on fried slices of bread-crumb masked with gratin stuffing. (Recipe 202)
When lemons accompany a roast, they should be served separately.
The mediæval custom of dishing game with the plumage has been abandoned.
Roast feathered game à l’anglaise is dished up with or without potato chips, and the three adjuncts are gravy, bread-crumbs, and bread-sauce.
In northern countries game roasts are always accompanied either by slightly sugared stewed apples, or by cherry or apricot jam.

notes.title: Fuel for Grills
content: The best is live coal or small pieces of charcoal. It is essential that it produce no smoke.

notes.title: The Bed of Charcoal
content: The arrangement must be regulated according to the size and kind of the products. It should be set in equal layers in the centre, and slightly raised on the sides.

notes.title: The Grill
content: The grill must always be placed over the glowing fuel in advance, and it should be very hot when the objects to be grilled are placed upon it, otherwise they would stick.

title: RED MEAT GRILLS
introduction: I submit as a principle that the golden rule in grills is to strictly observe the correct degree of heat which is proper to each treated object, never forgetting that the larger and richer in nutrition the piece of meat, the quicker and more thorough must be its initial setting.
notes: For large pieces of meat (beef or mutton), the better the quality, the more resisting must be the rissoled coating they receive. The fierceness of the fire should be proportionately abated the moment the initial rissoling has been effected.
For thinner pieces, a quick rissoling of their surfaces over a fierce fire, and a few minutes of subsequent cooking will be all they need.
Before placing meats on the grill, baste them slightly with clarified butter, and repeat this frequently during cooking.
Grilled red meat should always be turned by means of special tongs. Do not pierce the surface.
Cooking is complete when the meat resists pressure from a finger, or when little beads of blood appear upon the rissoled surface.

title: WHITE-MEAT GRILLS
introduction: Superficial rissoling is not as necessary as with red meats. For this kind of grills keep a moderate fire, so that the cooking and colouring of the meat may take place simultaneously.
notes: Baste fairly often with clarified butter while cooking, lest their outsides dry.
They are known to be cooked when the juice issuing from them is quite white.

title: FISH GRILLS
notes: Use a moderate fire and only grill after having copiously sprinkled them with clarified butter or oil. Sprinkle them similarly while cooking.
A grilled fish is cooked when the bones are easily separated from the meat.
Except for fatty fish, always roll fish to be grilled in flour before sprinkling with melted butter. This gives them a golden external crust and keeps them from drying.

title: THE GRILLING OF PRODUCTS COATED WITH BUTTER AND BREAD-CRUMBS
introduction: These grills generally consist of only small objects; they must be effected on a very moderate fire, with the view of enabling them to cook and acquire colour simultaneously. They should also be frequently besprinkled with clarified butter, and turned with care, so as not to break their coating, the object of which is to withhold their contained juices.

title: FRYINGS
introduction: Frying is one of the principal cooking processes. Its procedure is governed by stringent laws and rules which it is best not to break.

Utensils used in frying should be made of copper or other resisting metal; they should be in one piece, oval or round, and sufficiently large and deep to allow, while only half-filled with fat, of the objects being properly affected by the latter.
Utensils with vertical sides are preferable to those with slanting kind.

title: FRYING FAT—ITS PREPARATION
introduction: Any animal or vegetable grease is suitable for frying, provided it be quite pure and possess a resisting force allowing it to reach a very high temperature without burning. But for frying on a large scale, the use of cooked and clarified fats, such as the fat of “pot-au-feu” and roasts, should be avoided.
The fat of kidney of beef generally forms the base of the grease intended for frying on a large scale.
The grease used for frying ought not only to be melted down, but also thoroughly cooked, so that it may be quite pure.
notes: Cut the grease into pieces and then put it into the saucepan with 1 pint (473 ml) of water per every 10 lbs (4.5 kg).
The grease is cooked when the membranes are converted into greaves and it gives off smoke with a distinct smell.
At this stage, remove it from the fire for about ten minutes to cool, then strain it through a sieve or a coarse towel.

title: THE VARIOUS DEGREES OF HEAT REACHED BY THE FRYING MEDIUM, AND THEIR APPLICATION
introduction: The temperature reached by a frying medium depends upon its constituents and purity. The various degrees may be classified as moderately hot, hot, very hot.

notes.title: Testing Temperature
content: It is moderately hot when a sprig of parsley begins to bubble immediately; it is hot if it crackles when a slightly moist object is thrust into it; it is very hot when it gives off a thin white smoke.

notes.title: Moderately Hot (275°-284°F / 135°-140°C)
content: Used for all products containing vegetable water and for fish that require cooking by penetration before concentration.

notes.title: Hot (320°F / 160°C)
content: Used for all products that have undergone initial cooking, and for products that must be set immediately, such as those panés à l’anglaise or covered with batter (croquettes, fritters, etc.).

notes.title: Very Hot (356°F / 180°C)
content: Used for all objects that need a sharp and firm setting, and for all small objects whose cooking is effected in a few minutes, as in the case of whitebait.

title: FRYING MEDIUM FOR FISH
notes: Oil is best suited to the frying of fish, especially the very small kind.
The temperature should be regulated strictly in accordance with the size of the fish to be fried, in order that its cooking and colouring may be effected simultaneously.
Except Nonats and whitebait, which are simply rolled in flour, fish to be fried are previously steeped in slightly salted milk and then rolled in flour.
When finished, fried fish are drained, dried, slightly salted, and dished on a serviette or on paper, with a garnish of fried parsley-sprays and sections of channelled lemon.

title: THE QUANTITY OF THE FRYING MEDIUM
introduction: This should always be in proportion to the quantity or size of the objects to be fried, bearing in mind that these must always be entirely submerged. The greater the amount of fat, the higher the temperature reached, and the less one need fear a sudden cooling of the fat when the objects are immersed.

title: THE CARE OF THE FRYING MEDIUM
introduction: Every time a frying fat is used it should, after having been melted, be strained through a towel, for the majority of objects which it has served to cook must have left some particles behind them which might prove prejudicial to the objects that are to follow. Not only do these foreign substances disturb the clearness of the fat and render it liable to burn, but they are exceedingly detrimental to the objects that are treated later.

title: GRATINS
introduction: The various kinds of the order 'Gratins' are (1) the Complete Gratin; (2) the Rapid Gratin; (3) the Light Gratin; (4) Glazing, which is a form of Rapid Gratin.

title: COMPLETE GRATIN
introduction: This is the first example of the series; its principal constituent must be completely cooked, and its cooking must be coincident with the reduction of the sauce and the formation of the gratin proper.
notes: The base is almost invariably ordinary or Lenten duxelle sauce. (Recipe 223)
The object to be treated is laid on a buttered dish, surrounded with slices of raw mushrooms and chopped shallots, and covered with duxelle sauce.
The surface is then sprinkled with raspings, and copiously moistened with melted butter.
When withdrawing the gratin from the oven squeeze a few drops of lemon-juice over it, and besprinkle it with chopped parsley.
1. If too much sauce is used, the object will cook before the sauce reduces.
2. If the sauce is insufficient, it will reduce before the object is cooked.
3. The larger the piece, the more moderate the heat should be. Conversely, the smaller it is, the fiercer the fire should be.

title: RAPID GRATIN
notes: Proceed as above, with duxelle sauce, but the products treated are always cooked and warmed in advance.
Cover the object with the necessary quantity of sauce, besprinkle with raspings and butter, and set the gratin to form in a fierce oven.

title: LIGHT GRATIN
introduction: This is proper to farinaceous products, such as macaroni, lazagnes, noodles, gnocchi, &c., and consists of a combination of grated cheese, raspings, and butter. A moderate heat is all that is wanted. Also considered as light gratins are those which serve as the complement of stuffed vegetables such as tomatoes, mushrooms, egg-plant, and cucumber.

title: GLAZINGS
introduction: These are of two kinds—they either consist of a heavily buttered sauce, or they form from a sprinkling of cheese upon the sauce.
notes: In the first case, after pouring sauce over the object, place the dish on another dish containing a little water. The greater the quantity of butter used, the more intense the heat required, in order that a slight golden film may form almost instantaneously.

In the second case, the sauce used is always a Mornay. (Recipe 91) Cover the object with the sauce, besprinkle with grated cheese and melted butter, and place in fairly intense heat, so that a slight golden crust may form.

title: BLANCHINGS
introduction: The term blanchings is applied to three classes of operations:

notes.title: 1. The blanching of meats
content: This obtains mostly in the case of calf’s head and foot, sweet-bread, and trotters. These meats are first set to soak in cold, running water. They are then placed on the fire in a saucepan with enough cold water to cover, and the water is gradually brought to the boil. Boiling time varies by item. As soon as blanched, the meats are cooled in fresh water.

notes.title: 2. The blanching, or parboiling of certain vegetables
content: This term is wrongly applied to the cooking of green vegetables like French beans, which is more correctly termed 'à l’anglaise'.

notes.title: 3. The blanching of certain other vegetables
content: This consists in partly cooking vegetables in plenty of water to rid them of any bitter or pungent flavour. This is chiefly resorted to for lettuce, chicory, endives, celery, artichokes, cabbages, and out-of-season root vegetables. After blanching, these vegetables are always cooled in cold water.

title: THE TREATMENT OF DRY VEGETABLES
notes: It is wrong to soak dry vegetables if they are of good quality. They need only be put into a saucepan with enough cold water to cover, and with 1 oz (28 g) of salt per 5 quarts (4.7 L) of water.
Set to boil gently, skim, add the aromatic garnish (carrots, onions, faggot), and cook gently with lid on.
If the vegetables are old or inferior, they might be put to soak in soft water for about 1.5 hours. A prolonged soaking may give rise to incipient germination.

title: BRAISED VEGETABLES
notes: Vegetables to be braised must be first blanched, cooled, pared, and strung.
Garnish the bottom of a saucepan with blanched pork-rind, sliced carrots and onions, and a faggot. Cover the sides with thin slices of bacon.
Lay the vegetables upon the litter, and leave them to sweat in the oven for about ten minutes with lid on.
Now moisten enough to cover with white stock, and set to cook gently.
Drain, remove string, and cut to the shape required. Lay them in a sautépan, and cover them with their reduced stock from which the grease has been removed.
If prepared in advance, put them aside in basins, cover them with their cooking-liquor (strained, boiling, and with grease), and cover with buttered paper.

title: LEASON OF GREEN VEGETABLES WITH BUTTER
notes: First thoroughly drain the vegetables and toss them over the fire for a few minutes to rid them of moisture.
Season, add the butter away from the fire, and slightly toss, rolling the saucepan to mix the butter with the vegetables.

title: LEASON OF VEGETABLES WITH CREAM
notes: Vegetables must be kept somewhat firm. After draining, put them into a saucepan with enough boiling fresh cream to well moisten without covering them.
Finish their cooking process in the cream, stirring occasionally.
When the cream is almost entirely reduced, finish, away from the fire, with a little butter.
The leason may be slightly stiffened with a few tablespoonfuls of cream sauce if necessary.

title: VEGETABLE CREAMS AND PURÉES
notes: Purées of dry and farinaceous vegetables may be obtained by rubbing them through a sieve. Put the purée into a sautépan, dry it over a brisk fire, adding 1.5 oz (43 g) of butter per pint (473 ml) of purée; then add milk or cream until the required consistence is reached.
For purées of aqueous vegetables, such as French beans, cauliflowers, celery, &c., a quarter of their volume of mashed potatoes should be added to them to effect their leason.
In the case of vegetable creams, substitute for the mashed potatoes an equivalent quantity of succulent and stiff Béchamel sauce.

title: GARNISHES
introduction: In cookery, although garnishes only play a minor part, they are, nevertheless, very important, for, besides being the principal accompaniments to dishes, they are very often the adornment thereof, while it frequently happens that their harmonious arrangement considerably helps to throw the beauty of a fine joint or bird into relief.
A garnish may consist of one or more products. Be this as it may, its name, as a rule, distinctly denotes, in a word, what it is and how it is made.
In any case, it should always bear some relation to the piece it accompanies, either in the constituents of its preparation or with regard to the size of the piece constituting the dish.

The constituents of garnishes are supplied by vegetables, farinaceous products, quenelles of all kinds, cocks’ combs and kidneys, truffles and mushrooms, plain or stuffed olives, molluscs (mussels or oysters), shell-fish (crayfish, shrimps, lobster, &c.), butcher’s supplies, such as lamb’s sweet-bread, calf’s brains, and calf’s spine-marrow.

As a rule, garnishes are independent of the dish itself—that is to say, they are prepared entirely apart. At other times they are mixed with it, playing the double part of garnish and condimentary principle, as in the case of Matelotes, Compotes, Civets, &c.

title: BUTTERS AND CREAMS
notes: The seasoning of butters for hors-d’œuvres is effected when dishing them up. When prepared in advance, they ought to be placed in a bowl and put aside somewhere in the cool, covered with a piece of clean paper.

title: ANCHOVY BUTTER
notes: Wash twelve or fifteen anchovies in cold water, and dry them thoroughly. Remove the fillets from the bones, pound them smoothly with four oz. of butter, rub the whole through a fine sieve, smooth it with a spoon, and put it aside.

title: CAVIARE BUTTER
notes: Pound three oz. of pressed caviare with four oz. of butter, and rub through a fine sieve.

title: SHRIMP BUTTER
notes: Pound four oz. of shrimps with four oz. of butter; rub through a fine sieve first, then through muslin, after having softened the preparation.
This may also be made from the shelled tails of shrimps, which process, though it is easier, does not yield a butter of such delicate taste as the former.

title: CURRY BUTTER
notes: Soften four oz. of butter in a bowl, and add thereto sufficient curry-powder to ensure a decided taste. The exact quantity of curry cannot be prescribed, since the quality of the latter entirely governs its apportionment.

title: CRAYFISH BUTTER
notes: Cook the crayfish with _mirepoix_, as for Bisque. Finely pound the shells after having removed the tails, and add thereto four oz. of butter per two oz.; rub through a fine sieve first, then through muslin.
N.B.—The whole crayfish may be pounded, but the tails are usually laid aside with a view to supplying the garnish of the toasts for which the butter is intended.

title: RED-HERRING BUTTER
notes: Take the fillets of three red-herrings; remove the skins, and pound finely with three oz. of butter. Rub through a fine sieve.

title: LOBSTER BUTTER
notes: Pound four oz. of lobster trimmings and spawn, and a little of the coral with four oz. of butter. Rub through a fine sieve.

title: MILT BUTTER
notes: Poach four oz. of milt in a covered and buttered sauté-pan, with the juice of half a lemon; pound in the mortar, and add to the preparation its weight of butter and a teaspoonful of mustard. Rub through a fine sieve.

title: MONTPELLIER BUTTER (GREEN BUTTER)
introduction: See Compound Butter for Sauces (Recipe 153).

title: HORSE-RADISH BUTTER
notes: Grate two oz. of horse-radish and pound with four oz. of butter. Rub through a fine sieve.

title: SMOKED SALMON BUTTER
notes: Finely pound four oz. of smoked salmon with as much butter, and rub through a fine sieve.

title: PAPRIKA BUTTER
notes: Soften four oz. of butter in a bowl, and mix therewith a small teaspoonful of paprika infused in a few drops of white wine or consommé, with a view to strengthening the colour of the paprika.

title: PIMENTO BUTTER
notes: Pound four oz. of preserved or freshly-cooked capsicum; add as much butter thereto, and rub through a fine sieve.

title: CAVIARE CREAM
notes: Pound four oz. of preserved caviare and add thereto, little by little, two tablespoonfuls of fresh cream and two oz. of softened butter. Rub through a fine sieve, and finish the preparation by an addition of three tablespoonfuls of whisked cream.

N.B.—This cream and those that follow often take the place of the butters in the preparation of hors-d’œuvres. The addition of previously well-softened butter to these creams is necessary in order to make them sufficiently consistent when they cool.

title: LOBSTER CREAM
notes: Pound four oz. of lobster trimmings, spawn, and coral, and add thereto three tablespoonfuls of fresh cream and two oz. of softened butter.
Rub through a sieve, and complete the preparation with whisked cream, as above.

title: GAME CREAM
notes: Pound four oz. of cold, cooked game-meat with three tablespoonfuls of fresh cream and two oz. of softened butter. Rub through a sieve, and finish the preparation with three tablespoonfuls of whisked cream.

title: SMOKED SALMON CREAM
notes: Finely pound four oz. of smoked salmon, and add thereto, little by little, three tablespoonfuls of fresh cream and two oz. of softened butter. Rub the whole through a sieve, and finish with an addition of three tablespoonfuls of whisked cream.

title: TUNNY CREAM
notes: Finely pound four oz. of tunny in oil, and finish the cream similarly to that of the Smoked Salmon.

title: CHICKEN CREAM
notes: Finely pound four oz. of cold fowl (white parts only) and add thereto two tablespoonfuls of fresh cream and two oz. of softened butter. Rub through a sieve, and finish with three tablespoonfuls of whisked cream.
N.B.—This cream ought to be made and seasoned with salt immediately before being served.

title: MUSTARD SAUCE WITH CREAM
notes: Put three tablespoonfuls of mustard in a bowl with a little salt, pepper, and a few drops of lemon-juice. Mix the whole and add, little by little, the necessary quantity of very fresh cream.

title: ANCHOVY ALLUMETTES
notes: Roll some puff-paste trimmings into rectangular strips two and one-half inches wide and one-eighth inch thick. Spread thereon a thin coating of fish stuffing, finished with anchovy butter; lay the anchovy fillets, prepared beforehand, lengthwise on this stuffing, and cut into pieces about one inch wide. Place the pieces on a baking-tray, and set to bake in the oven for twelve minutes.

title: ANCHOVY FILLETS
notes: Cut each halved anchovy, which should have been previously _marinaded_ in oil, into two or three little fillets. Place them across each other in a hors-d’œuvre dish, after the manner of a lattice; garnish with chopped parsley and the chopped white and yolk of a hard-boiled egg, alternating the colours. Put a few capers on the fillets, and besprinkle moderately with oil. Anchovy fillets may also be served on a salad of _ciseled_ lettuce, for the sake of variety.

title: FRESH MARINADED ANCHOVIES
notes: Take a few live anchovies, cleanse them, and put them in salt for two hours. This done, plunge them in smoking oil, where they may remain only just long enough to stiffen. Drain, place them in a moderately acid _marinade_, and serve on a hors-d’œuvre dish with a little _marinade_.

title: ROLLED ANCHOVIES
notes: Turn some fine olives and stuff them with anchovy butter; when quite cold, encircle them with a ring of anchovy fillet, kept whole.

title: ANCHOVY MEDALLIONS
notes: Cut into discs, about the size of half-a-crown, potatoes boiled in water or baked beetroot. Cover their edges with fine anchovy fillets _marinaded_ in oil, and garnish their centres either with caviare, chopped hard-boiled egg, or milt purée, &c.

title: ANCHOVY PAUPIETTES
notes: Prepare some thick slices of _blanched_ and _marinaded_ cucumber, about the size of half-crowns, and hollow their centres slightly. Place rings composed of the fillets of anchovies in oil upon these slices, and fill up their centres with tunny cream or the cream of any fish or shell-fish.

title: ANCHOVY WITH PIMENTOS
notes: Prepare some anchovy fillets in oil, and place them across each other in a lattice, using fillets of pimento alternately with those of the anchovies. Garnish in the same way as for anchovy fillets, _i.e._, with the chopped white and yolk of a hard-boiled egg, and chopped parsley.

title: NORWEGIAN ANCHOVIES OR KILKIS
notes: These are found ready-prepared on the market. Place them on a hors-d’œuvre dish with some of their liquor, and without any garnish.

title: SMOKED EEL
notes: Serve it plain, cut into fillets.

title: EEL WITH WHITE WINE AND PAPRIKA
notes: Divide the eel into lengths of three and one-half inches; poach these in exactly the same way as for _matelote_, but with white wine and paprika seasoning. Let them cool in their cooking-liquor; cut the pieces lengthwise into large fillets, and cover them with the liquor after all grease has been removed therefrom and it has been clarified and cleared.

title: EEL AU VERT
notes: Stew in butter two oz. of sorrel, one-quarter oz. of parsley, as much chervil, a few tarragon leaves, a little fresh pimpernel, two oz. of tender nettle, one-quarter oz. of savory, a sprig of green thyme, and a few sage-leaves, all of which must be _ciseled_. Remove the skins from two lbs. of small eels, suppress the heads, and cut into pieces two inches long. Put these pieces with the herbs, stiffen them well, and add one pint of white wine and a little salt and pepper. Set to cook for ten minutes, thicken with the yolks of four eggs and a few drops of lemon-juice, and leave to cool in a bowl. This preparation of eel is served very cold.

title: EEL AU VERT A LA FLAMANDE
notes: Remove the skin from, and cut into small pieces, two lbs. of small eels. Stiffen the pieces in butter, moisten with one pint of beer, season, and set to cook for ten minutes. Add the herbs enumerated above, raw and roughly chopped. Once more set to cook for seven or eight minutes, thicken with fecula if the sauce is too thin, and transfer the whole to a bowl to cool. Serve very cold.

title: ARTICHOKES A LA GRECQUE
notes: Take some very small and tender artichokes. Pare them, cut the leaves short, and plunge them into a large saucepan of acidulated water. Set to parboil for eight or ten minutes, drain, cool in fresh water, and drain once more in a sieve.

For twenty artichokes prepare the following liquor:—one pint of water, one-quarter pint of oil, a little salt, the juice of three lemons, a few fennel and coriander seeds, some peppercorns, a sprig of thyme, and a bay-leaf. Set to boil, add the parboiled artichokes, and leave to cook for twenty minutes. Transfer to a bowl.
Serve these artichokes very cold upon a hors-d’œuvre dish, accompanied by a few tablespoonfuls of their cooking-liquor.

title: SMALL ARTICHOKE-BOTTOMS
notes: Remove the leaves and the hearts of some little artichokes; trim their remaining bases, and plunge each as soon as trimmed into acidulated water lest they blacken. Cook them “au blanc” (Recipe 167), and leave them to cool in their liquor.

Drain them well, dry them, place them in a pan, and _marinade_ them for twenty minutes in oil and lemon-juice. This done, garnish them, either with a _salpicon_ thickened with mayonnaise, a milt or other purée, a small _macédoine_, or a vegetable salad, &c. Place on a hors-d’œuvre dish with a garnish of parsley sprays.

title: BARQUETTES
notes: These are a kind of small Croustades with indented edges, made in very small, boat-shaped moulds, and they may be garnished in any conceivable way.
As their preparation is the same as that of Tartlets, see the latter (Recipe 387); also refer to “Frivolities” (Recipe 350).

title: SMOKED HAMBURG BEEF
notes: Cut it into very thin slices; divide these up into triangles, and roll the latter into the shape of cones. The slices may also be served flat.
Dish up at the last moment, and serve very cold.

title: CANAPÉS AND TOAST
notes: In the matter of hors-d’œuvres, the two above names have the same meaning. The preparation consists of small slices of the crumb of bread, about one-quarter inch thick, slightly toasted and with a garnish on one of their sides. The garnish is subject to the taste of the consumer, the resources at the disposal of the cook, or the latter’s fancy, which may here be fully indulged.

But the garnish, par excellence, for Canapés or Toast, is fresh butter combined with a fine mince of white roast chicken-meat, the meat of shell-fish or fish, or cheese, &c., as I pointed out above under the butters for hors-d’œuvres.

Whatever be the garnish of Canapés or Toast, and even when it would be unreasonable to let butter form a part of it, as, for example, in the case of _marinaded_ fish, anchovies, filleted herring, &c., it is always best to put plenty of butter on the pieces of toast while they are still hot, with the view of keeping them soft.

When the garnish consists of a purée, _i.e._, a compound butter, I should advise the use of a piping-bag fitted with a grooved pipe, for laying the preparation upon the toast. This method is both clean and expeditious, and lends itself to any fanciful arrangement which the varying shape of the toast may suggest.
The principal shapes given to the toast are as follows: round, square, rectangular, oval, triangular, crescented, star-like, crossed, &c.
They should never exceed one and one-half inches in diameter, and a corresponding size in the other shapes.
I shall only indicate here a few kinds of specially garnished toast, and leave the thousand and one other kinds for the operator himself to discover.

title: ANCHOVY TOAST
notes: Make the pieces of toast oval. Cover with anchovy butter, and place thereon, lattice-wise, some fillets of anchovy cut to the length of the toast. Garnish the pieces of toast all round with the separately chopped whites and yolks of hard-boiled eggs, alternating the colours.

title: CAVIARE TOAST
notes: Make the pieces of toast round; cover with caviare butter; garnish the edges with a thread of softened butter, laid on by means of a piping-bag fitted with a grooved pipe. Put fresh caviare in the centre.

title: SHRIMP TOAST
notes: Make the pieces of toast round; cover with shrimp butter, and garnish by means of a border composed of shelled shrimps’ tails with a caper in the centre.

title: CITY TOAST
notes: Make the pieces of toast round, and cover with a thick coating of the following preparation, viz.:—Four oz. of fresh butter, softened; two oz. of fresh Gruyère and two oz. of Parmesan, both grated; a dessertspoonful of cream, and a little salt and cayenne. Cover this preparation with two half-discs, which when juxtaposed are equal in circumference to the round of the toast. The half-discs should be cut respectively from a Lyons sausage and a Gruyère cheese; both should be thin, and equal in thickness.

title: DANISH TOAST
notes: Prepare some slices of brown bread, equal in thickness to the toast; but only heat, do not grill them. Spread some horse-radish butter over them, and cover with alternate strips of smoked salmon, caviare, and filleted herrings _marinaded_ in white wine. Now stamp the garnished slices with a sharp fancy-cutter, the shape of which is optional.

title: CRAYFISH TOAST
notes: Make the pieces of toast crescented; cover with crayfish butter, deck the edges with a string of softened butter, and garnish with a crayfish’s tail, cut into two lengthwise. The two halves of the tail should be placed in the middle of each crescent, close together and with their thickest side innermost.

title: TONGUE TOAST
notes: Prepare some slices of crumb of bread, equal in thickness, and toast them. Now garnish with a coating, half as thick as the slices themselves, of mustard butter. Cover the butter with thin slices of very red, salted tongue, and let the butter harden.

Stamp out the pieces of toast with a star-shaped fancy-cutter, which should be dipped from time to time in boiling water in order to facilitate the operation. Finally, make a rosette of mustard butter in the middle of each piece of toast.

title: LUCILE TOAST
notes: Make the pieces of toast oval, cover with mustard butter, and border their edges with a line of finely chopped and very red tongue. Garnish the middle of each with chopped white chicken-meat, and in the centre drop a pinch of chopped truffle.

title: VARIOUS CAROLINES
notes: These are very small éclairs of _pâte à choux_ without sugar. When quite cold, garnish them inside with a purée, either of tongue, fowl, game, or foie gras, &c., then coat them thinly with a chaud-froid sauce in keeping with the purée forming the inside garnish.
When the sauce has cooled, glaze it, by means of a brush, with a little cold melted jelly, with a view to making it glossy.
N.B.—Carolines are also used as a garnish for certain cold preparations, aspics, &c.

title: CAVIARE AND BLINIS
notes: Caviare is undoubtedly the richest and most delicate of hors-d’œuvres, granted, of course, that it be of good quality and consist of large, light-coloured, and transparent particles. Its price is always high, owing to the difficulty attending its importation. It is served very simply, either in a silver timbale or in its original receptacle, surrounded with ice, and accompanied by a dish of Blinis, whereof the preparation is as follows:—

Make a thin paste with one oz. of yeast and one lb. of sifted flour diluted with one pint of lukewarm milk. Leave this paste to ferment for two hours in a lukewarm atmosphere, and then add thereto one-half lb. of flour, the yolks of four eggs, a pinch of salt, one-half pint of tepid milk; mix the whole without letting it acquire any body, and finally add the whites of four eggs, whisked. Let the preparation ferment for half an hour, and, when about to serve, cook the Blinis quickly, after the manner of pancakes, in special little omelet-pans. Dish them up very hot on a napkin.

Failing fresh caviare, the pressed and salted kind may also be used for hors-d’œuvres. Some cooks serve finely-chopped onions with fresh caviare, but a worse practice could not be imagined. Fresh caviare, the flavour of which is perfect, does not need any supplementary condiment.

title: CELERY “A LA BONNE-FEMME”
notes: Take equal quantities of very tender celery sticks and peeled, quartered and cored russet apples. Finely mince the celery and apples, season with a mustard-and-cream sauce, and place on a hors-d’œuvre dish.

title: CELERY A LA GRECQUE
notes: Select a few hearts of celery, very equal; trim, wash, and parboil them in acidulated water, as directed under “artichokes à la Grecque.” Prepare the cooking-liquor from the same ingredients, using the same quantities thereof, and cook similarly.
Serve very cold on a crystal hors-d’œuvre dish with a portion of the cooking-liquor.

title: CELERIAC
notes: Quarter, peel, and cut the vegetable in _julienne_ fashion. Prepare the seasoning with mustard, salt, pepper, and vinegar; add the _julienne_ of Celeriac and mix thoroughly. When the roots are quite soft, a seasoning consisting of mustard-and-cream sauce is preferable.

title: MARINADED CÈPES
notes: Select some very small and fresh _cèpes_. Parboil them for eight minutes, drain and cool them, put them into a basin, and cover them with the boiling _marinade_ after having passed the latter through a strainer.

_Marinade for Two lbs. of Cèpes._—Put into a saucepan one pint of vinegar, one-third pint of oil, a crushed clove of garlic, a fragment of bay, and a little thyme, six peppercorns, a pinch of coriander, a few fennel leaves, and a small root of parsley. Set to boil for five minutes. Leave the mushrooms to _marinade_ for five or six hours before using them.

title: CHERRIES A L’ALLEMANDE
notes: Take five lbs. of Morella cherries, put them into a bottle, as in the case of cherry brandy, and add thereto three cloves, a fragment of cinnamon, some grated nutmeg, and a sprig of tarragon. Pour over the cherries two quarts of vinegar, boiled with one-half lb. of brown sugar and properly cooled. Cork the bottle, and leave the fruit to macerate for a fortnight.

title: BRAINS A LA ROBERT
notes: Cook well-cleansed sheep’s or lamb’s brains in _court-bouillon_, and cool. Divide them up into thin and regular slices, and place them on a hors-d’œuvre dish. Rub the brain remains through a fine sieve, combine the resulting purée with a mustard-and-cream sauce, and add thereto a fine _julienne_ of the white part only of celery.
Cover the slices of brain with the sauce.

title: CUCUMBER A LA DANOISE
notes: Cut the cucumber to the shape of small _cassolettes_ or _barquettes_, _blanch_ and _marinade_ them.
Garnish with a preparation composed of a purée of salmon mixed with fillets of herring and chopped, hard-boiled eggs in equal quantities.
Sprinkle a little chopped horse-radish over the garnish.

title: STUFFED CUCUMBERS
notes: Prepare them as above, in the shape of small _barquettes_ or _cassolettes_. Cook them, at the same time keeping them firm; _marinade_ them for twenty minutes, when they are quite cold, in oil and vinegar, and garnish them, by means of a piping-bag, either with a thick purée, some mince-meat thickened with mayonnaise, or a small vegetable _macédoine_, &c.

title: CUCUMBER SALAD
notes: Carefully peel the cucumbers, cut them into two lengthwise, remove their seeds, and mince finely. Place them in a bowl, sprinkle with table-salt, and leave them to exude their vegetable moisture for twenty-five minutes. This done, drain them, press them in a towel, season with pepper, oil, and vinegar, and add some chopped chervil.

title: CUCUMBER AND PIMENTO SALAD
notes: Select some very fresh, medium-sized cucumbers, peel them, and cut them into pieces two inches in length. Cut these pieces spirally, beginning at their peripheries and working towards their centres; then cut them diametrally, so as to produce curved strips of the vegetable. Add an equal quantity of pimentos cut into strips, and season as in the case of cucumber salad.

title: YORK CONES
notes: Cut slices from a York ham as thinly as possible, and trim them to the shape of triangles. Roll the triangles into cones, and garnish their insides (by means of a piping-bag fitted with a grooved pipe) with any butter or cream. (See Nos. 280 to 299.)

title: TONGUE CONES
notes: Proceed as for York Cones.

title: MOULDED CREAMS
notes: Prepare a hors-d’œuvre cream in accordance with any one of the recipes (Nos. 294 to 299). Put this cream into very small, slightly-oiled, and ornamented moulds, and leave it to set in the cool or on ice. Empty the moulds, at the moment of dishing up, either directly upon a dish, on tartlets garnished with a purée in keeping with the cream, or on toast. With these moulded creams, endless varieties of delicate and recommendable little hors-d’œuvres may be prepared, while in their preparation the moulds used in pastry for “petits fours” may serve a useful purpose.

title: SHRIMPS AND PRAWNS
notes: Get these very fresh and serve them on boat-shaped hors-d’œuvre dishes, arranging them so that they overlap one another. Either garnish the middle of the dishes with curled-leaf parsley, or lay the crustacean directly upon parsley.

title: DUCHESSES
notes: This hors-d’œuvre is almost equivalent to the Carolines (Recipe 325), except that the shape of the Duchesses is that of little _choux_, about the size of a pigeon’s egg, and that, as a rule, they are merely glazed with some melted jelly, and not covered with a chaud-froid sauce. Sprinkle them with chopped pistachios, and serve them very cold on ornamented dish-papers.

title: NANTUA DUCHESSES
notes: Stuff the little _choux_, referred to above, with crayfish purée, and sprinkle them, again and again, with cold, melted jelly, in order to cover them with a transparent film.

title: DUCHESSES A LA REINE
notes: Stuff the little _choux_ with a purée of fowl with cream. Glaze with jelly, as above, and sprinkle some very black, finely-chopped truffles over the jelly.

title: DUCHESSES A LA SULTANE
notes: Stuff the little _choux_ with a purée of fowl, completed with pistachio butter. Glaze with jelly, and sprinkle a little chopped pistachio upon each little _chou_.

title: CAVIARE DUCHESSES
notes: Stuff with fresh caviare or caviare cream. Glaze with jelly and serve iced.

title: SMOKED-SALMON DUCHESSES
notes: Stuff the little _choux_ with a purée of smoked salmon and butter, and glaze them with a maigre jelly.

title: NORWEGIAN DUCHESSES
notes: Stuff the _choux_ with a purée of Kilkis and butter, and glaze with jelly.

title: KAROLY ECLAIRS
notes: These are little éclairs stuffed with a purée made from the entrails of woodcock with champagne. The purée is buttered and slightly seasoned. Cover the éclairs with a brown chaud-froid sauce, mask them with game jelly, and serve them, iced, on ornamented dish-papers.

title: CRAYFISH EN BUISSON
notes: Prepare them in accordance with the recipes “à la nage” or “à la marinière,” and serve them very cold.

title: MARINADED SMELTS
notes: Fry some well-dried and floured smelts in oil; as soon as this is done, put them in a deep dish or a bowl. Add to the oil, per pint (which quantity should be allowed for every two lbs. of the fish), eight unpeeled garlic-cloves, an onion, and a carrot cut into thin, round slices, all of which vegetables should be slightly fried.
